Beatified by Pope Pius X in 1908 and canonized by Pope Benedict XV in 1920, he was named patron of Catholic youth and students, having sanctified the years of study; in 1959 Pope John XXIII declared him patron of the Abruzzi region, where he died and lies buried.
saints.knownFor: His hidden holiness and joyful devotion to Our Lady of Sorrows.

sources.text: Catholic Encyclopedia (1913), “Bl. Gabriel of Our Lady of Sorrows”
Vatican biography, Canonization of St. Gabriel of Our Lady of Sorrows (vatican.va)

saints.name: St. Romanus of Condat
saints.title: Abbot
saints.shortBlurb: A hermit of the Jura mountains whose solitude drew disciples and grew into the great monasteries of the region…
biography: Born about the year 400, Romanus withdrew at the age of thirty-five into the wild Jura mountains to live as a hermit, taking shelter beneath the firs of Condat. His younger brother Lupicinus followed him, and disciples gathered, among them the boy Eugendus, until the hermitage grew into a congregation of monks.

From it rose a family of houses: the abbey of Condat, around which grew the town now called Saint-Claude; Lauconne, later Saint-Lupicin, where Lupicinus was buried; the convent of La Balme for nuns, where Romanus himself was laid; and Romainmotier in what is now Switzerland.

Ordained priest by St. Hilary of Arles in 444, Romanus governed with a mildness that tempered the sterner temper of Lupicinus, and he was remembered for his tenderness toward lepers and the outcast. He died about 463; St. Gregory of Tours wrote his life in his Book of the Fathers.
saints.knownFor: Founding the monasteries of the Jura, among them Condat.

sources.text: Butler, Lives of the Saints (1866 ed.), 28 February

saints.name: St. Oswald of Worcester
saints.title: Bishop
saints.shortBlurb: A reforming English bishop of Danish blood who renewed the monastic life of his land and died washing the feet of the poor…
biography: Born about 925 of Danish stock and brought up by his uncle St. Oda, archbishop of Canterbury, Oswald was sent about 950 to the abbey of Fleury in France to learn the monastic life, and was ordained there in 959. Recalled to England, he found his uncle dead, but St. Dunstan procured his consecration as bishop of Worcester in 961.

With Dunstan and St. Ethelwold of Winchester he was a chief worker in the monastic revival under King Edgar. He replaced the married clerks of Worcester cathedral with monks, and founded the abbey of Ramsey about 971 on land given by the ealdorman Aethelwine, bringing Abbo of Fleury to teach in its school.

In 972 he was made archbishop of York while retaining Worcester, holding both until his death. His Lenten custom was to wash and feed the poor each day; on 29 February 992, kneeling at that service in Worcester, he died, and was buried in the church of St. Mary; because his day recurs only in leap years, his feast is commonly kept on 28 February.
saints.knownFor: The English Benedictine revival with Saints Dunstan and Ethelwold.

sources.text: Butler, Lives of the Saints (1866 ed.), 28 February

saints.name: St. David of Wales
saints.title: Bishop, Patron of Wales
saints.shortBlurb: The abbot-bishop of Menevia and patron of Wales, who taught his monks to be joyful and faithful in little things…
biography: David, in Welsh Dewi, was born about 500, the son of St. Non, and became a monk and famed teacher. He founded churches across Wales, chief among them his abbey at Mynyw, now St Davids, in Pembrokeshire, where his monks pulled the plough without oxen, lived on bread and water, and held nothing of their own.

At the Synod of Brefi about 550, tradition says, as he spoke against the Pelagian heresy the ground rose beneath him to form a hill and a white dove settled on his shoulder, and he was acclaimed primate of Wales.

He died on 1 March, in 589 or by another reckoning 601, his last words bidding his monks be joyful, keep the faith, and do the little things they had seen and heard in him; his cult was confirmed by Pope Callixtus II about 1120.

His shrine at St Davids drew pilgrims through the Middle Ages. As the chief teacher and father of the Welsh church he is venerated as the patron of Wales, his day on 1 March kept with the wearing of the leek.
saints.knownFor: Founding the monastery of Menevia and evangelizing Wales.

canonization.canonized: Canonized 1120 by Pope Callixtus II (per tradition)

sources.text: Butler, Lives of the Saints (1866 ed.), 1 March

saints.name: St. Chad
saints.title: Bishop of Lichfield
saints.shortBlurb: A disciple of St. Aidan who yielded his see in humility, then evangelized the Mercians on foot from his new seat at Lichfield…
biography: Chad, or Ceadda, a Northumbrian, was trained at Lindisfarne under St. Aidan and completed his formation among the monasteries of Ireland. When his brother Cedd died of the plague in 664, Chad succeeded him as abbot of Lastingham in Yorkshire.

That same year King Oswiu named him bishop of the Northumbrians, and he was consecrated by Wini of the West Saxons with two British bishops. When Wilfrid, the see's chosen bishop, returned from Gaul, Archbishop Theodore of Canterbury judged Chad's position irregular. Chad yielded it without protest and went back to Lastingham, and Theodore, struck by such humility, confirmed his ordination.

Later in 669 King Wulfhere of Mercia asked for a bishop, and Theodore sent Chad to the Mercians and the people of Lindsey; he fixed his see at Lichfield. He travelled his vast diocese on foot until Theodore ordered him to ride, once lifting him into the saddle with his own hands.

He had labored among the Mercians only two and a half years when he died in the plague on 2 March 672. Bede, who tells his story in the Ecclesiastical History, judged that Chad and his brother Cedd together had won Mercia to the faith.
saints.knownFor: Evangelizing Mercia from his see at Lichfield.

sources.text: Butler, Lives of the Saints (1866 ed.), 2 March

saints.name: St. Katharine Drexel
saints.title: Virgin, Foundress of the Sisters of the Blessed Sacrament
saints.shortBlurb: A Philadelphia heiress who gave her fortune to found schools and missions for Native and African Americans…
biography: Born in Philadelphia on 26 November 1858 into the banking family of Francis Anthony Drexel, Katharine lost her mother within weeks of her birth and grew up in a household where alms were distributed daily. Travel in the West opened her eyes to the misery of Native Americans.

In 1887, in an audience with Pope Leo XIII, she begged him to send missionaries to the Indians; he answered, "Why not become a missionary yourself?" She entered the Sisters of Mercy in 1889 and in February 1891 founded the Sisters of the Blessed Sacrament for Indians and Colored People, which she governed until 1937.

From her inherited fortune she financed more than sixty schools and missions for Native and African Americans, and from 1915 built up work in New Orleans that became Xavier University of Louisiana, the only historically Black Catholic university in the country.

She died at Bensalem, Pennsylvania, on 3 March 1955, aged ninety-six. Beatified in 1988 and canonized by Pope John Paul II on 1 October 2000, she was the first native-born American citizen declared a saint. Having spent her fortune on the oppressed, she is invoked as patron of racial justice and of philanthropists.
saints.knownFor: Devoting her inheritance and life to the education of Native and African Americans.

sources.text: Vatican biography, Canonization of St. Katharine Drexel (vatican.va)

saints.name: St. Casimir
saints.title: Prince of Poland
saints.shortBlurb: The chaste young prince of Poland who chose prayer and the poor over the ambitions of a crown…
biography: Born at Wawel Castle in Kraków on 3 October 1458, the second son of King Casimir IV of Poland and Elizabeth of Austria, Casimir was educated from the age of nine by the chronicler Jan Długosz in Latin, law, and history.

In 1471 his father sent him with an army of twelve thousand to take the crown of Hungary. Convinced the enterprise was unjust, he withdrew from the campaign and afterward refused to renew it; he likewise declined a marriage arranged with Kunigunde, daughter of the Emperor Frederick III, preferring celibacy.

Heir to the throne after his brother Vladislaus became king of Bohemia, he gave himself to prayer, fasting, and almsgiving, often found kneeling at locked church doors before dawn. A copy of the hymn "Omni die dic Mariae" was found in his coffin, and it is still called the Hymn of St. Casimir.

He died of tuberculosis at Grodno on 4 March 1484, aged twenty-five, and was buried in Vilnius Cathedral. Tradition holds that Pope Leo X canonized him in 1521 at the petition of his brother King Sigismund I. Prince of both nations and buried in the Lithuanian capital, he is venerated as patron of Poland and Lithuania.
saints.knownFor: His purity, devotion to Our Lady, and care for the poor.

canonization.canonized: Canonized 1521 (bull of Pope Leo X); confirmed 1602 by Pope Clement VIII

sources.text: Butler, Lives of the Saints (1866 ed.), 4 March

saints.name: St. John Joseph of the Cross
saints.title: Priest, Franciscan
saints.shortBlurb: A Franciscan of the Alcantarine reform who carried stones for his brethren and was known for miracles and prophecy…
biography: Born Carlo Gaetano Calosirto on the island of Ischia on 15 August 1654, John Joseph entered the Friars Minor at Naples before he was sixteen, the first Italian to join the Alcantarine reform founded in Spain by St. Peter of Alcántara, and took the name by which he is known.

In 1674 he was sent to found a friary at Piedimonte and labored at its building with his own hands. Ordained priest much against his will, he chose as superior the lowliest offices, slept but three hours a night, and never tasted wine.

When the Italian Alcantarines were formed into a separate province in 1702, he was made their vicar provincial and guided the fragile branch through its first trials. People of every rank were brought to him for healing, yet he bade those he cured take some medicine, that the cure might be ascribed to nature and not to him.

He died at Naples on 5 March, worn out by a life of austerity. Beatified by Pope Pius VI in 1789 and canonized by Pope Gregory XVI in 1839, he is venerated as patron of Ischia, where a chapel in the Aragonese Castle bears his name.
saints.knownFor: Restoring strict observance among the Italian Franciscans.

sources.text: Butler, Lives of the Saints (1866 ed.), 5 March
The Roman Martyrology (1914 English ed.; public domain)

saints.name: St. Colette
saints.title: Virgin, Reformer of the Poor Clares
saints.shortBlurb: A carpenter's daughter who restored the Poor Clares to their original poverty and founded a strict reform of the order…
biography: Born Nicolette Boellet at Corbie in Picardy on 13 January 1381, the daughter of a carpenter of the abbey, Colette was left an orphan at eighteen. After trying the Beguines and a Benedictine house, she took the habit of the Third Order of St. Francis in 1402 and lived four years as a recluse beside the abbey church.

Convinced by visions that she was called to restore the Poor Clares to their first poverty, she went in 1406 to Peter de Luna, acknowledged in France as Pope Benedict XIII, who received her at Nice, gave her the veil of the Second Order, and by a series of bulls empowered her to found and reform monasteries.

Beginning at Besançon in 1410, she founded or reformed eighteen monasteries in her lifetime, prescribing absolute poverty, bare feet, and perpetual abstinence; those of her obedience were called Colettines. In this work she was aided by her confessor, the Franciscan Henry de Beaume.

She died at Ghent on 6 March 1447, worn out by penance and travel, and her body rests in the church of her monastery there. Canonized by Pope Pius VII in 1807, she is invoked by childless couples and by expectant mothers.
saints.knownFor: The reform of the Poor Clares (the Colettines).

sources.text: Butler, Lives of the Saints (1866 ed.), 6 March

saints.name: Sts. Perpetua and Felicity
saints.title: Martyrs
saints.shortBlurb: A young noblewoman and her slave companion who went joyfully to the beasts at Carthage, leaving one of the earliest first-person accounts of martyrdom…
biography: In 203, during the persecution of Septimius Severus, five catechumens were arrested at Carthage: Vibia Perpetua, a well-born matron of twenty-two with an infant son at her breast; the slaves Felicity and Revocatus; and Saturninus and Secundulus. Their catechist Saturus gave himself up to join them.

In prison Perpetua wrote down her visions and the tears of her pagan father, who came repeatedly to beg her to sacrifice. Felicity, eight months with child, was delivered of a daughter two days before the games, lest she be left behind when her companions went to their death.

On 7 March they were exposed to the beasts at the games held for the birthday of Caesar Geta: the men were torn by leopards and bears, the women tossed by a maddened cow, and all were dispatched by the sword, Perpetua herself steadying the young gladiator's shaking blade to her throat.

The "Passion of Perpetua and Felicity," which preserves her diary, is among the earliest surviving Christian writings by a woman, and their names stand together in the Roman Canon of the Mass. Because one nursed her child and the other gave birth in chains, they are patrons of mothers and expectant mothers.
saints.knownFor: Their courage and the ancient “Passion” that records it.

sources.text: Butler, Lives of the Saints (1866 ed.), 6 March

saints.name: St. John of God
saints.title: Religious, Founder of the Brothers Hospitallers
saints.shortBlurb: A soldier and shepherd whose sudden conversion led him to spend his life nursing the sick and the poor of Granada…
biography: Born João Duarte Cidade at Montemor-o-Novo in Portugal on 8 March 1495, John was lost to his family as a child and grew up a shepherd near Oropesa in Spain, then a soldier under its Count, fighting the French at Fontarabia and the Turks.

After years of wandering and a season in Ceuta nursing an exiled family, he settled at Granada as a seller of books. On 20 January 1537 a sermon of St. John of Ávila pierced him; his public penance was so violent he was shut in the mad ward of the Royal Hospital, where the preacher bade him serve others rather than scourge himself.

He rented a house for the sick poor of Granada, begging for them in the streets by night and nursing them by day. Companions joined him, and from them grew the Brothers Hospitallers, approved by the Holy See in 1572.

He died at Granada on 8 March 1550, his fifty-fifth birthday, of pneumonia caught after plunging into a river to save a drowning youth. Canonized by Pope Alexander VIII in 1690, he is patron of hospitals, the sick, and nurses for this work of mercy, and of booksellers from his earlier trade.
saints.knownFor: Founding the Brothers Hospitallers and his heroic care of the sick.

sources.text: Butler, Lives of the Saints (1866 ed.), 8 March

saints.name: St. Frances of Rome
saints.title: Religious, Foundress of the Oblates
saints.shortBlurb: A Roman wife and mother who served the poor through plague and war and founded the Oblates of Mary…
biography: Born Francesca Bussa de' Leoni at Rome in 1384, Frances longed for the cloister but was married at about twelve to Lorenzo Ponziani, commander of papal troops. The arranged marriage proved happy and lasted forty years; with her sister-in-law Vannozza she made the palace a dispensary for the poor.

Through the wars of the Western Schism, plague that carried off two children, and famine, she opened her home as a hospital and drove her own wagon to gather wood and herbs. When Lorenzo returned ruined and wounded, she nursed him to the end.

In 1425 she gathered devout Roman women into the Oblates of Mary, bound by no vows and living in their own homes under the Benedictines of Santa Maria Nova; in 1433 she founded for them the monastery of Tor de' Specchi, approved by Pope Eugene IV. After his death in 1436 she joined the community as superior.

She died on 9 March 1440 and was canonized by Pope Paul V in 1608. Because her guardian angel was said to light her way with a lamp when she traveled at night, Pope Pius XI declared her patron of motorists in 1925; she is honored as patron of widows.
saints.knownFor: Uniting family life with heroic charity, and founding the Oblates of Mary.

sources.text: Butler, Lives of the Saints (1866 ed.), 9 March

saints.name: The Forty Martyrs of Sebaste
saints.title: Martyrs
saints.shortBlurb: Forty soldiers of a Roman legion who were left to freeze on a frozen lake near Sebaste rather than deny Christ…
biography: About the year 320, in the persecution under the Emperor Licinius, forty Christian soldiers of the Twelfth Legion, the Fulminata, garrisoned at Sebaste in Lesser Armenia, refused to offer sacrifice and were condemned to freeze, stripped naked through a bitter night on a frozen pond outside the city.

A warm bath was set on the shore as the price of apostasy. One of the forty broke and ran to it, dying as he entered the water; but a guard named Aglaius, watching from the bank, saw crowns descending upon the martyrs, confessed himself a Christian, and stripped to take the apostate's place, so that the number forty stood complete.

At dawn the stiffened bodies, some still breathing, were burned and the ashes cast into a river, yet Christians gathered the relics and spread them through many cities. Basil of Caesarea preached their praise within living memory of their death, and Gregory of Nyssa, who buried his own parents beside their shrine, left two homilies in their honor.
saints.knownFor: Their united constancy unto death.

sources.text: Butler, Lives of the Saints (1866 ed.), 10 March

saints.name: St. Eulogius of Córdoba
saints.title: Priest and Martyr
saints.shortBlurb: A learned priest of Córdoba who encouraged the martyrs under Muslim rule and was himself beheaded…
biography: Born before 819 into a family of the senatorial class of Córdoba, Eulogius was educated in the monastery of St. Zoilus and, ordained priest, became head of the city's chief ecclesiastical school. His fellow student and lifelong friend Alvarus would later write his life.

When about 850 the Emir Abd al-Rahman II loosed persecution on the Christians, many of whom were executed for reviling Muhammad, Eulogius, himself for a time imprisoned with his bishop, encouraged the confessors and recorded their sufferings in his "Memoriale Sanctorum," the chief witness to the Martyrs of Córdoba.

In 859 he sheltered Leocritia, a young woman of Muslim parentage who had been secretly baptized and fled her angry family. Discovered together, they were condemned to death; and Eulogius, though chosen for the vacant archbishopric of Toledo, was beheaded at Córdoba on 11 March 859 before he could be consecrated. Leocritia suffered four days later.

His relics were afterward translated to the cathedral of Oviedo. His writings preserve the names and constancy of a whole generation of Spanish martyrs, and his friend Alvarus remembered him as gentle and learned, humble enough to yield to the opinions of his lessers.
saints.knownFor: Chronicling and encouraging the Martyrs of Córdoba.

sources.text: Butler, Lives of the Saints (1866 ed.), 11 March

saints.name: St. Maximilian
saints.title: Martyr
saints.shortBlurb: A young North African who refused conscription into the Roman army for conscience's sake and was executed for the name of Christ…
biography: At Theveste in Numidia, the modern Tébessa of Algeria, on 12 March 295, Maximilian, son of the Christian veteran Fabius Victor, was brought before the proconsul Dion to be enrolled in the Roman army, for he had reached the age of twenty-one and owed the state his service.

"I cannot serve," he answered; "I am a Christian." When Dion offered the military seal, he refused it, saying he already bore the seal of Christ, and neither threats nor his father's presence moved him. Condemned, he was beheaded the same day; his father returned home, the Acts relate, giving thanks to God.

The "Acta Maximiliani," composed within a few years of his death and reckoned among the most authentic records of the early martyrs, preserve the dialogue of his trial. As the first Christian known to have died for refusing military service, he is invoked as the patron of conscientious objectors, and his name is kept on 12 March in the Roman Martyrology.
saints.knownFor: His witness of conscience recorded in the “Acta Maximiliani.”

sources.text: The Roman Martyrology (1914 English ed.; public domain)
Butler, Lives of the Saints (1866 ed.), 12 March

saints.name: St. Martin of Braga
saints.title: Bishop, Apostle of the Suevi
saints.shortBlurb: A monk from Pannonia who converted the Suevi of Galicia from Arianism and became archbishop of Braga…
biography: Born in Pannonia about 520, Martin became a monk on a pilgrimage to the Holy Land, and about 550 sailed to Gallaecia in the northwest of Spain, then ruled by the Arian Suevi. Near their capital at Braga he founded the monastery of Dumium and was made its bishop.

By his preaching King Miro and the Suevic people were won from Arianism to the Catholic faith. Martin sat in the First Council of Braga in 561 and, raised to the metropolitan see of Braga, presided over the Second in 572, which received his collection of eighty-four canons translated from the Greek.

Gregory of Tours judged him second to none in the learning of his age. He adapted Seneca in moral treatises, the "Formula Vitae Honestae," dedicated to King Miro, and "De Ira"; he translated the Sayings of the Egyptian Fathers from the Greek, and in "De Correctione Rusticorum" taught the bishops how to root out rural superstition.

He died about 580 and was buried at Dumium, the monastery he had founded. Posterity named him Apostle of the Suevi; and so exactly did his "Formula Vitae Honestae" follow Seneca that it was long mistaken for the philosopher's own work.
saints.knownFor: Converting the Suevi and reforming the Church of Galicia.

sources.text: The Roman Martyrology (1914 English ed.; public domain)

saints.name: St. Matilda
saints.title: Queen
saints.shortBlurb: The devout queen of Germany, wife of Henry the Fowler and mother of Otto the Great, known for her almsgiving…
biography: Born about 895 at Engern in Westphalia and brought up at the monastery of Erfurt, Matilda married in 909 Henry, duke of Saxony, afterward King Henry I of Germany, called the Fowler. She bore him five children, among them the emperor Otto I, Henry duke of Bavaria, and Bruno, later archbishop of Cologne.

Widowed in 936, she favored the claim of her son Henry to the crown against his brother Otto, and in later years both sons turned on her, charging that her lavish alms had impoverished the crown. She surrendered her dower lands and withdrew to her villa at Engern, yet was reconciled to her sons when misfortune overtook them.

Her chief monastic foundations were Quedlinburg, Nordhausen, Engern, and Pöhlde. She died at the convent of Quedlinburg on 14 March 968 and was buried beside her husband, venerated as a saint immediately after her death. A queen of unstinting charity and a long-widowed mother of kings, she is honoured as a patron of queens and of widows.
saints.knownFor: Her charity, monastic foundations, and patience amid family strife.

sources.text: Butler, Lives of the Saints (1866 ed.), 14 March

saints.name: St. Clement Mary Hofbauer
saints.title: Priest, Redemptorist
saints.shortBlurb: A baker who became the first Redemptorist north of the Alps and the tireless “Apostle of Vienna”…
biography: Born in 1751 at Tasovice in Moravia, the ninth of twelve children, John Hofbauer was apprenticed to a baker at Znojmo and for years baked at the Premonstratensian priory of Louka, kept from the seminary by poverty and by the religious laws of the Emperor Joseph II.

Making his way to Rome, he joined the Redemptorists, taking the name Clement Mary, and was ordained priest in 1785, the first of the congregation professed north of the Alps. Sent to Warsaw in 1787, he made the church of St. Benno a center of daily preaching, confession, and schooling for orphans, laboring there for twenty-one years.

Expelled with his brethren by Napoleon's order in 1808, he settled in Vienna, where his pulpit, confessional, and direction of students and converts so renewed Catholic life that he is called the Apostle of Vienna. He died there on 15 March 1820 and was canonized by Pius X in 1909; he is patron of Vienna and, from his early trade, of bakers.
saints.knownFor: Planting the Redemptorists in northern Europe and reviving the faith in Vienna.

sources.text: Butler, Lives of the Saints (1866 ed.), 15 March

saints.name: St. Heribert
saints.title: Archbishop of Cologne
saints.shortBlurb: The chancellor of Emperor Otto III who became a charitable archbishop of Cologne and builder of Deutz Abbey…
biography: Born about 970 at Worms, Heribert was schooled at the cathedral and at Gorze Abbey; his father forbade his first wish, to be a monk, and he was ordained priest in 994. Taken into the service of the Emperor Otto III, he served as chancellor first for Italy and from 998 for Germany.

Appointed archbishop of Cologne in 999, he stood at Otto's deathbed in 1002 and carried the imperial regalia back to Germany. Waylaid by the party of Henry II, he at first opposed the new king, then served him as chancellor and trusted counsellor.

In 1003 he founded Deutz Abbey on the Rhine, and his almsgiving was proverbial; tradition tells of a barefoot procession he led that ended a drought, for which he is invoked for rain. Struck by fever on a pastoral visitation, he died on 16 March 1021 and was buried at Deutz, the patron of his beloved city of Cologne.
saints.knownFor: His charity and pastoral care as archbishop of Cologne.

sources.text: Butler, Lives of the Saints (1866 ed.), 16 March

saints.name: St. Patrick
saints.title: Bishop
saints.shortBlurb: Carried off to Ireland as a slave and returning as its bishop, he won a nation to Christ and left behind his own Confession of God’s mercy…
biography: Born in Roman Britain late in the fourth century, Patrick was the son of Calpurnius, a deacon and town councillor, and the grandson of the priest Potitus. Seized by Irish raiders at sixteen, he herded flocks in slavery for six years, learning to pray without ceasing, before escaping to a ship some two hundred miles away.

After years of study in Gaul he returned to Ireland as a bishop — tradition dates his mission from 432 — baptizing thousands, ordaining clergy, and contending with kings and druids. Two of his writings survive: the Confessio, his account of God's mercy to him, and a letter excommunicating the soldiers of Coroticus, who had slain and enslaved his new converts.

He died, by the commonly received account, in 461 and is buried at Downpatrick. As the apostle who won Ireland to Christ he is its chief patron; the later legends that he drove the snakes from the island and taught the Trinity with a shamrock still cling to his memory.
saints.knownFor: The evangelization of Ireland; the Confessio; the “Breastplate” prayer attributed to him.

sources.text: Butler, Lives of the Saints (1866 ed.), 17 March

saints.name: St. Cyril of Jerusalem
saints.title: Bishop and Doctor of the Church
saints.shortBlurb: The bishop of Jerusalem whose Lenten “Catechetical Lectures” still teach the faith to those preparing for baptism…
biography: Born about 315 at or near Jerusalem, Cyril was ordained deacon by Bishop Macarius about 335 and priest by Maximus some eight years later, and about the year 350 he succeeded Maximus as bishop of the holy city of his birth.

His episcopate fell in the heat of the Arian controversy. Accused by Acacius of Caesarea of selling church treasures — sacred vessels he had sold, the historians say, to feed the starving — he was deposed in 357 and driven three times into exile under the emperors Constantius and Valens, returning for good in 378.

His fame rests on his Catechetical Lectures, eighteen instructions to candidates for baptism with five mystagogical lectures on the sacraments, preached in Constantine's basilica and still a chief witness to the creed and liturgy of the fourth-century Church. Present at the First Council of Constantinople in 381, he died in 386 and was declared a Doctor of the Church in 1883.
saints.knownFor: His Catechetical Lectures and his defense of orthodoxy.

canonization.canonized: Venerated from antiquity; declared Doctor of the Church 1883 by Pope Leo XIII

sources.text: Butler, Lives of the Saints (1866 ed.), 18 March

saints.name: St. Joseph
saints.title: Spouse of the Blessed Virgin Mary
saints.shortBlurb: The just man of Nazareth, guardian of the Redeemer and husband of Our Lady, patron of the universal Church…
biography: Joseph, a carpenter of Nazareth of the house of David, was espoused to Mary. Warned by an angel in a dream, he took her as his wife though she was found with child; again in dreams he was bidden to flee with the Child into Egypt from Herod, and to return after Herod's death.

Scripture records no word of his, only his ready obedience, and calls him a just man. He appears last in the Gospel at the finding of the twelve-year-old Jesus in the Temple, and tradition holds that he died before the Lord's public ministry, in the presence of Jesus and Mary.

Long venerated as guardian of the Redeemer, he was declared Patron of the Universal Church by Pius IX on 8 December 1870, and Pius XII in 1955 set his feast as model of workers on the first of May. Patron of workers and of fathers, he is invoked above all for a happy death, having died, as devotion holds, in the arms of Jesus and Mary.
saints.knownFor: Guarding the Holy Family in faithful, silent obedience.

canonization.canonized: Venerated from antiquity; Patron of the Universal Church (1870)

sources.text: Butler, Lives of the Saints (1866 ed.), 19 March

saints.name: St. Cuthbert
saints.title: Bishop of Lindisfarne
saints.shortBlurb: The shepherd turned monk of Lindisfarne, beloved wonderworker of Northumbria and lover of solitude…
biography: Born about 634 in the border country, Cuthbert was a shepherd on the hills near Melrose when, on the night in 651 that St. Aidan of Lindisfarne died, he saw in vision a soul borne to heaven by angels; soon after he entered the monastery of Melrose under the prior Boisil.

Made prior of Melrose and then, after the Synod of Whitby, of Lindisfarne, he journeyed tirelessly among the villages of Northumbria, winning the name of wonder-worker of Britain. Yet he yearned for solitude, and in 676 withdrew to the bare island of Inner Farne.

Elected bishop in 684 and consecrated at York by Archbishop Theodore in 685 — exchanging Hexham for Lindisfarne — he resigned within two years and died on Inner Farne on 20 March 687. His body, found incorrupt in 698, rests at Durham, and Bede wrote his life in verse and prose. He is the beloved patron of Northumbria.
saints.knownFor: His missionary charity and holiness in Northumbria.

sources.text: Butler, Lives of the Saints (1866 ed.), 20 March

saints.name: St. Nicholas of Flüe
saints.title: Hermit
saints.shortBlurb: A Swiss farmer, soldier, and magistrate who, with his wife's consent, became a hermit and peacemaker of the Confederation…
biography: Born in 1417 at Flüeli near Sachseln in Unterwalden, Nicholas was a farmer who fought as a soldier at Ragaz in 1446, rose to captain, and served his canton as councillor and judge, declining the office of Landammann. With his wife Dorothea he had ten children.

In 1467, past fifty and with Dorothea's consent, he left his household for a hermitage in the nearby Ranft gorge, moved by a vision of a lily devoured by a horse, which he read as the world's cares swallowing up the spirit. There for some twenty years he gave himself to prayer and penance, said to have taken no earthly food but the Eucharist.

His counsel was sought from across Europe, and in 1481 his intervention at the Diet of Stans reconciled the quarreling cantons and saved the Confederation from civil war. He died on 21 March 1487, surrounded by his wife and children, and was canonized by Pius XII in 1947 — the peacemaker who is honoured as patron of Switzerland.
saints.knownFor: His hidden life of prayer and his peacemaking at Stans.

sources.text: Butler, Lives of the Saints (1866 ed.), 21 March

saints.name: St. Lea of Rome
saints.title: Widow
saints.shortBlurb: A Roman widow who left the world for a life of prayer and penance, held up by St. Jerome as an example above worldly greatness…
biography: Lea was a noble Roman widow of the fourth century, known to us only through her friend St. Jerome. Left wealthy by an early widowhood, she renounced the world and joined the circle of ascetic women gathered about St. Marcella, shedding her riches and standing to live as a servant among consecrated virgins.

In time she became the superior of the community. Jerome recalls that she exchanged her rich attire for sackcloth, ceased to command others that she might obey, dwelt in a corner with a few pieces of furniture, and spent her nights in prayer, instructing her companions by example rather than by words.

She died in 384, while Jerome and Marcella were reading the seventy-third psalm together. In the letter that is our whole knowledge of her, Jerome set her hidden and holy death against the pomp of a Roman consul lately buried amid pagan honors, praising her as one who chose Christ over the world.
saints.knownFor: Her hidden life of penance, commended by St. Jerome.

sources.text: The Roman Martyrology (1914 English ed.; public domain)
Butler, Lives of the Saints (1866 ed.), 22 March

saints.name: St. Turibius of Mogrovejo
saints.title: Archbishop of Lima
saints.shortBlurb: The Spanish lawyer who became archbishop of Lima and a tireless reformer and evangelizer of colonial Peru…
biography: Born in 1538 at Mayorga in León, Turibius taught law at Salamanca and was serving as a lay judge of the Inquisition at Granada when Philip II named him, over his own protest, to the see of Lima. Ordained priest in 1578 and consecrated in 1580, he reached Peru in 1581.

Three times he traversed his vast archdiocese on foot, baptizing and confirming — among them St. Rose of Lima and St. Martín de Porres — learning the native tongues, and defending the Indians against the abuses of the colonists. He presided over the Third Council of Lima in 1582–83 and in 1591 founded the first seminary in the Americas.

Worn by fever on a visitation, he died at Zaña on 23 March 1606, repeating the Lord's own words, "into thy hands I commend my spirit." Canonized by Benedict XIII in 1726, he was proclaimed patron of the Latin American episcopate by John Paul II in 1983.
saints.knownFor: The evangelization and reform of the Church in Peru.

sources.text: Butler, Lives of the Saints (1866 ed.), 23 March

saints.name: St. Catherine of Sweden
saints.title: Virgin, Abbess of Vadstena
saints.shortBlurb: The daughter of St. Bridget of Sweden who followed her mother to Rome and led the new Bridgettine order at Vadstena…
biography: Born about 1331, the fourth child of St. Bridget of Sweden and Ulf Gudmarsson, Catherine was married at about twelve or thirteen to Lord Eggert van Kyren, a German nobleman, whom she persuaded to join her in a vow of perpetual chastity. In 1349 she accompanied her mother to Rome, and soon after their arrival her husband died.

For some twenty-five years she shared her mother's pilgrimages and works of charity, journeying with her as far as the Holy Land. When Bridget died in 1373, Catherine brought her body home to Sweden for burial at Vadstena and became the first abbess of the monastery her mother had founded there.

Returning to Rome, she labored for her mother's canonization and for the confirmation of the Bridgettine order, living five years in friendship with St. Catherine of Siena. She died at Vadstena on 24 March 1381; her cult was confirmed by Innocent VIII in 1484.
saints.knownFor: Leading the Bridgettine order at Vadstena.

canonization.canonized: Cult confirmed 1484 by Pope Innocent VIII

sources.text: Butler, Lives of the Saints (1866 ed.), 24 March

saints.name: The Annunciation of the Lord
saints.title: Solemnity of the Lord
saints.shortBlurb: The angel Gabriel announced to the Virgin Mary that she would bear the Son of God, and at her “yes” the Word was made flesh…
biography: In the sixth month of Elizabeth's pregnancy, the Gospel of Luke recounts, the angel Gabriel was sent from God to Nazareth, to a virgin espoused to Joseph of the house of David whose name was Mary. Greeting her as full of grace, he announced that she would conceive by the Holy Spirit and bear a son, Jesus, the Son of the Most High.

At her consent — "Behold the handmaid of the Lord: be it done to me according to thy word" — the eternal Word was made flesh in her womb. The feast thus honors at once the mystery of the Incarnation and the faith and obedience of the Virgin whose fiat made way for it.

Kept on 25 March, nine months before Christmas, the feast is first certainly attested in a canon of the Council of Toledo in 656 as celebrated throughout the Church, and the Council in Trullo in 692 exempted it alone, with Sundays, from the Lenten ban on feasts. In England it was long kept as Lady Day.
saints.knownFor: The Incarnation of the Word — “and the Word was made flesh.”

saints.name: St. Ludger
saints.title: Bishop, Apostle of Saxony
saints.shortBlurb: A Frisian disciple of Alcuin who evangelized the Saxons and Frisians and became the first bishop of Münster…
biography: Born about 742 at Zuilen near Utrecht of a noble Frisian family, Ludger was sent to the cathedral school of Gregory at Utrecht and later crossed to York, where he was ordained deacon and studied under Alcuin. Ordained priest at Cologne in 777, he was charged with the missions of East Frisia, centered on Dokkum, where Boniface had been martyred.

When the Saxon leader Widukind drove out the missionaries in 784, Ludger withdrew to Rome and Monte Cassino; recalled to the field, he declined the bishopric of Trier in 793 to evangelize the Saxons. About 800 he founded the abbey of Werden, and at Mimigernaford he built a monastery of canons around which the city of Münster grew.

Consecrated first bishop of Münster on 30 March 805, he converted more by gentleness, men said, than Charlemagne did by force. He died at Billerbeck on 26 March 809, having preached and celebrated Mass twice that day, and was buried at Werden.
saints.knownFor: Evangelizing the Saxons and founding the see of Münster.

sources.text: Butler, Lives of the Saints (1866 ed.), 26 March

saints.name: St. Rupert
saints.title: Bishop, Apostle of Bavaria
saints.shortBlurb: The missionary bishop who evangelized Bavaria and Austria and gave Salzburg its name and its Church…
biography: A Frankish bishop of Worms, Rupert was driven from that city by its still largely pagan people toward the end of the seventh century. Theodo, duke of Bavaria, then called him to Regensburg to preach the faith among the Bavarian tribes, and Rupert baptized the duke and many of his people.

He preached down the Danube as far as Lorch, the Roman Lauriacum, then made his seat in the ruined town of Juvavum, which he rebuilt and which came to be called Salzburg. There he restored the monastery of St. Peter, laid the foundations of the cathedral, and founded the nunnery of Nonnberg, where his niece Erentrude was first abbess.

From Duke Theodo he received estates at Reichenhall, where he fostered the saltworks that gave the city its name and him his emblem of a salt barrel. He died about 710; in 774 his successor Vergilius translated his relics to Salzburg Cathedral. He is honoured as apostle of the Bavarians and patron of Salzburg, the church he founded.
saints.knownFor: Founding the Church of Salzburg and evangelizing Bavaria.

sources.text: Butler, Lives of the Saints (1866 ed.), 27 March

saints.name: St. Guntram
saints.title: King of Burgundy
saints.shortBlurb: A Frankish king of the sixth century remembered for penance, almsgiving, and peacemaking among his warring kin…
biography: Born at Soissons in 532, a son of Chlothar I and grandson of Clovis, Guntram received a fourth of the Frankish realm at his father's death in 561 and ruled the kingdom of Orléans, later called Burgundy, for thirty-one years. Gregory of Tours, who knew him well, habitually calls him 'good king Gontrand'.

His early life was not blameless: he put away wives and lost his sons, two of them to dysentery in 577. Stricken with remorse, he gave himself to fasting, prayer, and almsgiving, open-handed above all in famine and plague, and he forgave even those who tried to take his life.

He built and endowed churches and monasteries, among them the church of St. Marcellus at Chalon-sur-Saône, and by the Treaty of Andelot in 587 secured peace with his nephew and adopted heir, Childebert II. He died at Chalon on 28 March 592 and was buried in his own foundation, his subjects at once acclaiming him a saint.
saints.knownFor: His penance, charity, and peacemaking as a Christian king.

sources.text: Butler, Lives of the Saints (1866 ed.), 28 March

saints.name: Sts. Jonas and Barachisius
saints.title: Martyrs
saints.shortBlurb: Two brothers of Beth-Asa in Persia who went to strengthen condemned Christians and were tortured to death under King Shapur II…
biography: Jonas and Barachisius were two brothers of the Persian city of Beth-Asa. In the eighteenth year of King Shapur II, when a fierce persecution was raging, they went to Hubaham to encourage the Christians lying under sentence of death, and after nine of these had been executed the brothers were themselves arrested for having strengthened them.

Commanded to worship the sun, fire, and water, they answered that it was better to obey the immortal King of heaven than a mortal prince. Jonas was beaten, kept a night in a frozen pond, mutilated limb by limb, crushed in a wooden press, and at last sawn in pieces; Barachisius, after fire and molten lead, died with boiling pitch poured into his mouth.

They suffered on 24 December 327, and a friend ransomed their bodies for five hundred drachms and three silk garments. Their acts were written down by an eyewitness, Esaias, son of Adabus of Arzun, and the Roman Martyrology keeps their memory on 29 March.
saints.knownFor: Their steadfastness under the Persian persecution.

sources.text: The Roman Martyrology (1914 English ed.; public domain)
Butler, Lives of the Saints (1866 ed.), 29 March

saints.name: St. John Climacus
saints.title: Abbot
saints.shortBlurb: The abbot of Mount Sinai whose “Ladder of Divine Ascent” has guided monks and pilgrims toward God for centuries…
biography: Born about 579, John came as a youth to the monastery of Mount Sinai, the present St. Catherine's, and was formed in the monastic life by an elder named Martyrius. After his master's death he withdrew to a hermitage at the foot of the mountain, where he spent long years in solitude, studying the lives of the saints.

When he was about sixty-five the monks persuaded him to be their abbot. At the request of John, abbot of Raithu on the Red Sea, he wrote the work from which he takes his surname: the Klimax, or Ladder of Divine Ascent, which pictures the soul's climb to God in thirty steps, answering to the thirty years of Christ's hidden life. A shorter companion treatise, To the Pastor, also survives.

The Ladder became one of the most beloved books of Byzantine spirituality and is read to this day in Orthodox monasteries during Great Lent, whose fourth Sunday is dedicated to him. He died about 649, and East and West alike keep his feast on 30 March.
saints.knownFor: Writing “The Ladder of Divine Ascent.”

sources.text: Butler, Lives of the Saints (1866 ed.), 30 March

saints.name: St. Benjamin
saints.title: Deacon and Martyr
saints.shortBlurb: A Persian deacon who would not stop preaching the Gospel and was martyred with cruel torture under King Bahram V…
biography: Benjamin was a deacon of the Persian church during the forty years of persecution that began under King Yazdegerd I and raged more fiercely under his son Bahram V. Imprisoned for a year for the faith, he was released through the intercession of an ambassador of the Roman emperor Theodosius II, on condition that he preach Christ no more.

Benjamin answered that he could not be silent about Christ. Seized again, he was put to tortures recorded by the church historian Sozomen: sharpened reeds were driven beneath the nails of his hands and feet and into the tenderest parts of his body, and at last a knotty stake ended his sufferings, about the year 424.

His constancy under such torments made him one of the most renowned martyrs of the Persian church. The Roman Martyrology keeps his name on 31 March, and the churches of East and West alike venerate him as a martyr of Christ.
saints.knownFor: Refusing to be silent about the Gospel, unto martyrdom.

sources.text: The Roman Martyrology (1914 English ed.; public domain)
Butler, Lives of the Saints (1866 ed.), 31 March

saints.name: St. Hugh of Grenoble
saints.title: Bishop
saints.shortBlurb: The reforming Bishop of Grenoble who welcomed St. Bruno and gave the Carthusians their first home…
biography: Born in 1053 at Châteauneuf-sur-Isère near Valence, Hugh was a canon of Valence while still a layman. Elected bishop of Grenoble at the Council of Avignon in 1080, he was conducted to Rome and ordained by Pope Gregory VII himself, and found his see ruined in morals and in goods.

For fifty-two years he laboured against simony and the laxity of his clergy, restoring discipline and recovering the patrimony of his church, long disputed by Count Guigues III of Albon until an accord in 1099. Once he sought to resign his see for the cloister of Cluny, but the pope ordered him back to his charge.

In 1084, after dreaming of seven stars, he welcomed Bruno of Cologne and six companions and gave them the wild Alpine valley of the Chartreuse, where the Carthusian Order began; Hugh remained its lifelong protector. He died on 1 April 1132 and was canonized only two years later by Innocent II.
saints.knownFor: Reforming his diocese and giving the Carthusians the valley of the Chartreuse.

sources.text: Butler, Lives of the Saints (1866 ed.), 1 April

saints.name: St. Francis of Paola
saints.title: Hermit and Founder
saints.shortBlurb: A Calabrian hermit whose penance and miracles founded the Order of Minims, the “least” of religious…
biography: Born at Paola in Calabria on 27 March 1416 to poor parents who had begged a son through the intercession of Francis of Assisi, he spent a year among the Franciscans of San Marco Argentano and then, from 1432, lived alone as a hermit in a cave on the Tyrrhenian shore.

When two companions joined him about 1436, the order that would be called Minims began; Alexander VI later confirmed the rule and gave them that name, 'the least' in the household of God. To the usual vows Francis added a fourth, a perpetual Lenten abstinence from flesh, eggs, and dairy. He was never ordained a priest.

Renowned for prophecy and healing, he was summoned to France by the dying Louis XI and went only when the pope commanded. He prepared the king for death and remained at the French court as counsellor to Charles VIII and Louis XII.

He died at Plessis-les-Tours on Good Friday, 2 April 1507, and was canonized by Leo X in 1519. Because tradition holds that, refused passage by a boatman, he crossed the Strait of Messina on his spread cloak, Pius XII named him patron of the seafarers of Italy in 1943.
saints.knownFor: Founding the Order of Minims and a life of extreme penance.

sources.text: Butler, Lives of the Saints (1866 ed.), 2 April

saints.name: St. Richard of Chichester
saints.title: Bishop
saints.shortBlurb: The devoted Bishop of Chichester whose prayer still asks to know, love, and follow Christ more nearly…
biography: Born about 1197 near Droitwich and orphaned young, Richard de Wych laboured on his brother's farm to restore the impoverished family estate, then gave it up for study at Oxford, Paris, and Bologna. Returning to England, he became chancellor of Oxford and, in 1237, chancellor of Canterbury under Edmund of Abingdon, whose exile at Pontigny he shared.

Elected bishop of Chichester in 1244, he was opposed by Henry III, who seized the see's revenues; Innocent IV consecrated him at Lyons in 1245, but for two years Richard lived on charity, lodging with a parish priest at Tarring and visiting his diocese on foot. Restored, he reformed his clergy by exact statutes and gave himself to almsgiving and personal austerity.

He died at the Maison Dieu in Dover on 3 April 1253, sent to preach a crusade, and was canonized by Urban IV in 1262; his shrine at Chichester drew pilgrims until Henry VIII destroyed it in 1538. The deathbed prayer ascribed to him — to know Christ more clearly, love him more dearly, follow him more nearly — is still beloved, and he is patron of his own diocese.
saints.knownFor: His pastoral holiness and the prayer that bears his name.

sources.text: Butler, Lives of the Saints (1866 ed.), 3 April

saints.name: St. Isidore of Seville
saints.title: Bishop and Doctor of the Church
saints.shortBlurb: The last of the Latin Fathers, whose learning gathered the wisdom of the ancient world for a new age…
biography: Born at Cartagena about 560, Isidore belonged to a family of saints: his brothers Leander and Fulgentius and his sister Florentina are all venerated. Educated in the cathedral school of Seville, he succeeded Leander as archbishop in 600 and governed that see for more than thirty years.

He laboured to weld Goths and Romans into one Catholic people, completing the conversion of the Visigoths from Arianism. He presided over the Second Council of Seville in 619 and over the Fourth Council of Toledo in 633, which ordered every bishop to establish a school in his cathedral city for the study of the liberal arts.

His Etymologies, an encyclopedia in twenty books, preserved the learning of antiquity and was the most popular compendium in medieval libraries; he also wrote a history of the Goths. He died on 4 April 636 and was proclaimed Doctor of the Church in 1722. Because he gathered all knowledge for learners, he is patron of students and has even been proposed as patron of the Internet.
saints.knownFor: His Etymologies and his labour to preserve ancient learning.

canonization.canonized: Venerated from antiquity; Doctor of the Church (1722)

sources.text: Butler, Lives of the Saints (1866 ed.), 4 April

saints.name: St. Vincent Ferrer
saints.title: Priest
saints.shortBlurb: The Dominican “Angel of the Judgment,” whose preaching of penance stirred all of Western Europe…
biography: Born at Valencia on 23 January 1350, Vincent entered the Order of Preachers at eighteen and was ordained priest at Barcelona in 1379; after teaching theology at Lleida he gave himself wholly to preaching. For some twenty years he journeyed through Spain, France, Switzerland, and Italy, drawing vast crowds by his sermons on sin, death, and judgment, whence men called him the Angel of the Judgment.

He lived through the Western Schism and long upheld the Avignon claimant Benedict XIII, whom he served as apostolic penitentiary; but when Benedict refused every path of reunion, Vincent publicly withdrew his obedience, helping to open the way to the settlement reached at the Council of Constance. Multitudes of sinners, and many Jews and Muslims, were reconciled to the Church by his preaching.

Worn out by travel, he died at Vannes in Brittany on 5 April 1419 and was canonized by Callixtus III in 1455. He is honoured as a patron of builders, for he spent his life building up the Church and mending its broken unity.
saints.knownFor: His preaching of repentance and his part in healing the Western Schism.

sources.text: Butler, Lives of the Saints (1866 ed.), 5 April

saints.name: Pope St. Celestine I
saints.title: Pope
saints.shortBlurb: The pope who upheld the title Mother of God at Ephesus and sent the faith toward Britain and Ireland…
biography: A Roman deacon under Innocent I, Celestine was elected bishop of Rome in 422. His ten-year pontificate was a sustained defence of the inherited faith: he curbed the Novatians at Rome, insisting that pardon never be refused to a dying sinner who sincerely asked it, and continued the condemnation of Pelagian teaching on grace.

Above all he moved against Nestorius of Constantinople, whose preaching denied Mary the title Theotokos, Mother of God. A Roman synod in 430 condemned the error, and Celestine commissioned Cyril of Alexandria to act in his name; the next year his legates joined the Council of Ephesus, which upheld the title.

His care reached the ends of the Christian world: he sent Germanus of Auxerre to Britain in 429 against Pelagianism and, in 431, the deacon Palladius as first bishop to the believing Scots of Ireland, before St. Patrick. He died in 432 and was buried on the Via Salaria; his body now rests in Santa Prassede at Rome.
saints.knownFor: Backing the Council of Ephesus and the defence of Mary as Mother of God.

sources.text: The Roman Martyrology (1914 English ed.; public domain), 6 April

saints.name: St. John Baptist de la Salle
saints.title: Priest
saints.shortBlurb: A French canon who gave up rank and wealth to found free schools and train the teachers of the poor…
biography: Born at Reims in 1651, the son of a wealthy family, John Baptist de la Salle was made a cathedral canon at sixteen and ordained priest in 1678. His life turned in 1679 when he helped the schoolmaster Adrian Nyel open a school for poor boys; he went on to house the teachers in his home, resign his canonry, and sell his inheritance to feed the famine-stricken poor of Champagne.

With those schoolmasters he formed the Institute of the Brothers of the Christian Schools, the first religious institute with no priests among its members, bound to teach the poor gratuitously. He trained his masters in what is reckoned the first normal school, opened at Reims in 1685, and pioneered teaching in the vernacular, in classes rather than one by one.

Harassed by the schoolmasters' guilds and by churchmen opposed to a community of laymen teaching 'together and by association', he died at Saint-Yon near Rouen on Good Friday, 7 April 1719. Leo XIII canonized him in 1900; Pius XII declared him patron of all teachers of youth in 1950 — the founder of modern popular schooling made patron of those who continue it.
saints.knownFor: Founding the De La Salle Brothers and modern teacher training.

sources.text: Catholic Encyclopedia (1913), “St. John Baptist de la Salle”
Butler, Lives of the Saints (1866 ed.), 7 April

saints.name: St. Julie Billiart
saints.title: Virgin and Founder
saints.shortBlurb: A French peasant woman, long paralyzed, who rose to found the Sisters of Notre Dame de Namur…
biography: Born at Cuvilly in Picardy in 1751, a farmer's daughter, Julie Billiart knew the catechism by heart at seven and soon taught it to others. In 1774 she witnessed a shot fired at her father; the shock brought on an illness that slowly paralyzed her, and by 1784 she was bedridden — yet from her bed she taught catechism and prepared children for first communion.

During the Revolution she sheltered hunted priests and had to be smuggled out of Cuvilly under straw in a wagon, reaching Amiens, where in 1794 she met the noblewoman Françoise Blin de Bourdon. With her and Catherine Duchâtel she founded the Sisters of Notre Dame at Amiens on 2 February 1804 to teach poor girls; that same year, after a novena prescribed by her confessor, she was completely cured.

The motherhouse moved to Namur in 1809, and as the Sisters of Notre Dame de Namur the institute spread: in twelve years Julie founded fifteen convents and made a hundred and twenty journeys, her watchword 'How good is the good God'. She died at Namur on 8 April 1816, was beatified by Pius X in 1906, and canonized by Paul VI in 1969.
saints.knownFor: Founding the Sisters of Notre Dame de Namur for the education of poor girls.

sources.text: Vatican biography, Canonization of St. Julie Billiart (vatican.va)

saints.name: St. Waltrude
saints.title: Abbess
saints.shortBlurb: A noblewoman of Hainaut whose convent became the seed of the city of Mons…
biography: Born at Cousolre in Hainaut, daughter of the nobles Walbert and Bertilia and sister of Aldegonde, foundress of Maubeuge, Waltrude married Vincent Madelgarus, count of Hainaut, and bore him four children — Landry, Dentelin, Aldetrude, and Madelberta — who with their parents were all venerated as saints.

About 656, after young Dentelin's death, the couple resolved to part: Vincent became a monk in the monastery he had founded at Hautmont. Waltrude gave herself to prayer and almsdeeds, ransoming captives at her own cost, and gathered a company of virgins at Castrilocus — Châteaulieu, the 'castle place' — the hill around which the city of Mons grew up.

She died on 9 April about the year 688. Her relics rest in the collegiate church of Sainte-Waudru at Mons, and each year the city draws her shrine through its streets on a gilded cart, the car d'or, in the festival called the Ducasse. Because the town grew from her convent, she is honored as mother and patroness of Mons.
saints.knownFor: Founding the community that grew into the city of Mons.

sources.text: Butler, Lives of the Saints (1866 ed.), 9 April

saints.name: St. Fulbert of Chartres
saints.title: Bishop
saints.shortBlurb: The bishop and teacher who made Chartres a beacon of learning and rebuilt its great cathedral…
biography: Born about 960, of humble stock and probably in Picardy, Fulbert studied at the cathedral school of Reims, where a fellow student was the future king Robert the Pious, and by tradition under Gerbert of Aurillac, later Pope Sylvester II. Called to Chartres, he directed its cathedral school and drew scholars from many lands; his pupils named him the 'venerable Socrates'.

Made deacon in 1004 and bishop of Chartres in 1006, he governed for twenty-two years, counselling kings and prelates in letters still read; that to Duke William V of Aquitaine, on the mutual duties of lord and vassal, became a classic of feudal law. When his cathedral burned in 1020 he raised the funds to rebuild it; his crypt survives beneath the present church.

A fervent servant of the Virgin, whose relic the Sancta Camisia Chartres treasured, he spread the feast of her Nativity through his sermon Approbate consuetudinis and left the Easter hymn Chorus novae Jerusalem ('Ye choirs of new Jerusalem'). He died on 10 April 1028; never formally canonized, he is honored as a saint at Chartres and stands in the Roman Martyrology.
saints.knownFor: The school of Chartres and the rebuilding of its cathedral.

sources.text: Butler, Lives of the Saints (1866 ed.), 10 April

saints.name: St. Stanislaus
saints.title: Bishop and Martyr
saints.shortBlurb: The Bishop of Kraków slain at the altar for rebuking a king, and the patron of Poland…
biography: Born at Szczepanów in 1030, the only son of the nobles Wielisław and Bogna, Stanislaus studied at Gniezno and, by tradition, at Paris. Ordained by Bishop Lambert II, he rose to be canon, preacher, and vicar-general of Kraków, and on the bishop's death in 1072 was chosen his successor at the command of Pope Alexander II.

One of the first native Poles to hold a bishopric, he restored Gniezno's metropolitan see, making possible Bolesław II's coronation as king in 1076. Yet he did not spare that king: rebuking Bolesław the Bold for his crimes, he at last excommunicated him, whereupon the royal court condemned the bishop to death for treason.

On 11 April 1079, as he celebrated Mass in the chapel of Saint Michael on Skałka outside Kraków, the king's men dared not touch him and Bolesław struck him down himself; the body was hacked to pieces. The outrage cost Bolesław his throne.

Canonized by Innocent IV at Assisi in 1253, he became patron of Poland; Poles read in the legend of his scattered and reunited members a prophecy that their riven nation would be made whole, and their kings were crowned kneeling before his shrine at Wawel.
saints.knownFor: Dying a martyr for the Church's freedom against a king.

sources.text: Butler, Lives of the Saints (1866 ed.), 11 April

saints.name: Pope St. Julius I
saints.title: Pope
saints.shortBlurb: The pope who sheltered St. Athanasius and stood for Nicaea against the Arian tide…
biography: A Roman by birth, Julius was chosen bishop of Rome on 6 February 337, after the see had stood vacant four months. His pontificate fell in the thick of the Arian controversy: when Athanasius of Alexandria, deposed and driven out by the Arian party, fled to Rome about 340, Julius received him and made his cause his own.

A synod he assembled at Rome about 341, of more than fifty bishops, acquitted Athanasius; and in his letter to the Eastern bishops Julius rebuked them for deposing a bishop without reference to Rome — 'Can you be ignorant,' he wrote, 'that this is the custom, that we should be written to first, so that from here what is just may be defined?'

Through his influence the Council of Sardica was assembled in 343, which vindicated the exiled bishops and confirmed the right of appeal to the Roman see. He built several churches in Rome and died on 12 April 352. A later tradition, resting on a letter now judged spurious, credits him with fixing 25 December as the feast of the Nativity.
saints.knownFor: Defending St. Athanasius and the Nicene faith against Arianism.

sources.text: The Roman Martyrology (1914 English ed.; public domain), 12 April

saints.name: Pope St. Martin I
saints.title: Pope and Martyr
saints.shortBlurb: The last pope to die a martyr, exiled and starved for condemning heresy about Christ's will…
biography: Born near Todi in Umbria, Martin had served Pope Theodore I as apocrisiarius, his legate at the imperial court of Constantinople, when he was himself elected; he was consecrated on 21 July 649 without waiting for the emperor's confirmation — a deliberate defiance. Within three months he summoned the bishops of the West to the Lateran.

That council, 105 bishops in October 649, condemned Monothelitism — the doctrine that Christ had but one will — together with the Ecthesis of Heraclius and the Typos by which Constans II forbade the whole dispute. Constans struck back: in June 653 the exarch Theodore Calliopas seized the ailing pope in the Lateran basilica and shipped him prisoner to Constantinople.

Tried there for treason, publicly degraded, and condemned to death, he saw his sentence commuted to exile; in May 655 he reached Cherson in the Crimea, where famine and neglect killed him within months, on 16 September 655. The Church venerates him as the last of the martyr popes, and the East keeps him as Saint Martin the Confessor.
saints.knownFor: Condemning Monothelitism and dying in exile for the faith.

sources.text: Butler, Lives of the Saints (1866 ed.), 13 April

saints.name: St. Lidwina of Schiedam
saints.title: Virgin
saints.shortBlurb: A Dutch maiden whose thirty-eight years of illness became a school of redemptive suffering…
biography: Born at Schiedam in Holland on 18 April 1380, one of a laborer's nine children, Lidwina fell while skating at fifteen and broke a rib. The injury never healed; sickness crept over her limb by limb until she lay bedridden — by her biographers' account paralyzed but for one hand — for the last thirty-eight years of her life.

She offered her sufferings for sinners and lived in union with the Passion; her fasts grew so extreme that the magistrates of Schiedam drew up a document, which survives, attesting that she took almost no nourishment. Cures and multiplied alms were credited to her prayers, and the sick of Holland came to her bedside as to a shrine.

She died on 14 April 1433, aged fifty-two, and her grave became a place of pilgrimage; the friar John Brugman wrote her life, and Thomas à Kempis spread her fame. Leo XIII granted her equipollent canonization on 14 March 1890. Because her passion began on the ice she is patroness of skaters; because she bore it thirty-eight years, of the chronically ill.
saints.knownFor: Bearing long illness as an offering of redemptive suffering.

canonization.canonized: Cult confirmed 1890 by Pope Leo XIII

sources.text: Butler, Lives of the Saints (1866 ed.), 14 April

saints.name: St. Hunna
saints.title: Matron
saints.shortBlurb: A noblewoman of Alsace called “the Holy Washerwoman” for washing the clothes of the poor with her own hands…
biography: Hunna was a noblewoman of seventh-century Alsace, the daughter of a duke, who married Huno, a nobleman of Hunawihr. She raised her son under the guidance of St. Deodatus, the former bishop of Nevers then living as a hermit in the Vosges, who baptized the boy and gave him his own name.

Mistress of a great household, she spent herself on her poorer neighbors: she nursed the sick, taught the faith, and cooked, cleaned, and washed for those who had no one else. Because she carried home the dirty clothes of the poor and brought them back clean, the country people called her 'the Holy Washerwoman'.

She died about 679 at Hunawihr and was buried there; her son became a monk in Deodatus's monastery at Ebersheim and was himself venerated as a saint. Pope Leo X canonized her in 1520, when her relics were raised on 15 April, her feast day; and for the lowly service that was her glory she is invoked as patroness of laundresses.
saints.knownFor: Serving the poor by washing their clothes with her own hands.

sources.text: The Roman Martyrology (1914 English ed.; public domain), 15 April
Butler, Lives of the Saints (1866 ed.), 15 April

saints.name: St. Bernadette Soubirous
saints.title: Virgin
saints.shortBlurb: The poor miller's daughter of Lourdes to whom the Immaculate Conception appeared…
biography: Born at Lourdes on 7 January 1844, the eldest of a miller's nine children, Bernadette Soubirous grew up in poverty, the family lodging in a disused jail. Frail from cholera and asthma, she was gathering firewood at the grotto of Massabielle on 11 February 1858 when she saw 'a small young lady'.

Eighteen apparitions followed, ending 16 July. At her word Bernadette scraped in the mud and uncovered a spring; and on 25 March, asked her name, the lady answered in the local dialect, 'I am the Immaculate Conception' — a dignity defined by Rome only four years before, unknown to the unlettered girl. In 1862 the Church judged the apparitions worthy of belief.

To escape notice she entered the Sisters of Charity at Nevers in 1866 as Sister Marie-Bernarde, serving in the infirmary and as sacristan. Wasted by asthma and tuberculosis, she died on 16 April 1879, aged thirty-five; her body, exhumed in 1909, was found incorrupt.

Pius XI beatified her in 1925 and canonized her on 8 December 1933, the feast of the Immaculate Conception, honoring in her not the visions but a life of humility. The shrine of Lourdes now draws some five million pilgrims every year.
saints.knownFor: The apparitions of Our Lady of Lourdes and her hidden holiness.

sources.text: Vatican biography, Canonization of St. Bernadette Soubirous (vatican.va)

saints.name: Pope St. Anicetus
saints.title: Pope and Martyr
saints.shortBlurb: An early pope who received St. Polycarp and kept charity amid the dispute over Easter…
biography: A Syrian from Emesa, the modern Homs, Anicetus governed the Roman church in the middle of the second century, from about 157 to 168, when Gnostic teachers such as Valentinus and Marcion were troubling it; against them he held fast to the apostolic faith. The Liber Pontificalis recalls even his ruling that the clergy must not wear long hair.

His pontificate is lit by the visit, about 155, of the aged Polycarp of Smyrna, disciple of the Apostle John. They could not agree about Easter — the churches of Asia kept it on the fourteenth of Nisan with the Passover, Rome on the Sunday — yet neither broke communion: Anicetus in deference let Polycarp celebrate the Eucharist in his own church, and they parted in peace.

The traveler Hegesippus also visited Rome in his days, a sign of the see's early eminence. Anicetus died in April about the year 168 and was buried, the Liber Pontificalis says, in the cemetery of Callixtus on the Appian Way; later tradition counts him among the martyrs, though his martyrdom is not historically attested.
saints.knownFor: His charity toward St. Polycarp in the early Easter controversy.

sources.text: The Roman Martyrology (1914 English ed.; public domain), 17 April

saints.name: St. Apollonius the Apologist
saints.title: Martyr
saints.shortBlurb: A learned Roman senator who defended the faith before the Senate and died for it…
biography: Apollonius was a Roman of rank and learning — a senator, the sources say, and a man versed in philosophy — living under the Emperor Commodus. Denounced as a Christian by one of his own slaves to the praetorian prefect Perennis, he was called upon to answer before the Senate.

There, far from recanting, he read a reasoned defense of Christianity — 'a remarkable volume', Jerome calls it — maintaining that he did not fear death, since eternal life awaits those who have lived well on earth. His judges heard him patiently in two hearings three days apart; but the rescript of Trajan against the Christians stood, and he was condemned to death.

The defense itself, translated into Greek, is lost, though Eusebius preserves the story of his trial in the Ecclesiastical History. He suffered about the year 185 — beheaded, one ancient account says — and stands among the first men of Roman learning to answer persecution with a public and reasoned confession of the faith.
saints.knownFor: His reasoned defense of the faith before the Roman Senate.

sources.text: The Roman Martyrology (1914 English ed.; public domain), 18 April

saints.name: St. Alphege of Canterbury
saints.title: Bishop and Martyr
saints.shortBlurb: An archbishop who forbade his own ransom and was slain by Danish raiders…
biography: Born in 954, Alphege — Ælfheah in Old English — left his widowed mother for the monastery of Deerhurst and afterward lived as an anchorite at Bath, where he became abbot. In 984 he was made Bishop of Winchester, and in 994 he gave confirmation to Olaf of Norway at Andover.

Raised to Canterbury in 1006, he was taken prisoner in September 1011 when a Danish army sacked and burned the city. Held for months while a heavy ransom was demanded, he forbade his impoverished people to buy his life at their cost.

On 19 April 1012, at Greenwich, his captors, drunk with wine and enraged that the ransom was refused, pelted him with the bones of their feast and with stones, until one of them, named Thurm, dispatched him with an axe.

His body rested eleven years in St. Paul's, London, before King Canute translated it to Canterbury. Canonized in 1078, he found a defender of his martyrdom in Anselm of Canterbury, who taught that he who dies for truth and justice dies for Christ.
saints.knownFor: Refusing to let the poor be taxed for his ransom, and dying at Danish hands.

sources.text: Butler, Lives of the Saints (1866 ed.), 19 April

saints.name: St. Agnes of Montepulciano
saints.title: Virgin
saints.shortBlurb: A Tuscan prioress and mystic whom St. Catherine of Siena honoured as a mother in religion…
biography: Born about 1268 near Montepulciano in Tuscany, Agnes entered a monastery at nine years old, giving herself to prayer with a fervour beyond her age. Four years later she was sent to assist in founding a new convent at Proceno, and at fifteen, by papal dispensation, she was made its prioress.

At the entreaty of her native town she returned to Montepulciano and in 1298 established there a convent of Dominican nuns, which she governed as prioress for nearly twenty years until her death, famed for prayer, severe austerity, and the miracles reported at her intercession.

She died on 20 April 1317, aged about forty-nine, and her tomb became a place of pilgrimage. Nearly two centuries later Catherine of Siena journeyed to Montepulciano to venerate her body, which remains incorrupt, reverencing her as a mother in religion. Agnes was canonized in 1726 by Pope Benedict XIII, himself a Dominican.
saints.knownFor: Her mystical life and her monastery at Montepulciano.

sources.text: Butler, Lives of the Saints (1866 ed.), 20 April

saints.name: St. Anselm of Canterbury
saints.title: Bishop and Doctor of the Church
saints.shortBlurb: The father of scholastic theology, who sought faith seeking understanding…
biography: Born at Aosta about 1033, Anselm crossed the Alps and in 1060 became a monk of Bec in Normandy, drawn by the fame of Lanfranc. Prior in 1063 and abbot in 1078, he wrote in those years the Monologion and the Proslogion, with its celebrated argument for the existence of God.

His was a theology of prayerful reason — 'faith seeking understanding'. Named Archbishop of Canterbury in 1093, he resisted William Rufus and then Henry I in defence of the Church's liberty, enduring two exiles; during the first he finished Cur Deus Homo, his masterwork on the Redemption, and at the Council of Bari in 1098 defended the Latin doctrine of the Holy Spirit.

The long investiture struggle ended in 1107, when Henry surrendered the claim to invest bishops while the Church allowed prelates to do homage for their temporal holdings. Anselm died on 21 April 1109; Clement XI declared him a Doctor of the Church in 1720, and he is honoured as a father of scholastic theology and a patron of theologians.
saints.knownFor: “Faith seeking understanding” and the birth of scholastic theology.

canonization.canonized: Venerated from antiquity; Doctor of the Church (1720)

sources.text: Butler, Lives of the Saints (1866 ed.), 21 April

saints.name: Sts. Soter and Caius
saints.title: Popes and Martyrs
saints.shortBlurb: Two early popes sharing one feast, one famed for Rome's ancient charity, the other buried on the eve of the last persecution…
biography: Soter governed the Roman Church from about 166 to 174. St. Dionysius of Corinth, in a letter preserved by Eusebius, thanked him for upholding and increasing Rome's immemorial custom — 'the traditional custom of the Romans' — of sending alms to churches in every city and relief to the brethren labouring in the mines.

Dionysius adds that Soter's own letter was read aloud in the church of Corinth, like the earlier letter of Clement; it is now lost, though some have sought it in the so-called Second Epistle of Clement. A fifth-century writer credits Soter with a book against the Montanists, on uncertain authority.

Caius reigned twelve years, from 17 December 283 to 22 April 296, and was buried in the chapel of the popes in the cemetery of Callixtus. Later legend made him a kinsman of Diocletian and a martyr, but the fourth-century Depositio Episcoporum names him only among the bishops, for he died in the peace before the last persecution.

The two popes have shared a single commemoration on 22 April from the earliest martyrologies; in later centuries forged decretals were circulated under both their names — testimony to the weight their memory carried in the Roman Church.
saints.knownFor: Their governance of the early Roman Church and their witness to Christ.

sources.text: The Roman Martyrology (1914 English ed.; public domain), 22 April

saints.name: St. George
saints.title: Martyr
saints.shortBlurb: The soldier-martyr of the early Church, honoured across East and West as a model of courage…
biography: George was a martyr who suffered at or near Lydda, called Diospolis, in Palestine, traditionally about 303 in the persecution of Diocletian. Nothing certain is known of his life beyond his martyrdom, yet pilgrims from the sixth century onward venerated his tomb at Lydda, and churches in Syria, Egypt, and the West already bore his name.

A decree of Pope Gelasius about 495 already numbered him among those saints 'whose names are justly reverenced among men, but whose actions are only known to God'. The dragon legend — the knight who frees a king's daughter and converts her city — appears no earlier than the twelfth century and was spread by the Golden Legend.

Honoured as a soldier-martyr, he was seen, crusaders believed, fighting beside them with St. Demetrius at Antioch in 1098, and became a patron of soldiers and of chivalry. When Edward III founded the Order of the Garter under his patronage about 1347, George became the patron of England, whose banner still bears his red cross.
saints.knownFor: His witness as a soldier-martyr and his patronage of soldiers and England.

sources.text: The Roman Martyrology (1914 English ed.; public domain), 23 April

saints.name: St. Fidelis of Sigmaringen
saints.title: Priest and Martyr
saints.shortBlurb: A lawyer turned Capuchin, the “advocate of the poor” who died preaching the faith to the Grisons…
biography: Born Mark Rey at Sigmaringen in 1577, the burgomaster's son, he studied at Freiburg, travelled France and Italy as a nobleman's tutor, and in 1611 took the doctorate in canon and civil law. An advocate who pleaded the cause of the poor without fee, he left the bar, sickened by the corruption of the courts.

Ordained priest in 1612, he entered the Capuchins at Freiburg, taking the name Fidelis. He served as guardian of the convents of Rheinfelden, Freiburg, and Feldkirch and won fame as a preacher against the Calvinism spreading through the Alpine valleys.

In 1621 he was sent to the Grisons, where Calvinism had taken root, and the new Congregation for the Propagation of the Faith made him mission superior. On 24 April 1622, after Mass at Grüsch, he was preaching at Seewis when an armed mob broke in; refusing apostasy, he answered, 'I came to extirpate heresy, not to embrace it', and was cut down.

The first martyr of Propaganda Fide, he was buried at Feldkirch, his head and arm kept at Chur. Beatified in 1729 and canonized by Benedict XIV in 1746, he is a patron of lawyers in memory of his first calling.
saints.knownFor: Dying as the first martyr of the missions of Propaganda Fide.

sources.text: Butler, Lives of the Saints (1866 ed.), 24 April

saints.name: St. Mark
saints.title: Evangelist
saints.shortBlurb: The evangelist whose brief, vivid Gospel preserves the preaching of St. Peter, and traditional founder of the Church of Alexandria…
biography: Mark, the John Mark of the Acts of the Apostles, was the son of Mary, in whose Jerusalem house the first Christians gathered to pray, and a cousin of Barnabas. He accompanied Paul and Barnabas as an assistant on their first journey but turned back at Perga, a failing that later drove the two apostles apart.

Reconciled to Paul, he is found beside the apostle during the Roman imprisonment, and Peter greets the churches with 'Mark my son'. Papias, early in the second century, records that Mark became Peter's interpreter and wrote down accurately, though not in order, the apostle's preaching — the shortest of the four Gospels.

Ancient tradition sends him to Egypt as founder and first bishop of the Church of Alexandria, where, his later Acts relate, he was martyred, dragged through the streets, about the year 68. In 828 Venetian merchants bore his relics from Alexandria to Venice, whose patron he became; the winged lion of the evangelist is her emblem still.
saints.knownFor: Writing the Gospel that preserves Peter's preaching.
