sources.text: Butler, Lives of the Saints (1866 ed.), 25 April

saints.name: St. Paschasius Radbertus
saints.title: Abbot
saints.shortBlurb: The Benedictine abbot who wrote the first great treatise on the Eucharist…
biography: Born about 785 at Soissons and exposed as a child, Paschasius was raised by Benedictine nuns and became a monk of Corbie under Abbot Adalhard, whom he accompanied in 822 to found New Corvey in Saxony. A deacon all his life, he refused priestly ordination out of humility.

Made abbot of Corbie about 844, he resigned after some seven years to give himself to study. Besides commentaries on Matthew, the Psalms, and Lamentations and lives of the abbots Adalhard and Wala, he wrote the Church's first systematic treatise on the Eucharist, On the Body and Blood of the Lord.

Composed in 831 for the monks of New Corvey and presented in revised form to the Emperor Charles the Bald in 844, the book taught the real presence of Christ's true Body and Blood and provoked the first great Eucharistic controversy, answered by Ratramnus and Rabanus Maurus, and vindicated by Gerbert, afterwards Pope Sylvester II.

He died at Corbie about 865 and was buried in the church of St. John. When miracles multiplied at his tomb, his relics were solemnly translated by order of Pope Gregory VII on 12 July 1073; his feast is kept on 26 April.
saints.knownFor: The first systematic treatise on the Real Presence in the Eucharist.

sources.text: The Roman Martyrology (1914 English ed.; public domain), 26 April

saints.name: St. Zita
saints.title: Virgin
saints.shortBlurb: A humble maidservant of Lucca who made a lifetime of housework a path to holiness…
biography: Born about 1212 to a poor family of Monsagrati, a village near Lucca, Zita entered at twelve the service of the Fatinelli, a prosperous household of that city, and remained their servant for some forty-eight years, sanctifying housework by prayer and by quiet gifts of food to the poor.

Her exactness at first earned only the jealousy of the other servants, whose accusations turned her employers against her, but her patient goodness outlasted their malice, and in time she was set over the whole household — generous in almsgiving, yet careful to relieve only genuine need.

She died at Lucca on 27 April 1272, in her sixtieth year, and miracles at her intercession made her so dear that Dante could style Lucca simply 'Santa Zita'. Her tomb in San Frediano was opened in 1580, and Innocent XII confirmed her cult in 1696. Because she spent her life as a maidservant, she is the patroness of domestic workers.
saints.knownFor: Sanctifying humble domestic service through charity and prayer.

canonization.canonized: Cult confirmed 1696 by Pope Innocent XII

sources.text: Butler, Lives of the Saints (1866 ed.), 27 April

saints.name: St. Louis Marie de Montfort
saints.title: Priest
saints.shortBlurb: A tireless missionary of the poor whose “True Devotion” shaped modern Marian piety…
biography: Born at Montfort in Brittany on 31 January 1673, Louis-Marie Grignion studied with the Jesuits at Rennes and walked to Paris at nineteen for his theology, giving away his money and vowing to live on alms. Ordained in 1700, he found his vocation in 1705 as a preacher of parish missions.

For seventeen years he walked the villages of Brittany and the Vendée, preaching with fire, reviving the Rosary, and raising with his people's hands a monumental calvary at Pontchâteau that the government, stirred by Jansenist intrigue, ordered demolished. Poisoned once at La Rochelle, he never fully recovered his health.

He founded the Daughters of Wisdom at Poitiers in 1703 for the care of the sick poor and the Company of Mary in 1713 for missionary priests, and in his Treatise on True Devotion to the Blessed Virgin he taught total consecration to Jesus through Mary, a teaching that has shaped Catholic devotion ever since.

Worn out by his labours, he died at Saint-Laurent-sur-Sèvre on 28 April 1716, aged forty-three, leaving his two congregations only a handful of members. He was beatified by Leo XIII in 1888 and canonized by Pius XII in 1947.
saints.knownFor: His missions to the poor and his teaching on consecration to Christ through Mary.

sources.text: Catholic Encyclopedia (1913), “Blessed Louis-Marie Grignion de Montfort”
Butler, Lives of the Saints (1866 ed.), 28 April

saints.name: St. Catherine of Siena
saints.title: Virgin and Doctor of the Church
saints.shortBlurb: A Dominican mystic of Siena whose letters and Dialogue moved popes, and who helped bring the papacy home from Avignon…
biography: Born at Siena on 25 March 1347, daughter of the dyer Giacomo di Benincasa, Catherine consecrated herself to God in childhood and at sixteen took the habit of the Dominican tertiaries, living three years in prayer in a little room of her father's house.

After her mystical espousals she left her cell to nurse the sick and serve the poor, and her counsel was soon sought by princes. At Pisa in 1375 she received the stigmata, invisible at her own prayer, and in 1376 she went to Avignon, where her pleading moved Gregory XI to return the papacy to Rome in January 1377.

Peacemaker in a divided Italy, she dictated at Siena her Dialogue of Divine Providence, and when the Great Schism opened in 1378 she gave herself wholly to Urban VI, who summoned her to Rome. There, spent by penance and by her labours for the Church's unity, she died on 29 April 1380, aged thirty-three.

Canonized by Pius II in 1461, she was named patroness of Italy in 1939, declared a Doctor of the Church in 1970, and made co-patroness of Europe in 1999; her nursing of the sick makes her a patron of nurses.
saints.knownFor: Recalling the popes to Rome and her mystical writings.

canonization.canonized: 1461 by Pope Pius II; Doctor of the Church (1970)

sources.text: Butler, Lives of the Saints (1866 ed.), 30 April

saints.name: Pope St. Pius V
saints.title: Pope
saints.shortBlurb: The Dominican pope who carried out the reforms of Trent and gave the Church the feast of the Rosary…
biography: Born Antonio Ghislieri on 17 January 1504 at Bosco near Alessandria, he entered the Dominicans, taking the name Michele, and was ordained in 1528. Paul IV made him Bishop of Sutri in 1556 and, in 1557, cardinal and inquisitor general of all Christendom.

Elected pope on 7 January 1566, he lived as a friar in the Vatican and made the decrees of the Council of Trent his life's work, publishing the Roman Catechism in 1566, the reformed Breviary in 1568, and in 1570 the restored Roman Missal that ordered the Latin liturgy for four centuries.

He excommunicated Elizabeth of England in 1570 and, against the Turks, bound Spain and Venice to the Holy See in the Holy League, whose fleet under Don John of Austria broke Ottoman power at Lepanto on 7 October 1571. Crediting the victory to the Rosary, he founded the feast now kept as Our Lady of the Rosary.

He died worn out by a painful ailment on 1 May 1572, repeating, 'O Lord, increase my sufferings and my patience'. Beatified by Clement X in 1672 and canonized by Clement XI in 1712, he is commemorated on 30 April.
saints.knownFor: Enforcing the Council of Trent and the victory of Lepanto.

sources.text: Butler, Lives of the Saints (1866 ed.), 30 April

saints.name: St. Joseph the Worker
saints.title: Spouse of the Blessed Virgin Mary
saints.shortBlurb: The carpenter of Nazareth, guardian of the Holy Family, whose daily labor sanctifies all honest work…
biography: Joseph of Nazareth, a descendant of David, was the husband of Mary and the foster-father of Jesus. The Gospels call him a 'just man' who obeyed without hesitation each word of the angel: to take Mary as his wife, to flee with her and the child into Egypt, and to return and dwell at Nazareth. Of his own voice Scripture records not a single word.

Matthew's Gospel names his trade tekton — carpenter or craftsman — and in his workshop the child Jesus grew up and learned to work. Joseph appears last at the finding of the twelve-year-old in the Temple; because by ancient tradition he died in the arms of Jesus and Mary, he is invoked as the patron of a happy death.

His cult grew late in the West: the feast of 19 March is attested from the tenth century, and in 1870 Pius IX declared him Patron of the Universal Church. In 1955 Pius XII added the memorial of Saint Joseph the Worker on the first of May — patron of workers for the toil that fed the Holy Family, and of fathers for his guardianship of the Son.
saints.knownFor: The dignity of human labor, sanctified in the carpenter of Nazareth.

saints.name: St. Athanasius
saints.title: Bishop and Doctor of the Church
saints.shortBlurb: The unbending bishop of Alexandria who stood “against the world” for the divinity of Christ through five exiles…
biography: Born at Alexandria about 296, Athanasius became deacon and secretary to Bishop Alexander, whom he accompanied to the Council of Nicaea in 325. There the assembled bishops condemned the teaching of Arius that the Son was a creature, confessing Him instead to be of one being with the Father.

On Alexander's death in 328 Athanasius, barely thirty, was chosen bishop of Alexandria. For forty-five years he defended the Nicene faith, suffering five exiles under four emperors — to Trier, to Rome, and three times into hiding in Egypt — whence the saying Athanasius contra mundum, 'Athanasius against the world'.

In exile and at home he wrote without ceasing: the treatise On the Incarnation, composed in his youth; the Life of Antony, which carried Egyptian monasticism to the West; and the festal letter of 367, the first surviving list of the twenty-seven books of the New Testament.

He died at Alexandria on 2 May 373, and the Council of Constantinople in 381 sealed the faith he had kept. Numbered among the four great Doctors of the Eastern Church, he is honored as patron of theologians, for none labored longer to hand on the apostolic faith entire.
saints.knownFor: His lifelong defense of Christ's divinity against Arianism.

canonization.canonized: Venerated from antiquity; Doctor of the Church

sources.text: Butler, Lives of the Saints (1866 ed.), 2 May

saints.name: Sts. Philip and James
saints.title: Apostles
saints.shortBlurb: Two of the Twelve, joined in a single feast because their relics were together enshrined at Rome…
biography: Philip was a native of Bethsaida in Galilee, the town of Peter and Andrew. Called directly by the Lord, he at once brought Nathanael to Him; it was Philip who reckoned the cost of feeding the five thousand, whom the Greeks approached wishing to see Jesus, and who prayed, 'Lord, show us the Father'.

After Pentecost, tradition sends Philip to Phrygia, where he was crucified at Hierapolis under Domitian. James, the son of Alphaeus, called the Less, governed the church of Jerusalem as its first bishop and wrote the Epistle that bears his name; about the year 62 he was thrown from the pinnacle of the Temple and clubbed to death as he prayed for his murderers.

The relics of the two apostles have rested together in the Roman basilica of the Holy Apostles since the sixth century, whence they share a single feast. Long kept on 1 May, the day of that basilica's dedication, it was moved in 1969 to 3 May, the first of May being given to St. Joseph the Worker.
saints.knownFor: Their apostolic witness to Christ, sealed in martyrdom.

saints.name: St. Florian
saints.title: Martyr
saints.shortBlurb: A Roman officer in Noricum who confessed Christ and was drowned in the Enns during Diocletian's persecution…
biography: Born about 250, Florian rose to high office in the Roman administration of Noricum, in what is now Upper Austria, and dwelt at Aelium Cetium, the modern St. Pölten. When Diocletian's persecution reached the province and the governor Aquilinus imprisoned some forty Christians at Lauriacum, Florian hastened thither to stand with them.

Seized by his former comrades, he professed the faith openly and refused to sacrifice; he was scourged, his shoulders flayed, and condemned to the water. On 4 May 304 a millstone was hung about his neck and he was drowned in the river Enns below Lauriacum, the Lorch of today.

A matron named Valeria is said to have buried his body where the abbey of St. Florian stands near Linz. In the twelfth century portions of his relics were carried to Poland, and he is honored as a patron of that land and of Upper Austria. Because legend tells that he once saved a burning house with one pitcher of water, he is invoked against fire, the patron of firefighters.
saints.knownFor: His steadfast confession under Diocletian and his patronage of firefighters.

sources.text: The Roman Martyrology (1914 English ed.; public domain)

saints.name: St. Hilary of Arles
saints.title: Bishop
saints.shortBlurb: A monk of Lérins raised young to the see of Arles, austere in life and famed for his eloquence…
biography: Born about 401 of a distinguished family in northern Gaul, Hilary seemed marked out for worldly honors when his kinsman Honoratus, founder of the abbey of Lérins, won him to the monastic life. He later told of the struggle between the Lord calling him and the world offering its charms.

When Honoratus, by then bishop of Arles, died in 429, Hilary succeeded him at about twenty-eight and presided over the councils of Orange and Vaison. He lived as a monk on the episcopal throne, going barefoot, working with his hands, and selling the vessels of the Church to ransom captives; his panegyric on his master, the Life of St. Honoratus, survives.

In 444 his zeal outran his jurisdiction: he deposed Chelidonius, bishop of Besançon, though Besançon lay in another province, and Pope Leo the Great reversed the sentence and stripped Hilary of his metropolitan powers. Hilary submitted, kept his see, and died at Arles on 5 May 449, not yet fifty; Leo himself praised his holiness.
saints.knownFor: His ascetic zeal and eloquent preaching as Bishop of Arles.

sources.text: Butler, Lives of the Saints (1866 ed.), 5 May

saints.name: St. Dominic Savio
saints.title: Youth
saints.shortBlurb: A boy of the Oratory under St. John Bosco who resolved to “die rather than sin,” dead before his fifteenth year…
biography: Born on 2 April 1842 at Riva near Turin, the son of a blacksmith and a seamstress, Dominic Savio made his first Communion at seven and at twelve met John Bosco, who received him into the Oratory at Valdocco. The boy resolved at once upon holiness, taking for his motto, 'Death rather than sin'.

At the Oratory he served Mass daily and in 1856 gathered companions into the Sodality of the Immaculate Conception. When two boys who had stuffed the school stove with rubbish threw the blame on him, he bore the punishment in silence rather than accuse them; he is therefore invoked as patron of the falsely accused.

His health, never strong, gave way; sent home to Mondonio and weakened by the bleedings then in fashion, he died on 9 March 1857, not yet fifteen, saying he saw something wonderful. John Bosco wrote his life; Pius X advanced his cause; Pius XII beatified him in 1950 and canonized him in 1954, and the Church has named him patron of young people and of choirboys.
saints.knownFor: Youthful holiness formed under St. John Bosco.

sources.text: Vatican biography, Canonization of St. Dominic Savio (vatican.va)

saints.name: St. John of Beverley
saints.title: Bishop
saints.shortBlurb: The Northumbrian bishop and teacher who ordained the Venerable Bede and ended his days in the monastery he founded…
biography: Born of noble parents at Harpham in Yorkshire, John studied at Canterbury under Archbishop Theodore and the abbot Adrian, then lived for a time among St. Hilda's community at Whitby. Consecrated bishop of Hexham in 687, he won renown as a preacher and teacher, withdrawing for retreat to Erneshow across the Tyne.

Translated to York in 705, he ordained the young Bede first deacon and then priest. Bede repaid his master by recording his miracles in the Ecclesiastical History — among them the dumb youth with a scabbed head, whom John taught to speak and made whole.

About 717 he resigned his see to Wilfrid the Younger and retired to the monastery he had founded at Inderawuda, the wood of the Deiri, later called Beverley. There he died on 7 May 721. His tomb drew pilgrims for centuries; he was canonized by Benedict IX in 1037, and on 25 October, the day of his translation, Henry V won Agincourt and gave the saint the credit.
saints.knownFor: His holy episcopate and the ordination of the Venerable Bede.

sources.text: Butler, Lives of the Saints (1866 ed.), 7 May

saints.name: St. Peter of Tarentaise
saints.title: Archbishop
saints.shortBlurb: A Cistercian monk drawn from his cloister to govern the see of Tarentaise, beloved for his boundless charity…
biography: Born in 1102 at Saint-Maurice near Vienne, Peter became one of the first monks of the Cistercian abbey of Bonnevaux, and in 1132 was sent into Savoy to found Tamié, which he governed as abbot for ten years. In 1142, urged by St. Bernard and the chapter of his order, he was made archbishop of Tarentaise against his will.

He found the diocese in ruin, its churches and tithes seized by laymen, and spent thirteen years restoring it. He rebuilt his cathedral, founded a hospital at Tamié for the sick poor and for strangers, and established the May bread, a distribution of loaves to the poor in the lean weeks before harvest that survived until the Revolution.

He fled in 1155 to a distant house of his order, hoping to live unknown as a lay brother, but was discovered and brought back. He labored for Pope Alexander III against the antipope Victor IV and sought peace between Louis VII of France and Henry II of England; dying at Bellevaux Abbey on that mission in 1174, he was canonized by Celestine III in 1191.
saints.knownFor: His Cistercian sanctity and charity as Archbishop of Tarentaise.

sources.text: Butler, Lives of the Saints (1866 ed.), 8 May

saints.name: St. Pachomius
saints.title: Abbot
saints.shortBlurb: The Egyptian soldier-turned-hermit who gathered the desert solitaries into community and wrote monasticism's first Rule…
biography: Born of pagan parents in the Egyptian Thebaid about 292, Pachomius was conscripted at twenty into the army and held with other recruits at Thebes, where Christians brought the wretched youths food and comfort. Astonished at such charity toward strangers, he prayed to the Christians' God and vowed to serve Him all his days.

Released and baptized about 314, he placed himself under the aged hermit Palemon, from whom he learned the solitary life. About 320 he settled at Tabennisi on the Nile and there gathered his disciples into an ordered community, writing for them a Rule of prayer, labor, and common life — the earliest written rule of monasticism.

The work grew swiftly: before his death Pachomius governed nine monasteries of men and two of women, numbering many thousands of monks. Carried off by an epidemic in 348, he left a pattern that Basil shaped for the East and that Jerome, by translating the Rule into Latin, carried to the West, where it prepared the way for Benedict.
saints.knownFor: Founding cenobitic (communal) monasticism and its first written Rule.

sources.text: The Roman Martyrology (1914 English ed.; public domain)

saints.name: St. Damien of Molokai
saints.title: Priest
saints.shortBlurb: The Belgian missionary who gave his life to the abandoned lepers of Molokai and died one of them…
biography: Jozef De Veuster was born on 3 January 1840 at Tremelo in Belgium, a farmer's son. Entering the Congregation of the Sacred Hearts, he took the name Damien and, when his brother Pamphile fell too ill to sail, volunteered in his place for the Hawaiian mission; ordained at Honolulu in 1864, he labored nine years on the island of Hawaii.

In 1873 Bishop Maigret sought priests for Kalaupapa, the peninsula of Molokai to which the government exiled its lepers. Damien went with three companions and begged to stay when the others were relieved. For sixteen years he was priest, doctor, carpenter, and gravedigger to the outcasts, building houses and churches, dressing ulcers, and shaping coffins with his own hands.

In 1885 he greeted his flock with the words 'We lepers': he had taken the disease. He died at Kalaupapa on 15 April 1889, aged forty-nine, and his body was borne back to Louvain in 1936. Beatified in 1995 and canonized in 2009, he is the patron of lepers and outcasts, for he made himself one of them.
saints.knownFor: A life laid down for the lepers of Molokai.

sources.text: Vatican biography, Canonization of St. Damien de Veuster (vatican.va)

saints.name: St. Mamertus
saints.title: Bishop
saints.shortBlurb: The Bishop of Vienne in Gaul who instituted the Rogation Days of penitential prayer and procession…
biography: Mamertus was archbishop of Vienne in Dauphiné in the fifth century, reckoned the eighteenth bishop of that see; his brother Claudianus, a learned monk, he ordained priest to share his labors. His people were scourged by wars, earthquakes, and fires, while wild beasts prowled even the marketplaces of the city.

When a great fire in Vienne defied all efforts to quench it, it ceased at the bishop's prayers — a deliverance his successor Avitus called miraculous. Taking the calamities as a summons to penance, Mamertus, about 470, appointed three days of fasting, litanies, and processions before the feast of the Ascension.

These were the Rogation Days. The observance spread from Vienne through Gaul — the First Council of Orleans prescribed it in 511 — and about 800 Pope Leo III extended it to Rome and the whole Western Church. Mamertus died about 475; his relics, carried to Orleans in the next century, were destroyed by the Calvinists.
saints.knownFor: Instituting the Rogation Days of prayer and procession.

sources.text: Butler, Lives of the Saints (1866 ed.), 11 May

saints.name: St. Pancras
saints.title: Martyr
saints.shortBlurb: A boy of about fourteen who was beheaded at Rome rather than sacrifice to the gods…
biography: His acts are late and uncertain, but tradition holds that Pancras was born about 289 at Synnada in Phrygia. Orphaned young, he was brought to Rome by his uncle Dionysius, and there both were converted to Christ; the boy is said to have freed his slaves and given largely to the poor.

Under Diocletian, about 304, he was denounced as a Christian; refusing to sacrifice, he was beheaded on the Aurelian Way at about fourteen years of age. A matron named Octavilla took up his body by night, anointed it with balsam, and laid it in her cemetery on the Via Aurelia.

Over his tomb Pope Symmachus raised a basilica about 500, and his cult spread far: Pope Vitalian sent his relics to England, where the first church Augustine built at Canterbury was dedicated to him, and the ancient church of St. Pancras in London has given his name to a district and a railway station. For the steadfastness of his confession he is invoked as patron of fidelity to oaths.
saints.knownFor: His youthful martyrdom at Rome under Diocletian.

sources.text: The Roman Martyrology (1914 English ed.; public domain)

saints.name: Our Lady of Fatima
saints.title: Marian Memorial
saints.shortBlurb: The 1917 apparitions of the Virgin Mary to three shepherd children at Fatima, calling the world to prayer and penance…
biography: On 13 May 1917, while the First World War raged, three shepherd children — Lúcia dos Santos, ten, and her cousins Francisco and Jacinta Marto, nine and seven — were watching their flocks at the Cova da Iria near Fatima in Portugal when a Lady brighter than the sun appeared above a holm oak.

She came again on the thirteenth of each month until October, asking for the daily Rosary, prayer, and penance for the conversion of sinners and the peace of the world, and in July confiding three secrets, among them a vision of hell and the consecration of Russia to her Immaculate Heart.

On 13 October, before some seventy thousand onlookers, the sun seemed to dance and plunge toward the earth — the Miracle of the Sun, reported by the secular press. Francisco and Jacinta died of influenza, in 1919 and 1920, and were canonized at Fatima by Pope Francis in 2017; Lúcia, a Carmelite nun, died in 2005.

The Bishop of Leiria declared the apparitions worthy of belief in 1930. On 13 May 1981, the feast itself, John Paul II was shot; he credited her hand with turning the bullet, which now lies in the crown of her image.
saints.knownFor: The call to prayer, penance, and the Rosary given at Fatima in 1917.

sources.text: Vatican biography, Canonization of the Shepherds of Fatima (vatican.va)

saints.name: St. Matthias
saints.title: Apostle
saints.shortBlurb: Chosen by lot to take the place of Judas among the Twelve, a witness to the Lord from His baptism to the Ascension…
biography: His name, from the Hebrew Mattithiah, means gift of Yahweh. One of the seventy disciples, Matthias had companied with the Lord from His baptism by John to the Ascension, and so Peter, standing among about a hundred and twenty brethren after the Ascension, proposed that one be chosen to take the place of the traitor Judas.

Two were put forward, Joseph called Barsabbas, surnamed Justus, and Matthias; having prayed, they cast lots, and the lot fell on Matthias, who was numbered with the eleven Apostles. Of his later labours Scripture says nothing, and tradition divides: one account sends him first to Judea, then to preach among the peoples of Ethiopia, where he was crucified; another holds that he was stoned at Jerusalem and beheaded.

His relics are said to have been brought to Rome by St. Helena, and a portion is venerated at Trier. Long kept on 24 February, his feast was moved to 14 May in the 1969 revision of the Roman calendar. In art he bears the axe of his martyrdom, under which sign he is patron of carpenters; he is also invoked against alcoholism.
saints.knownFor: Completing the Twelve after the Ascension.

sources.text: Butler, Lives of the Saints (1866 ed.), 24 February

saints.name: St. Isidore the Farmer
saints.title: Layman
saints.shortBlurb: A day-laborer of Madrid who sanctified the plough and the field with unceasing prayer…
biography: Isidore was born about 1070 at Madrid to poor parents, who named him for St. Isidore of Seville. He passed his whole life as a hired labourer on the farm of the landowner Juan de Vargas, who came to make him bailiff of his estate, and tradition tells of angels guiding his plough while he was at Mass.

With his wife, María Torribia — venerated in Spain as María de la Cabeza — he shared his bread with the poor; their only son died young. Isidore died on 15 May 1130, and when his body was exhumed in 1212 it was found incorrupt, whereupon his tomb drew pilgrims and cures.

Beatified by Paul V in 1619, he was canonized by Gregory XV on 12 March 1622 in the same ceremony as Ignatius of Loyola, Francis Xavier, Teresa of Ávila, and Philip Neri. A farmworker who never left his fields, he is patron of Madrid and of farmers; in 1947 the National Catholic Rural Life Conference placed the farmers of the United States under his patronage.
saints.knownFor: Sanctity found in the daily labor of the fields.

sources.text: Butler, Lives of the Saints (1866 ed.), 15 May

saints.name: St. John Nepomucene
saints.title: Priest and Martyr
saints.shortBlurb: The priest of Prague who was drowned in the Vltava, remembered as a martyr of the seal of confession…
biography: John was born about 1345 at Pomuk, since called Nepomuk, in Bohemia. After studies at the University of Prague and in canon law at Padua, he entered the service of the Archbishop of Prague, Jan of Jenštejn, who made him his vicar-general in 1393.

That year King Wenceslaus IV, resolved to seize the rich Benedictine abbey of Kladruby for a favourite, came into open conflict with the archbishop, who had his own candidate confirmed as abbot. John stood with his archbishop; arrested and tortured, on 20 March 1393 he was thrown bound from the Charles Bridge into the Vltava, and his body was buried in St. Vitus Cathedral.

Later tradition made him the queen's confessor, drowned for refusing to betray the seal of confession — a story first told more than half a century after his death, yet one that fixed his fame as a martyr of the confessional. Beatified in 1721 and canonized by Benedict XIII in 1729, he is patron of confessors, of those unjustly slandered, and of bridges and those in danger from water.
saints.knownFor: Dying rather than betray the seal of confession.

sources.text: Butler, Lives of the Saints (1866 ed.), 16 May

saints.name: St. Paschal Baylon
saints.title: Religious
saints.shortBlurb: A Spanish shepherd-boy turned Franciscan lay brother, burning with love for the Blessed Sacrament…
biography: Paschal was born at Torrehermosa in Aragon on 16 May 1540, the feast of Pentecost, for which he was named. From his seventh to his twenty-fourth year he kept sheep in the fields, teaching himself to read so that he might say the Little Office, and sharing his scant dinner with the poor.

In 1564 he was received among the reformed Franciscans as a lay brother, professing the next year at the friary of Orito. Refusing the priesthood, he served as porter, cook, gardener, and gatherer of alms; on a journey through France he defended the Real Presence against Calvinist preachers and barely escaped a Huguenot mob. His nights were often spent kneeling before the Blessed Sacrament.

He died at Villarreal on 17 May 1592 — again Pentecost — while Mass was sung, tradition says, within hearing of his cell. Canonized by Alexander VIII in 1690, he was proclaimed by Leo XIII in 1897 patron of Eucharistic congresses and confraternities, in honour of the devotion that had ruled his life; shepherds also claim him, remembering his boyhood.
saints.knownFor: His ardent devotion to the Blessed Sacrament.

sources.text: Butler, Lives of the Saints (1866 ed.), 17 May

saints.name: Pope St. John I
saints.title: Pope and Martyr
saints.shortBlurb: A pope sent unwillingly on an embassy by an Arian king, who died a prisoner on his return…
biography: A Tuscan, a native of Siena, John was a deacon of the Roman Church when he was elected to the See of Peter on 13 August 523. Italy was then ruled by the Ostrogoth Theodoric, an Arian, and the peace between Ravenna and Constantinople was wearing thin.

When the Emperor Justin I in 523 moved against the Arians of the East, Theodoric compelled the frail pope to head an embassy to Constantinople demanding their relief, threatening reprisals against the Catholics of Italy. John was the first pope to journey to the imperial city; Justin received him honourably, granting all, save that those who had passed from Arianism to the Catholic faith should not be forced back.

On his return Theodoric, suspecting him of collusion with the emperor, cast him into prison at Ravenna, where he died of neglect and ill usage on 18 May 526. His body was carried to Rome and buried in St. Peter's, and he has been venerated as a martyr ever since; the king himself died within the year.
saints.knownFor: His witness unto death amid the Arian conflict.

sources.text: The Roman Martyrology (1914 English ed.; public domain)

saints.name: St. Dunstan
saints.title: Bishop
saints.shortBlurb: The Abbot of Glastonbury and Archbishop of Canterbury who revived English monastic life in the tenth century…
biography: Dunstan was born about 909 at Baltonsborough, near Glastonbury, and schooled by the Irish monks who kept cells among the old abbey's ruins. He served at the court of King Æthelstan until rivals drove him out, then took the monastic habit and lived as a hermit at Glastonbury, working as a silversmith, scribe, and harpist.

King Edmund made him Abbot of Glastonbury about 943, and there he restored the Rule of St. Benedict, the seed of an English monastic revival. Exiled by the young King Eadwig, he spent two years at Mont Blandin near Ghent, where he saw the Cluniac observance at first hand; recalled by Edgar in 957, he was made Bishop of Worcester and of London, and in 959 Archbishop of Canterbury.

With Æthelwold of Winchester and Oswald of Worcester he reformed the English Church, planting monks in the cathedrals and founding monasteries; in 973 he crowned Edgar at Bath with a rite that underlies the English coronation service to this day. He died at Canterbury on 19 May 988. Because he had wrought church plate with his own hands he is patron of goldsmiths and smiths; as a harpist, of musicians.
saints.knownFor: The revival of English monastic life as Archbishop of Canterbury.

sources.text: Butler, Lives of the Saints (1866 ed.), 19 May

saints.name: St. Bernardine of Siena
saints.title: Priest
saints.shortBlurb: The Franciscan preacher who carried the Holy Name of Jesus across Italy on his famous tablet…
biography: Bernardino degli Albizzeschi was born of a noble Sienese family at Massa Marittima on 8 September 1380 and orphaned at six. When plague struck Siena in 1400 he took charge of the hospital of Santa Maria della Scala for four months; in 1402 he entered the Observant Franciscans and was ordained priest in 1404.

For more than thirty years he travelled Italy on foot, drawing crowds so great that pulpits were set up in the marketplaces, preaching against usury, faction, and gambling until his hearers burned cards and dice in bonfires of the vanities. Above all he spread devotion to the Holy Name of Jesus, holding up a tablet bearing the monogram IHS on a blazing sun to displace the badges of the factions.

Summoned to Rome in 1426 to answer for this devotion, he was acquitted and preached there daily for eighty days. He refused the bishoprics of Siena, Ferrara, and Urbino, and as vicar-general from 1438 raised the Observants from 130 friars to over 4,000. He died at L'Aquila on 20 May 1444 and was canonized by Nicholas V in 1450. From his emblem comes his patronage of advertisers.
saints.knownFor: Preaching the Holy Name of Jesus across Italy.

sources.text: Butler, Lives of the Saints (1866 ed.), 20 May

saints.name: St. Christopher Magallanes and Companions
saints.title: Priests and Martyrs
saints.shortBlurb: A Mexican parish priest and his fellow martyrs, killed in the persecution of the Church during the Cristero years…
biography: Cristóbal Magallanes Jara was born to farming parents at San Rafael, Totatiche, in Jalisco on 30 July 1869, and worked as a shepherd before entering the seminary of Guadalajara. Ordained in 1899, he was made parish priest of his native Totatiche, where he founded schools and carpentry shops and gave himself to the evangelization of the Huichol people.

When the government closed the seminary of Guadalajara, he opened a clandestine house of studies, the Auxiliary Seminary of Totatiche, in 1915. Though he wrote and preached against armed rebellion, he was accused of fomenting the Cristero rising; arrested on 21 May 1927 while on his way to celebrate Mass, he was shot without trial at Colotlán four days later, with the young priest Agustín Caloca, prefect of his seminary.

He gave his few possessions to his executioners, absolved them, and declared: 'I die innocent, and ask God that my blood may serve to unite my Mexican brethren.' Beatified in 1992, he was canonized by John Paul II on 21 May 2000 with twenty-four companions, priests and laymen martyred in the persecution of the Church in Mexico between 1915 and 1937.
saints.knownFor: Faithful priests martyred in Mexico's persecution of the Church.

sources.text: Vatican biography, Canonization of St. Cristóbal Magallanes and Companions (vatican.va)

saints.name: St. Rita of Cascia
saints.title: Religious
saints.shortBlurb: The wife, mother, and widow who became an Augustinian nun, honored as the saint of impossible causes…
biography: Margherita Lotti — Rita — was born in 1381 at Roccaporena, a hamlet of Cascia in Umbria, to parents honoured as peacemakers. Given in marriage young to Paolo Mancini, a man of violent temper, she bore him eighteen years of patience and two sons. When he was murdered in a feud, she forgave his killers at his funeral; her sons, bent on vengeance, died of dysentery within the year.

Thrice refused by the Augustinian nuns of Cascia, who dreaded the feud her name carried, she was admitted on one condition: that she reconcile the families. She made peace where men had failed, and at thirty-six entered, to live forty years in prayer and penance. Meditating before the crucifix when about sixty, she received on her forehead a wound as from a thorn of Christ's crown.

She died at Cascia on 22 May 1457. A cousin who asked what she wished from her old home was sent, in January, for a rose, and found one blooming in the snow. Canonized by Leo XIII on 24 May 1900, she was named Patroness of Impossible Causes, for the hopeless knots her own life had untangled; her body rests incorrupt at Cascia.
saints.knownFor: Patient endurance and intercession in impossible causes.

sources.text: Butler, Lives of the Saints (1866 ed.), 22 May

saints.name: St. John Baptist de Rossi
saints.title: Priest
saints.shortBlurb: A Roman priest who gave himself wholly to the poor, the sick, and the outcasts of the city…
biography: Giovanni Battista de' Rossi was born on 22 February 1698 at Voltaggio, in the Genoese territory, the last of four children of poor but pious parents. Brought to Rome in 1711, he studied under the Jesuits of the Collegium Romanum and the Dominicans of the Minerva. Epilepsy, which first struck him then, dogged him all his life, and he was ordained on 8 March 1721 only by special dispensation.

He gave himself to the neglected of Rome: he founded a hospice for homeless women near San Galla, and sought out prisoners, the sick, and the carters and herdsmen who came in from the Campagna. Canon of Santa Maria in Cosmedin from 1737, he sold his cousin's fine house and gave the money to the poor.

Long afraid to hear confessions lest a seizure interrupt them, he became one of the most sought-after confessors in Rome, called a second Philip Neri, and Clement XII freed him from choir duties for the confessional's sake. Worn out by labour and by strokes, he died on 23 May 1764. He was beatified by Pius IX in 1860 and canonized by Leo XIII on 8 December 1881.
saints.knownFor: His tireless ministry to Rome's poor and in the confessional.

sources.text: Catholic Encyclopedia (1913), “St. John Baptist de Rossi”
Butler, Lives of the Saints (1866 ed.), 23 May

saints.name: St. Vincent of Lérins
saints.title: Monk
saints.shortBlurb: The monk of Lérins who gave the Church its enduring test of authentic tradition…
biography: Vincent was born at Toulouse to a noble family and is thought to have been the brother of St. Lupus, Bishop of Troyes. After a secular, perhaps military, career he withdrew to the island monastery of Lérins, off the southern coast of Gaul, which then drew the best minds of the West.

There, about 434, three years after the Council of Ephesus, he wrote under the name Peregrinus the Commonitorium, a brief guide for discerning true Catholic doctrine from heresy. His rule was that the faith be proved by antiquity, universality, and consent — that we hold what has been believed everywhere, always, and by all, quod ubique, quod semper, quod ab omnibus creditum est.

This Vincentian Canon has served theologians ever since as a test of authentic tradition. Himself wary of novelty, Vincent stood apart from Augustine's teaching on predestination, for which some later writers suspected him of semi-Pelagian leanings; he had also defended the title Mother of God against Nestorius. He died at Lérins before the year 450, and his feast is kept on 24 May.
saints.knownFor: The rule for discerning authentic Catholic teaching — held everywhere, always, by all.

sources.text: Butler, Lives of the Saints (1866 ed.), 24 May

saints.name: St. Bede the Venerable
saints.title: Priest and Doctor of the Church
saints.shortBlurb: The monk of Jarrow whose history first told the story of the English Church, the “Father of English History”…
biography: Bede was born about 673 on the lands of Wearmouth monastery in Northumbria, and at seven was given by his kinsfolk to Abbot Benedict Biscop, and afterwards to Ceolfrith of Jarrow. In that twin monastery he passed his whole life, as he wrote, amid the observance of the Rule and the daily singing of the Church, delighting to learn, to teach, or to write.

Ordained deacon at nineteen and priest at thirty by St. John of Beverley, he poured out commentaries on Scripture and treatises on chronology and the natural order. His crown is the Ecclesiastical History of the English People, finished in 731, which gathered ancient documents, the traditions of elders, and his own knowledge into the chief source for the conversion of England, whence he is called the Father of English History.

Dying on the vigil of the Ascension, 26 May 735, he dictated an English rendering of St. John's Gospel; when the boy Wilbert wrote the last sentence, Bede answered, 'It is finished,' and breathed his last singing the Glory be. Within two generations he was styled Venerable; Leo XIII declared him Doctor of the Church in 1899, and he is patron of historians and scholars.
saints.knownFor: His Ecclesiastical History of the English People.

canonization.canonized: Venerated from antiquity; Doctor of the Church (1899)

sources.text: Butler, Lives of the Saints (1866 ed.), 27 May

saints.name: St. Philip Neri
saints.title: Priest
saints.shortBlurb: The joyful “Apostle of Rome” and founder of the Oratory, who won souls through cheerfulness and charity…
biography: Born at Florence in 1515, Philip was educated by the Dominicans of San Marco. Sent at eighteen to a rich uncle at San Germano to learn trade, he underwent a sudden conversion, and in 1533 went to Rome, where for seventeen years he lived as a layman, nursing the sick and speaking of God with workmen in the streets.

In 1548 he founded the Confraternity of the Most Holy Trinity of Pilgrims and Convalescents, and in 1551 was ordained priest, dwelling at San Girolamo della Carita. His evening gatherings of prayer, readings, and song, for which Palestrina composed music and from which the oratorio takes its name, grew into the Congregation of the Oratory, approved by Pope Gregory XIII in 1575 at Santa Maria in Vallicella, the Chiesa Nuova.

Cheerful, blunt, and tender with penitents, he became so beloved in the city that he was called the Apostle of Rome. He died on 26 May 1595 and was canonized by Pope Gregory XV in 1622 on the same day as Ignatius of Loyola, Francis Xavier, Teresa of Avila, and Isidore the Farmer. Because of his unfailing gaiety in holiness, he is honoured as a patron of joy.
saints.knownFor: The joyful Apostle of Rome and founder of the Oratory.

sources.text: Butler, Lives of the Saints (1866 ed.), 26 May

saints.name: St. Augustine of Canterbury
saints.title: Bishop
saints.shortBlurb: The Roman monk sent by Pope Gregory the Great to convert the English, and first Archbishop of Canterbury…
biography: Prior of St. Andrew's monastery on the Caelian Hill in Rome, Augustine was chosen by Pope Gregory the Great in 595 to lead a band of monks to the English. They landed on the Isle of Thanet in Kent in 597 and were received by King Ethelbert, whose Frankish wife Bertha was already a Christian.

Ethelbert was baptized, and at Christmas in 597 thousands of his people followed him. Consecrated bishop at Arles, Augustine fixed his see at Canterbury, built the cathedral of Christ Church, and founded outside the walls the monastery of Sts. Peter and Paul, later called St. Augustine's Abbey. Reinforcements sent by Gregory in 601 let him set up further sees at London and Rochester in 604.

His attempts to bring the old British Christians into Roman observance failed, but the see he planted endured. He died about the year 604 and was buried in the monastery he had founded. As the first Archbishop of Canterbury and leader of Gregory's mission, he is venerated as the Apostle of the English and a patron of England.
saints.knownFor: The conversion of the English and the founding of the see of Canterbury.

sources.text: Butler, Lives of the Saints (1866 ed.), 26 May

saints.name: St. Bernard of Menthon
saints.title: Priest
saints.shortBlurb: The archdeacon of Aosta who built the Alpine hospices that sheltered travelers for a thousand years…
biography: Born in 923, by tradition at the castle of Menthon near Annecy in Savoy, Bernard refused an arranged marriage and became a priest under Peter, archdeacon of Aosta, whose office he later inherited. For forty-two years he preached through the mountain villages, his charge including the care of the poor and of travellers.

The passes toward Italy were deadly with snow, cold, and robbers. For the safety of pilgrims and merchants he founded a hostel and a community of canons at the summit of the pass that came to bear his name, the Great St. Bernard, nearly 8,000 feet above the sea, and later a second on the Little St. Bernard. The rescue dogs of the hospice grew famous only in later centuries.

He died at Novara in 1008 and was canonized by Pope Innocent XI in 1681. In 1923 Pope Pius XI confirmed him patron of the Alps; and because his hospices guarded those who climb, ski, or journey in high mountains, he is invoked as patron of mountaineers and of all who travel the heights.
saints.knownFor: The Alpine hospices that sheltered travelers for centuries.

canonization.canonized: Venerated from antiquity; named patron of Alpinists in 1923 by Pope Pius XI

sources.text: Butler, Lives of the Saints (1866 ed.), 28 May

saints.name: St. Paul VI
saints.title: Pope
saints.shortBlurb: The pope who carried the Second Vatican Council to its close and steered the Church through its reforms…
biography: Giovanni Battista Montini was born at Concesio, near Brescia, in 1897. Ordained in 1920, he served more than thirty years in the Secretariat of State and was among the closest advisers of Pope Pius XII, who named him Archbishop of Milan in 1954. Created a cardinal in 1958, he was elected pope in 1963 and took the name Paul VI.

He reconvened the Second Vatican Council and brought it to its close on 8 December 1965, then gave his pontificate to carrying out its reforms. The first pope of modern times to journey abroad, he embraced the Patriarch Athenagoras in the Holy Land in 1964, addressed the United Nations in New York in 1965, and travelled widely in Asia, Africa, and the Americas.

His 1968 encyclical Humanae Vitae, reaffirming the Church's teaching on married love, cost him much sympathy, yet he bore opposition with patience. He died at Castel Gandolfo on 6 August 1978 and was canonized by Pope Francis on 14 October 2018.
saints.knownFor: Guiding the Church through the close of the Second Vatican Council.

sources.text: Vatican biography, Canonization of St. Paul VI (vatican.va)

saints.name: St. Joan of Arc
saints.title: Virgin
saints.shortBlurb: The peasant girl who, led by heavenly voices, lifted the siege of Orléans and died at the stake at nineteen…
biography: Born about 1412 at Domrémy on the borders of Lorraine, the daughter of peasants, Joan never learned to read or write. From the age of thirteen she heard the voices of Sts. Michael, Catherine, and Margaret, who bade her go to the aid of the dauphin Charles and drive the English from France.

In 1429, after winning over the captain at Vaucouleurs and then the dauphin himself at Chinon, she led a relief army into besieged Orléans; the English raised the siege nine days after her arrival. The victory at Patay opened the road to Reims, where Charles VII was crowned in July 1429 with Joan standing by the altar.

Captured by the Burgundians at Compiègne in May 1430 and sold to the English, she was tried for heresy at Rouen under Pierre Cauchon, Bishop of Beauvais, and burned in the marketplace on 30 May 1431, about nineteen years old. A retrial quashed the sentence in 1456. Canonized in 1920 by Pope Benedict XV, the maiden-soldier who kept faith to the pyre is a patron of France and of soldiers.
saints.knownFor: The Maid of Orléans who freed France and died at the stake.

sources.text: Butler, Lives of the Saints (1866 ed.), 30 May

saints.name: The Visitation of the Blessed Virgin Mary
saints.title: Feast of the Blessed Virgin Mary
saints.shortBlurb: Mary's journey to her cousin Elizabeth, where the unborn John leapt for joy and the Magnificat was sung…
biography: St. Luke records that after the Annunciation Mary went with haste into the hill country, to a city of Juda, where her kinswoman Elizabeth was six months with child. At Mary's greeting the unborn John leapt in his mother's womb, and Elizabeth, filled with the Holy Ghost, cried out, 'Blessed art thou among women, and blessed is the fruit of thy womb' (Luke 1:39-45).

Mary answered with the Magnificat, 'My soul doth magnify the Lord', the hymn the Church sings daily at Vespers; and she stayed about three months before returning home. The meeting is honoured as the second Joyful Mystery of the Rosary.

The feast was first kept among the Franciscans in 1263; in 1389 Pope Urban VI, at the urging of John of Jenstein, Archbishop of Prague, set it in the Roman calendar for 2 July, hoping to end the Great Western Schism. The 1969 calendar reform moved it to 31 May, between the Annunciation, 25 March, and the Nativity of St. John the Baptist, 24 June.
saints.knownFor: Mary's visit to Elizabeth and the song of the Magnificat.

sources.text: Catholic Encyclopedia (1913), “Feast of the Visitation of the Blessed Virgin Mary”

saints.name: St. Justin Martyr
saints.title: Martyr
saints.shortBlurb: A philosopher who found in Christ the true wisdom he had long sought, and sealed his teaching with his blood…
biography: Born of pagan parents about the year 100 at Flavia Neapolis, the ancient Shechem, in Samaria, Justin passed through the schools of the Stoics, Peripatetics, Pythagoreans, and Platonists in search of truth. A talk with an old man by the sea, and the sight of the constancy of the martyrs, brought him to the prophets and to Christ about the year 130.

Still wearing the philosopher's cloak, he taught at Rome that the Gospel is the one sure philosophy, and that whatever was true in Plato belonged to the Christians. His two Apologies, addressed to the emperors Antoninus Pius and Marcus Aurelius, and his Dialogue with Trypho the Jew, are the earliest reasoned defences of the faith and preserve precious accounts of early Christian worship.

Denounced as a Christian, he was examined by the prefect Rusticus and, refusing to sacrifice, was scourged and beheaded at Rome about 165 with six companions. Because he sought wisdom in the pagan schools and found it fulfilled in Christ, he is honoured as the patron of philosophers and apologists.
saints.knownFor: His Apologies defending the faith to the pagan world.

sources.text: The Roman Martyrology (1914 English ed.; public domain)

saints.name: Sts. Marcellinus and Peter
saints.title: Martyrs
saints.shortBlurb: A Roman priest and an exorcist who died together under Diocletian and are still named in the Canon of the Mass…
biography: Marcellinus, a priest, and Peter, an exorcist, suffered at Rome in the persecution of Diocletian in the year 304. Pope St. Damasus, who as a boy had heard their story from the executioner himself, records that they were led to a thicket three miles from the city so that their bodies might not be found, and that they joyfully cleared the briars from the place where they were to die.

Beheaded and buried on the spot, they were found by two devout women, Lucilla and Firmina, who laid them in the catacombs on the Via Labicana that still bear their names, at the place called Ad Duas Lauros. Damasus adorned their tomb with a metrical epitaph, and Constantine built a basilica over it, near which his mother St. Helena was later buried.

Their feast was kept on 2 June from the earliest sacramentaries, and their names passed into the Canon of the Roman Mass, where they are still invoked today in the prayer Nobis quoque peccatoribus, among the martyrs and saints of the Roman Church.
saints.knownFor: Their witness under Diocletian; named in the Roman Canon.

sources.text: The Roman Martyrology (1914 English ed.; public domain)

saints.name: St. Charles Lwanga and Companions
saints.title: Martyrs
saints.shortBlurb: The young royal pages of Buganda who chose death by fire rather than betray their baptism…
biography: Charles Lwanga was born about 1860 in the kingdom of Buganda, in present-day Uganda, and rose to be chief of the royal pages at the court of King Mwanga II. In 1885 the king had the Anglican bishop James Hannington killed, then beheaded Joseph Mukasa, the Catholic catechist who reproached him; Charles and about a hundred catechumens sought baptism from the White Fathers, Charles himself on 15 November.

In May 1886 Mwanga, enraged that his pages would neither renounce their faith nor yield to his immoral demands, condemned the Christians to death. Charles secretly baptized the boys still unbaptized, among them the youngest, Kizito; on the march to the execution ground at Namugongo, three of the company were killed.

On 3 June 1886 Charles was burned alive apart from the rest, and twelve more Catholics, together with nine Anglicans, perished in the flames, while others died by the club or in the later persecution. Twenty-two Catholic martyrs of Uganda were canonized by Pope Paul VI on 18 October 1964, the first canonized martyrs of modern Africa, honoured as patrons of converts and of African youth.
saints.knownFor: The first canonized martyrs of sub-Saharan Africa.

sources.text: Vatican biography, Canonization of St. Charles Lwanga and Companions (vatican.va)

saints.name: St. Francis Caracciolo
saints.title: Priest and Founder
saints.shortBlurb: An Italian nobleman who founded a religious order devoted above all to the Blessed Sacrament…
biography: Born Ascanio Caracciolo at Villa Santa Maria in the Abruzzi in 1563, he was cured of a sickness thought mortal after vowing his life to God, and went to Naples to study for the priesthood, where he took the name Francis in a confraternity serving condemned prisoners. A letter of John Augustine Adorno, delivered to him by mistake, he read as God's call to found a new order.

The Clerics Regular Minor, approved by Pope Sixtus V in 1588, added to the three usual vows a fourth: never to seek any dignity or office. Their life joined works of charity with perpetual adoration of the Blessed Sacrament day and night. Superior general from 1593, after Adorno's death, Francis begged in the streets for the poor, spent hours before the tabernacle, and refused a bishopric from Pope Paul V.

In 1608 he went to Agnone to open a new house, pausing to pray the night at the Holy House of Loreto, and died there of a fever on 4 June. Canonized by Pope Pius VII in 1807, he rests at Naples, which chose him in 1838 as one of her patrons.
saints.knownFor: Founding the Clerks Regular Minor and Eucharistic devotion.

sources.text: The Roman Martyrology (1914 English ed.; public domain)

saints.name: St. Boniface
saints.title: Bishop and Martyr
saints.shortBlurb: The English monk who became the apostle of Germany, felled the sacred oak of Thor, and died a martyr in Frisia…
biography: Born Wynfreth in Devon about 675 and trained in the monasteries of Exeter and Nursling, he went to Rome in 719, where Pope Gregory II gave him the name Boniface and sent him as missionary bishop to the Germans. Consecrated in 722, he preached in Hesse and Thuringia under the protection of Charles Martel.

At Geismar near Fritzlar he felled the sacred oak of Thor, and when no thunderbolt struck him down, the people asked for baptism; of its wood he built a chapel. Raised to archbishop in 732 and given the see of Mainz in 745, he organized the German Church, reformed the Frankish clergy in synods, and saw his disciple Sturm found the abbey of Fulda.

In old age he resigned his see to finish his first mission among the Frisians. As he waited near Dokkum to confirm a company of converts, a band of heathen robbers fell on the camp and killed him with fifty-two companions on 5 June 754. His body rests at Fulda, and the Apostle of the Germans is honoured as patron of Germany, whose Church he planted.
saints.knownFor: Evangelizing and organizing the Church in Germany.

sources.text: Butler, Lives of the Saints (1866 ed.), 5 June

saints.name: St. Norbert
saints.title: Bishop and Founder
saints.shortBlurb: A worldly cleric converted by a brush with death, who became a great preacher and founded the Premonstratensians…
biography: Born at Xanten on the Rhine about 1080, of a noble family, Norbert held a canonry and a post as almoner at the court of the Emperor Henry V, living for pleasure. Thrown from his horse when lightning struck beside him in 1115, he took the shock as God's summons, resigned his benefices, gave his goods to the poor, and was ordained priest.

As a wandering preacher of penance he won followers and enemies alike. At the wish of Pope Calixtus II he settled his disciples in a valley near Laon called Prémontré, where on Christmas Day 1120 he founded a community of canons under the Rule of St. Augustine, the Premonstratensians. At Antwerp he confuted the errors of Tanchelm, who denied the Real Presence, leaving the city fervent in Eucharistic devotion.

In 1126 he was made Archbishop of Magdeburg against his will, and his reforms of a lax clergy were answered with plots against his life. He died at Magdeburg on 6 June 1134 and was canonized by Pope Gregory XIII in 1582. His relics were carried in 1627 to Strahov Abbey in Prague, where they rest still; hence he is honoured as a patron of Bohemia.
saints.knownFor: Founding the Premonstratensian canons; devotion to the Eucharist.

sources.text: Butler, Lives of the Saints (1866 ed.), 6 June

saints.name: St. Robert of Newminster
saints.title: Abbot
saints.shortBlurb: An English Cistercian abbot of gentle rule and great austerity, friend of the hermit St. Godric…
biography: Born at Gargrave in Yorkshire about 1100, Robert is said to have studied at Paris before serving as rector of his native village, and then entered the Benedictine abbey of Saint Mary in York. In 1132 he was among the monks expelled from York who, on land given by Archbishop Thurstan, founded Fountains Abbey in the valley of the Skell, which soon joined the Cistercian reform.

About 1138 he led a colony from Fountains into Northumberland, where Ranulf de Merlay and his wife Juliana gave land near Morpeth for a new house. As first abbot of Newminster he ruled for twenty-one years, and from it sent out monks to found Pipewell in 1143, Roche in 1147, and Sawley in 1148.

Remembered for austerity, gentleness, and a gift of prophecy, he was the close friend of the hermit Godric of Finchale, who is said to have seen Robert's soul carried up to heaven on the night of his death. Robert died at Newminster on 7 June 1159, and his tomb in the abbey church became a place of pilgrimage.
saints.knownFor: First abbot of Newminster; Cistercian holiness.

sources.text: Butler, Lives of the Saints (1866 ed.), 7 June
The Roman Martyrology (1914 English ed.; public domain)

saints.name: St. Medard
saints.title: Bishop
saints.shortBlurb: One of the most beloved bishops of ancient Gaul, remembered for his charity and long woven into French folklore…
biography: Born at Salency in Picardy about 456, of a Frankish father and a Gallo-Roman mother, Medard was ordained priest about 489 and consecrated bishop of Vermand in 530; his twin brother Gildard became bishop of Rouen. Amid the disorders of the age he transferred his see to Noyon, and from 532 he also governed the church of Tournai.

Famed for his charity, he gave the religious veil to Radegund, the queen who had fled her husband King Clotaire, and by tradition he founded at Salency the festival of the Rosière, at which the worthiest maiden of the parish was crowned each year. Legend tells that an eagle once spread its wings over him to shelter him from a storm.

He died at Noyon about 545, and his relics were later translated to Crouy, near Soissons, where the abbey of Saint-Médard arose. The tale of the sheltering eagle made him a master of rain in French lore: rain on his feast, 8 June, is said to mean forty days more, a saying like that of Swithin in England.
saints.knownFor: His charity as a bishop of ancient Gaul.

sources.text: Butler, Lives of the Saints (1866 ed.), 8 June

saints.name: St. Ephrem the Syrian
saints.title: Deacon and Doctor of the Church
saints.shortBlurb: The “Harp of the Holy Spirit,” whose hymns taught the faith and adorned the worship of the Syriac Church…
biography: Born at Nisibis in Roman Mesopotamia about 306, Ephrem was baptized young and served his church as deacon and teacher under Bishop Jacob. He lived through three Persian sieges of his city, and when the Emperor Jovian ceded Nisibis to Persia in 363 he went into exile with its Christian people, settling at Edessa.

There he taught in the famous school and poured out hymns, verse homilies, and commentaries in Syriac, defending the Nicene faith against Arians, Marcionites, Manichees, and the followers of Bardaisan. His teaching hymns were sung by choirs of women in the churches; more than four hundred survive, besides his commentary on the Diatessaron.

For the sweetness of that song he was called the Harp of the Spirit, and the Syriac Church reveres him as its greatest father. In 370 he visited Basil at Caesarea. Worn out by ministry to the famine-stricken and sick of Edessa, he died there in 373; Benedict XV declared him a Doctor of the Church in 1920.
saints.knownFor: His hymns and the title “Harp of the Holy Spirit.”

canonization.canonized: Venerated from antiquity; declared a Doctor of the Church in 1920

sources.text: The Roman Martyrology (1914 English ed.; public domain)

saints.name: St. Landericus of Paris
saints.title: Bishop
saints.shortBlurb: The bishop of Paris who founded the city's first hospital out of love for the poor…
biography: Landericus, in French Landry, was chief clerk of the royal chancery before he succeeded Audobertus as bishop of Paris in 650. When famine struck in 650 and 651 he sold all that he had, and even the plate and sacred vessels of his church, to buy bread for the poor.

He built the first hospital of Paris, a house for the sick poor dedicated to the martyr Christopher, which grew into the Hôtel-Dieu that stood for centuries beside Notre-Dame. He is also credited with raising the first church of Saint-Germain-l'Auxerrois, afterward the parish of the kings of France.

In 653 he was among the bishops who subscribed the charter of Clovis II exempting the abbey of Saint-Denis from episcopal jurisdiction. He died about 660 and was buried at Saint-Germain-l'Auxerrois; in 1408 two of his bones were given to the neighboring parish of Saint-Landry, near the house where he had been wont to pray, and Paris honours him as the father of its hospitals.
saints.knownFor: Founding the Hôtel-Dieu, the first hospital of Paris.

sources.text: Butler, Lives of the Saints (1866 ed.), 10 June
The Roman Martyrology (1914 English ed.; public domain)

saints.name: St. Barnabas
saints.title: Apostle
saints.shortBlurb: The “son of encouragement,” a Levite of Cyprus who vouched for Paul and carried the Gospel to the Gentiles…
biography: A Levite of Cyprus named Joseph, he sold a field and laid the price at the apostles' feet, and they surnamed him Barnabas, 'son of encouragement' (Acts 4:36-37). When the Church at Jerusalem still feared the newly converted Paul, it was Barnabas who vouched for him and brought him to the apostles.

Sent to Antioch, he fetched Paul from Tarsus, and they taught there a year. Set apart by the Spirit, they made the first missionary journey through Cyprus and Asia Minor; at Lystra the crowds took Barnabas for Zeus, and Acts calls him an apostle (14:14). Present with Paul at the Council of Jerusalem, he later parted from him over John Mark and sailed with Mark for Cyprus.

Tradition holds that he was stoned to death at Salamis in his native island and is honoured as the founder of the Church of Cyprus. His name and his reconciling of Paul with the apostles have made him a patron of peacemakers; he is likewise the patron of Cyprus and is invoked against hailstorms.
saints.knownFor: Encouraging the young Church and befriending St. Paul.

sources.text: Butler, Lives of the Saints (1866 ed.), 11 June

saints.name: St. John of Sahagún
saints.title: Priest
saints.shortBlurb: An Augustinian friar and fearless preacher who made peace in the feuding city of Salamanca…
biography: Born at Sahagún in the kingdom of León in 1419, John González de Castrillo was educated by the Benedictines of his native town and then by Alfonso de Cartagena, bishop of Burgos, who ordained him priest in 1445 and made him a canon of his cathedral. Scrupulous over the holding of many benefices, John resigned all but one poor chaplaincy and went to Salamanca to study theology.

A grave illness there moved him to vow the religious life; in 1463 he entered the Hermits of St. Augustine, making profession the next year, and rose to be master of novices and, in 1471, prior. Devoted above all to the Eucharist, he became the most powerful preacher in that university city.

He scourged without fear the feuds of Salamanca's noble factions and the vices of the great, and his preaching reconciled the blood-divided city, which honours him as its patron. He died on 11 June 1479 — later lives say poisoned by a woman whose paramour he had converted — and Alexander VIII canonized him in 1690.
saints.knownFor: Preaching peace to feuding Salamanca.

sources.text: Butler, Lives of the Saints (1866 ed.), 12 June

saints.name: St. Anthony of Padua
saints.title: Priest and Doctor of the Church
saints.shortBlurb: A Portuguese Franciscan of dazzling preaching and learning, invoked the world over for the finding of what is lost…
biography: Born Fernando Martins de Bulhões at Lisbon in 1195, Anthony entered the Augustinian canons at fifteen and was ordained priest at Coimbra. Moved by the relics of five Franciscans martyred in Morocco, he joined the Friars Minor in 1220, taking his new name from their chapel of Anthony the Great, and sailed for Morocco, only to be driven by illness and storm back to Italy.

His gifts lay hidden until an impromptu sermon at Forlì in 1222 revealed a preacher of rare power. Francis of Assisi himself entrusted to him the theological training of the friars — the order's first lector — and he taught at Bologna, Montpellier, and Toulouse, preached against heresy in France and Italy, and served as provincial of northern Italy.

He died at Arcella, on the road to Padua, on 13 June 1231, aged thirty-five, and Gregory IX canonized him at Spoleto the following May; Pius XII named him a Doctor of the Church in 1946. Because a novice who stole his annotated psalter was moved by his prayer to return it, he is invoked the world over for the finding of lost things.
saints.knownFor: His preaching and learning; patron of lost things.

canonization.canonized: 1232 by Pope Gregory IX; Doctor of the Church (1946)

sources.text: Butler, Lives of the Saints (1866 ed.), 13 June

saints.name: St. Methodius I of Constantinople
saints.title: Patriarch
saints.shortBlurb: The patriarch who saw the final restoration of the holy images after long years of iconoclasm…
biography: Born of wealthy parents at Syracuse about the year 800, Methodius was sent to Constantinople for a court career but became a monk, and then abbot, in Bithynia. When the iconoclast persecution revived under Leo the Armenian, he went to Rome in 815 as envoy of the deposed Patriarch Nicephorus.

On his return in 821 he was exiled by Michael II; under Theophilus he was imprisoned again for his defense of the holy images, and escaping, was hidden by friends until the emperor's death in 842. The next year the Empress Theodora, regent for her young son Michael III, deposed the iconoclast patriarch John and raised Methodius to the throne of Constantinople.

On 11 March 843, after a synod had confirmed the ancient teaching, he led the empress and the people in procession from Blachernae to Hagia Sophia to restore the images — the Triumph of Orthodoxy, kept ever since in the East on the first Sunday of Lent. He governed mildly toward reconciled iconoclasts and died on 14 June 847.
saints.knownFor: The restoration of sacred images in 843.

sources.text: The Roman Martyrology (1914 English ed.; public domain)

saints.name: St. Vitus
saints.title: Martyr
saints.shortBlurb: A boy martyr of the early Church, one of the Fourteen Holy Helpers invoked in sickness…
biography: According to his legend, Vitus was the young son of a pagan senator of Sicily, secretly brought to the faith by his tutor Modestus and his nurse Crescentia. Fleeing his father's anger, the three came to Lucania and there died of their tortures in the persecution of Diocletian, about the year 303, Vitus being yet a boy.

Their cult is ancient: the fifth-century Martyrology of Jerome joins their names in Sicily, and Gregory the Great speaks of a monastery of Vitus there. In 836 some of his relics were carried from Saint-Denis to the abbey of Corvey in Saxony, whence his devotion spread through Germany; in 925 King Henry I gave relics of Vitus to Wenceslaus of Bohemia, still enshrined in Prague's cathedral of St. Vitus.

Numbered among the Fourteen Holy Helpers, he is invoked against epilepsy and against the nervous disorder that bears his name: for on his feast the Germans danced before his statue, whence he became the patron of dancers, and the dancing sickness came to be called St. Vitus's Dance.
saints.knownFor: One of the Fourteen Holy Helpers; patron of dancers.

sources.text: The Roman Martyrology (1914 English ed.; public domain)

saints.name: St. John Francis Regis
saints.title: Priest
saints.shortBlurb: A tireless Jesuit missionary of the French mountains, apostle of the poor and of the forsaken…
biography: Born at Fontcouverte in Languedoc on 31 January 1597, John Francis Regis entered the Jesuit novitiate at Toulouse in 1616 and was ordained priest in 1630. After first labors among the plague-stricken of Toulouse and the poor and Huguenots of Montpellier, he was sent in 1633, at the bishop's invitation, into the mountain diocese of Viviers.

Until his death he evangelized more than fifty districts of the Vivarais, Forez, and Velay, tramping through the snow to remote villages, catechizing children, reconciling sinners, and converting many Huguenots. He founded the Confraternity of the Blessed Sacrament to collect bread and alms for the poor, and opened refuges where fallen women learned lacemaking — whence he is honoured as the patron of lacemakers.

He longed for the missions of Canada but spent himself for France. Worn out by a winter journey, he died of pneumonia at Lalouvesc on the last day of 1640, aged forty-three; Clement XII canonized him in 1737, and his shrine at Lalouvesc remains a place of pilgrimage.
saints.knownFor: His missions among the poor of the French highlands.

sources.text: The Roman Martyrology (1914 English ed.; public domain)

saints.name: St. Botulph
saints.title: Abbot
saints.shortBlurb: An English abbot whose name lives on in the town of Boston, “Botolph's town”…
biography: Born of noble Saxon parents in the early seventh century, Botulph, or Botolph, was educated with his brother Adulph under Fursey at Cnobheresburg and became a Benedictine on the Continent. Returning to England, he found favour with a king of the southern Angles, who granted him a tract of desolate land on which to build a monastery.

The Anglo-Saxon Chronicle records under the year 654 that 'Botolph began to build the church at Ikanho.' His monastery of Icanho — 'ox hill,' identified with Iken in Suffolk — drew many disciples, and the biographer of Ceolfrith, writing in Bede's day, remembers him as a man of remarkable life and learning. He died about 680 and was buried at his own foundation.

In 970 his relics were moved inland for fear of the Danes, and in time they rested at Thorney Abbey. More than sixty ancient English churches bear his name, four of them at the gates of London, where travelers prayed for a safe journey — whence he is the patron of travelers. Boston, 'Botolph's town,' keeps his name in two hemispheres.
saints.knownFor: Founding the abbey of Icanho; patron of travelers.

sources.text: Butler, Lives of the Saints (1866 ed.), 17 June
The Roman Martyrology (1914 English ed.; public domain)

saints.name: Sts. Mark and Marcellian
saints.title: Martyrs
saints.shortBlurb: Twin brothers of Rome strengthened in their last trial by the encouragement of St. Sebastian…
biography: Their legend makes Mark and Marcellian twin brothers of a distinguished Roman house and deacons of the Church, arrested under Diocletian about the year 286. When their pagan parents Tranquillinus and Martia came to the prison pleading with them to yield, Sebastian exhorted the brothers to constancy — and won the wavering parents themselves to Christ.

The same acts tell how the prefect Chromatius and his household were converted at that time, and how the brothers, hidden by the Christian officer Castulus, were betrayed by the apostate Torquatus and seized again. Condemned by the new prefect, they were hung head downward from pillars with nails through their feet, and after hanging thus for a full day were dispatched with lances.

They were buried on 18 June in the cemetery of Balbina on the Via Ardeatina, and their bodies were later translated to the church of Santi Cosma e Damiano, where they were found again in 1583. Their names stood in the Roman calendar for 18 June from before the Tridentine reform; removed in 1969, they remain in the Roman Martyrology.
saints.knownFor: Their steadfast martyrdom at Rome.

sources.text: The Roman Martyrology (1914 English ed.; public domain)

saints.name: St. Romuald
saints.title: Abbot
saints.shortBlurb: A nobleman of Ravenna who became a hermit and founded the Camaldolese, wedding the monastic and eremitic life…
biography: Born about 951 at Ravenna into the ducal house of the Onesti, Romuald was about twenty when he saw his father Sergius kill a kinsman in a duel over property. In penance he fled to the Benedictine abbey of San Apollinare in Classe, and after three years, finding its observance too mild, placed himself under a hermit named Marinus near Venice.

About 978 he persuaded Peter Orseolo, the doge of Venice, to resign his office in repentance, and followed him to the abbey of Cuxa in the Pyrenees, living as a hermit nearby. Back in Italy he spent some four decades wandering the peninsula, reforming monasteries and planting or renewing colonies of hermits, Val di Castro, Fonte Avellana, and Sitria among them.

About 1012, in the Casentino hills above Arezzo, a nobleman named Maldolus gave him the estate where he built Camaldoli, the field of Maldolus, whence the name, joining a hermitage of solitary cells to a monastery of the common life. From this wedding of the two ways grew the Camaldolese Benedictines. Romuald died at Val di Castro on 19 June 1027.
saints.knownFor: Founding the Camaldolese Benedictines.

sources.text: The Roman Martyrology (1914 English ed.; public domain)

saints.name: Pope St. Silverius
saints.title: Pope and Martyr
saints.shortBlurb: A pope deposed and exiled for refusing to restore a heretic, who died in banishment for the faith…
biography: Born at Frosinone, the son of Pope Hormisdas before the latter entered the clergy, Silverius was still a subdeacon when the Gothic king Theodahad thrust him into the papal chair; he was consecrated on 8 June 536. His brief pontificate fell amid Justinian's war to wrest Italy from the Goths.

When the general Belisarius entered Rome in December 536, the Empress Theodora demanded that the pope restore Anthimus, the Monophysite patriarch of Constantinople deposed under his predecessor. Silverius refused to reinstate a condemned heretic. Charged then with plotting to surrender the city to the Goths, he was summoned to the Pincian palace in March 537, stripped of the pallium, clothed in a monk's habit, and pronounced deposed.

He was banished first to Patara in Lycia, whose bishop moved Justinian to order his return for a just hearing; but Vigilius, the deacon who had supplanted him by Theodora's favor, shipped him instead to the barren island of Palmarola, where he died of hardship before the close of 537. The Church has honored him from antiquity as a martyr for the faith.
saints.knownFor: Suffering exile rather than betray the faith.

sources.text: The Roman Martyrology (1914 English ed.; public domain)

saints.name: St. Aloysius Gonzaga
saints.title: Religious
saints.shortBlurb: A young prince who renounced a marquisate for the Society of Jesus and died nursing the plague-stricken…
biography: Born on 9 March 1568 at Castiglione delle Stiviere in the duchy of Mantua, Aloysius was heir to his father's marquisate and was bred for arms; at five he delighted his father by marching at a military camp at the head of a platoon. Yet the boy turned early to prayer, receiving his first Communion from Charles Borromeo in 1580.

His father raged, but in November 1585 Aloysius renounced his inheritance in favor of his brother Rodolfo and entered the Society of Jesus at Rome on the twenty-fifth of that month, with Robert Bellarmine as his confessor. His purity, obedience, and penance were the admiration of the novitiate.

When plague struck Rome in 1591 he nursed the sick in the Jesuit hospital, carrying the dying in from the streets, caught the contagion, and died on 21 June 1591, aged twenty-three. Canonized by Benedict XIII in 1726 and declared by him in 1729 patron of youth and students, he is the Church's model for the young: innocence kept amid courts, a life given in charity.
saints.knownFor: His purity and self-sacrifice; patron of youth.

sources.text: Butler, Lives of the Saints (1866 ed.), 21 June

saints.name: St. Paulinus of Nola
saints.title: Bishop
saints.shortBlurb: A Roman senator and poet who gave away his wealth to serve Christ and the tomb of St. Felix…
biography: Born about 354 at Bordeaux into a senatorial family with estates across Gaul, Spain, and Italy, Pontius Meropius Paulinus was schooled by the poet Ausonius and rose to be suffect consul about 377 and governor of Campania, where he first honored the martyr Felix of Nola, building a road and a hospice for pilgrims to his tomb.

After the Emperor Gratian's murder in 383 he withdrew from public life, married Therasia of Barcelona, and was baptized by Delphinus of Bordeaux. When their only child died eight days after birth, the pair renounced their fortune. Ordained priest at Barcelona about 394, he settled the next year at Nola beside Felix's tomb, restoring its basilicas and honoring the saint's feast each year with a new poem.

After Therasia's death he was chosen bishop of Nola about 409 and governed some twenty years, corresponding with Augustine, Jerome, and Sulpicius Severus; Augustine sent him his works to be copied in Italy. He died on 22 June 431. Later ages credited him with the first church bells, whence the old bell-names nola and campana.
saints.knownFor: His poetry and his renunciation of wealth for Christ.

sources.text: Butler, Lives of the Saints (1866 ed.), 22 June

saints.name: St. Etheldreda
saints.title: Abbess
saints.shortBlurb: An East Anglian princess who kept her vow of virginity through two marriages and founded the abbey of Ely…
