She bore the future emperor Constantine at Naissus about 272, and was put away when his father Constantius rose in the empire and took a wife of higher rank.

Her son's victory restored her: she returned to court, was named Augusta in 324, and embraced the Christian faith with an ardor her rank let her spend freely. About 326 she journeyed to the Holy Land, where she raised the Church of the Nativity at Bethlehem and that of the Ascension on the Mount of Olives.

Writers of the late fourth century, Rufinus and Ambrose among them, credit her with finding the True Cross near the Lord's tomb, three crosses lying hidden there. She died about 330 with her son at her side and was buried in her mausoleum on the Via Labicana. For her excavations at the holy places she is invoked by archaeologists, and for her late conversion, by converts.
saints.knownFor: Her pilgrimage and the tradition of finding the True Cross.

saints.name: St. John Eudes
saints.title: Priest
saints.shortBlurb: A French missionary priest who spread devotion to the Sacred Hearts of Jesus and Mary…
biography: Born at Ri in Normandy on 14 November 1601, John Eudes joined the Oratory in 1623 and was ordained in 1625. He won fame as a mission preacher — Jean-Jacques Olier called him the prodigy of his age — and during the plagues of 1627 and 1631 ministered to the stricken, lodging in a cask in an open field to spare his brethren.

Grieved by the plight of penitent women, he founded at Caen in 1641 the Order of Our Lady of Charity to shelter them, and in 1643 he left the Oratory to found the Congregation of Jesus and Mary, the Eudists, for the forming of priests in seminaries and the preaching of missions.

Above all he gave the Church the liturgical worship of the Hearts of Jesus and Mary, composing their Mass and Office; the feast of the Heart of Mary was kept from 1648, that of the Sacred Heart of Jesus from 1672. He died at Caen on 19 August 1680; Leo XIII later named him author of the liturgical worship of the Sacred Hearts.
saints.knownFor: Promoting devotion to the Sacred Hearts and founding the Eudists.

saints.name: St. Bernard of Clairvaux
saints.title: Abbot and Doctor of the Church
saints.shortBlurb: The great Cistercian abbot and preacher whose eloquence and sanctity swayed the whole of Christendom…
biography: Born in 1090 at Fontaine-lès-Dijon of Burgundian nobility, Bernard in 1113 led some thirty companions, his brothers among them, into the reformed monastery of Cîteaux. Two years later he was sent as abbot to found Clairvaux, which under his rule sent out more than sixty daughter houses, and at Troyes in 1128 he shaped the Rule of the new Knights Templar.

The cloister could not hold him. When a double election split the papacy in 1130, Bernard judged for Innocent II and wore down the backers of Anacletus until the schism died with its claimant in 1138; in 1141 he worsted Abelard at the Council of Sens; and in 1146, at Vézelay before King Louis VII, he preached the Second Crusade at the bidding of Eugene III, once his own monk.

His eighty-six Sermons on the Song of Songs and treatises such as On Loving God and On Consideration won him the name of Mellifluous, honey-flowing, Doctor, and so he is counted patron of beekeepers. He died at Clairvaux on 20 August 1153, was canonized by Alexander III in 1174, and was declared a Doctor of the Church in 1830.
saints.knownFor: His preaching, mystical writing, and leadership of the Cistercians.

canonization.canonized: 1174 by Pope Alexander III; Doctor of the Church (1830)

saints.name: St. Pius X
saints.title: Pope
saints.shortBlurb: A pope of humble birth who took as his motto to restore all things in Christ…
biography: Giuseppe Melchiorre Sarto was born on 2 June 1835 at Riese in the Veneto, then under Austria, the second of ten children of the village postman. Ordained in 1858, he rose slowly — chancellor of Treviso, bishop of Mantua in 1884, cardinal and Patriarch of Venice in 1893 — and was elected pope on 4 August 1903 after Austria's veto had broken Cardinal Rampolla's candidacy.

Taking as his motto 'To restore all things in Christ,' he restored Gregorian chant by the motu proprio Tra le sollecitudini (1903), urged frequent Communion, admitted children of the age of reason to the Eucharist by Quam singulari (1910), ordered catechism teaching in every parish (Acerbo nimis, 1905), set in motion the first Code of Canon Law, and reorganized the Curia in 1908.

Against the errors he named Modernism, the synthesis of all heresies, he published the decree Lamentabili and the encyclical Pascendi in 1907. He died on 20 August 1914, as the First World War broke over Europe, and was canonized by Pius XII in 1954, the first pope so honored in more than two centuries. It is for those decrees that catechists and first communicants claim him as patron.
saints.knownFor: Promoting frequent Communion and defending the faith against Modernism.

sources.text: Vatican biography, Canonization of St. Pius X (vatican.va)

saints.name: The Queenship of the Blessed Virgin Mary
saints.title: Memorial of Our Lady
saints.shortBlurb: The Church's celebration of Mary as Queen of heaven and earth, reigning beside her Son…
biography: That Mary reigns as Queen beside her Son the King is a confession far older than its feast. Ephrem the Syrian saluted her as Queen in the fourth century, the title grew common from the sixth, and the Middle Ages sang it in the Salve Regina and the litanies that name her Queen of angels, of patriarchs, of all saints.

The ground of the title is her divine motherhood, vindicated at Ephesus in 431: the mother of the King is queen mother of his kingdom, reigning by grace, as Pius XII taught, where her Son reigns by nature; the rosary keeps her crowning as the last of its Glorious Mysteries.

Pius XII gave the devotion its own feast by the encyclical Ad Caeli Reginam of 11 October 1954, fixing it on 31 May. Paul VI moved it in 1969 to 22 August, the octave day of the Assumption, so that her crowning is kept as the fruit of her being taken up to her Son — the Queen of the universe of the Second Vatican Council.
saints.knownFor: Honoring Mary as Queen alongside her Son the King.

sources.text: Pius XII, Encyclical Ad Caeli Reginam (1954, vatican.va)

saints.name: St. Rose of Lima
saints.title: Virgin
saints.shortBlurb: The first canonized saint of the Americas, a Dominican tertiary of Lima given to penance and prayer…
biography: Isabel Flores de Oliva was born at Lima on 20 April 1586, one of eleven children of a Spanish soldier and a criolla mother, and was nicknamed Rose from infancy, a servant having seen her face flower into a rose. Confirmed in 1597 by Archbishop Toribio de Mogrovejo, himself later a saint, she took Rosa as her name.

Taking Catherine of Siena for her pattern, she fasted three days a week and, to turn away suitors drawn by her beauty, cropped her hair and roughened her face with pepper. Her father forbidding the convent, she became a Dominican tertiary in her twentieth year, vowed virginity, and lived as a recluse in a garden hermitage, earning the family's bread by needlework and the sale of her flowers.

She gathered the sick and the destitute into her room to nurse them, slept but two hours a night to give the rest to prayer, and is said to have foretold the day of her death. She died on 24 August 1617, aged thirty-one, and in 1671 Clement X canonized her as the first saint born in the Americas, declaring her patroness of the Americas, the Philippines, and the Indies.
saints.knownFor: Being the first canonized saint of the Americas.

saints.name: St. Bartholomew
saints.title: Apostle
saints.shortBlurb: One of the Twelve, often identified with Nathanael, “an Israelite in whom there is no guile,” martyred for the faith…
biography: Bartholomew — the name is Aramaic for 'son of Tolmai' — is named among the Twelve in all four apostolic lists, and from the early centuries he has been commonly identified with Nathanael of Cana, the disciple whom Philip brought to Jesus and of whom the Lord said, 'Behold an Israelite indeed, in whom there is no guile.'

Of his later ministry Scripture says nothing. Eusebius preserves the tradition that he carried the Gospel to India, where he left a copy of the Gospel of Matthew; other ancient accounts send him to Mesopotamia, and finally to Armenia with the apostle Jude Thaddeus — the two are honoured there as the nation's first evangelists.

Tradition places his martyrdom at Albanopolis in Armenia, where he is said to have been flayed alive and then beheaded. His relics were translated to Benevento in 838 and in part to the Roman church of San Bartolomeo all'Isola in 983. Because he was flayed, he is the patron of tanners, leather-workers, and bookbinders, and his emblem in art is the flaying knife.
saints.knownFor: Preaching the Gospel to the point of martyrdom.

sources.text: Butler, Lives of the Saints (1866 ed.), 24 August

saints.name: St. Louis IX
saints.title: King of France
saints.shortBlurb: The crusader king of France whose justice and charity made him the model of a Christian ruler…
biography: Born at Poissy in 1214, Louis was twelve when the death of his father Louis VIII brought him to the throne, crowned at Reims under the regency of his mother, Blanche of Castile. In 1234 he married Margaret of Provence, who bore him eleven children.

He governed with rare devotion to justice, hearing the pleas of the humble in person, reforming the royal officers by the great ordinance of 1254, and forbidding the judicial duel in his courts. To house the Crown of Thorns, bought from the Latin emperor of Constantinople, he built the Sainte-Chapelle in Paris, consecrated in 1248.

He fed the poor at his own table, founded the hospital of the Quinze-Vingts for the blind, and was a Franciscan tertiary. Taking the cross after a grave illness, he sailed in 1248, took Damietta, and was captured with his army in Egypt in 1250; ransomed, he spent four more years strengthening the fortresses of the Holy Land.

On a second crusade he died of dysentery before Tunis on 25 August 1270. Canonized by Boniface VIII in 1297, the only king of France so honoured, he is patron of France and, as a tertiary, of the Secular Franciscan Order.
saints.knownFor: Ruling France with justice and dying on crusade.

saints.name: St. Zephyrinus
saints.title: Pope
saints.shortBlurb: A pope of the early third century who guided the Roman Church through fierce doctrinal storms…
biography: A Roman by birth, Zephyrinus was bishop of Rome from 199 to 217, through the persecution of Septimius Severus, whose edict of 202 forbade conversion to Christianity under the severest penalties. He leaned heavily on his deacon Callixtus, whom he set over the public cemetery on the Appian Way that still bears that deacon's name; Callixtus would succeed him as pope.

His pontificate was tried by the Adoptionist sect of Theodotus the Tanner, condemned by his predecessor, and by the Monarchians, who so pressed the unity of God that they denied the distinction of Persons in the Trinity. A writer quoted by Eusebius honours him as a defender of the divinity of Christ; the scholar Hippolytus, in his Philosophumena, denounced him as an ignorant man governed by Callixtus.

He died on 20 December 217 and was buried in his own cemetery near that of Callixtus on the Appian Way. Long venerated as a martyr, his feast of 26 August was removed from the general calendar in 1969, for he had died a natural death; the Roman Martyrology now keeps his memory on 20 December.
saints.knownFor: Guiding the Roman Church amid early Trinitarian controversies.

saints.name: St. Monica
saints.title: Widow
saints.shortBlurb: The mother of St. Augustine, whose tears and prayers over many years won her son to Christ…
biography: Born about 331 at Thagaste in Numidia, of Berber stock, Monica was married to Patricius, a pagan town official of violent temper and loose life, whom she bore with patience and finally won to baptism before his death. Among their children was Augustine, who as a student at Carthage fell into Manichaeism and broke her heart.

For some seventeen years she prayed and wept for his conversion. When a bishop, wearied by her entreaties, answered her, 'the child of those tears shall never perish,' she received the words as an oracle. She followed Augustine from Africa to Rome and on to Milan, where through the ministry of St. Ambrose he was converted and baptized at Easter 387.

At Ostia, awaiting the voyage home, mother and son were lifted together at a window into a foretaste of heaven, as the Confessions records. There she died in that same year 387, asking only to be remembered at the altar. Her relics were brought to Rome in 1430 and rest in the church of Sant'Agostino; the long-suffering wife and importunate mother is honoured as patron of wives and mothers.
saints.knownFor: Her persevering prayer for her son's conversion.

sources.text: Butler, Lives of the Saints (1866 ed.), 4 May

saints.name: St. Augustine of Hippo
saints.title: Bishop and Doctor of the Church
saints.shortBlurb: Bishop of Hippo and the West’s greatest theologian, whose restless heart found rest in God at last and left the Church the Confessions and the City of God…
biography: Born in 354 at Thagaste in Numidia to a pagan father and the Christian Monica, Augustine studied rhetoric and was fired with the love of wisdom by Cicero's Hortensius, yet spent nine years among the Manichaeans. Teaching at Carthage, Rome, and Milan, he heard Ambrose preach, and in a garden at Milan the child's cry of 'tolle, lege' brought him at last to surrender.

Baptized by Ambrose at the Easter Vigil of 387, he returned to Africa after Monica's death at Ostia, was ordained in 391, and made bishop of Hippo in 396. From that small see he fought Manichaeans, Donatists, and Pelagians for thirty-four years.

His Confessions laid his restless heart before God; his City of God, begun after the sack of Rome in 410, set the passing city of man against the city that endures. His books, letters, and sermons made him the master of Western theology, and for his doctrine of grace he is called the Doctor of Grace.
He died on 28 August 430 as the Vandals besieged Hippo, and was named a Doctor of the Church in 1298. The patron of theologians, he taught the West that the heart is restless until it rests in God.
saints.knownFor: The Confessions; the doctrine of grace; the City of God.

canonization.canonized: Pre-Congregation; declared a Doctor of the Church in 1298 by Pope Boniface VIII

sources.text: Butler, Lives of the Saints (1866 ed.), 28 August

saints.name: The Passion of St. John the Baptist
saints.title: Prophet and Forerunner
saints.shortBlurb: The commemoration of the beheading of the Forerunner, who died for rebuking a king's sin…
biography: This memorial keeps the martyrdom of John the Baptist, the Forerunner who prepared the way of the Lord and baptized him in the Jordan. John had openly rebuked Herod Antipas, tetrarch of Galilee, for putting away his lawful wife and taking Herodias, the wife of his brother Philip; for this the tetrarch threw him into prison.

At Herod's birthday feast, the Gospel relates, the daughter of Herodias — Salome, Josephus names her — so pleased the company with her dancing that the king swore to give her whatever she asked, even to half his kingdom. At her mother's prompting she demanded the head of John the Baptist on a platter; and Herod, sorry yet ashamed before his guests, sent and had him beheaded in the prison, about the year 28 or 29.

The Jewish historian Josephus confirms the substance, placing the imprisonment and death at the fortress of Machaerus and adding that many Jews judged Herod's later defeat a punishment for the deed. John's disciples buried him at Sebaste in Samaria, where his tomb was venerated by the fourth century, and the day was long associated with the dedication of the basilica built over it.
saints.knownFor: Dying a martyr for the truth as the forerunner of Christ.

saints.name: Sts. Felix and Adauctus
saints.title: Martyrs
saints.shortBlurb: A Roman priest and an unknown bystander who joined him in confessing Christ unto death…
biography: Felix was a priest of Rome, martyred about the year 303 in the Great Persecution of Diocletian. Tradition relates that, condemned for refusing to sacrifice to the gods, he was led out to execution, and that a stranger in the crowd, moved by his constancy, stepped forward and openly declared himself a Christian.

The nameless man was seized and beheaded together with Felix; and because his name was never known, the faithful called him Adauctus, Latin for 'the added one' — added to Felix in martyrdom. The two have been honoured in one memory ever since, and are named in the most ancient sacramentaries and martyrologies.

They were buried in the catacomb of Commodilla on the Via Ostiensis, near the basilica of St. Paul Outside the Walls, where Pope Damasus honoured them with an inscription and a church rose over their graves. Their relics were afterward carried north: some to the abbey of Eschau in Alsace about 850, others to St. Stephen's Cathedral in Vienna in 1361.
saints.knownFor: A martyrdom shared by a priest and an unnamed convert.

sources.text: The Roman Martyrology (1914 English ed.; public domain), 30 August

saints.name: St. Raymond Nonnatus
saints.title: Mercedarian Priest
saints.shortBlurb: A Mercedarian friar who spent himself ransoming Christian captives from slavery, even offering his own body as pledge…
biography: Born in 1204 at Portell in Catalonia, Raymond was taken living from the womb of his dead mother — whence his byname Nonnatus, 'not born.' Drawn to religion, he joined at Barcelona the young Order of Our Lady of Mercy, founded by St. Peter Nolasco to ransom Christians enslaved by the Moors, and was ordained priest in 1222.

As the order's ransomer he redeemed captives in Spain and North Africa — by its tradition, 140 at Valencia and 250 at Algiers — and at Tunis, when his money ran out, he gave himself as hostage for twenty-eight prisoners, keeping the order's fourth vow. Legend tells that his captors bored his lips with a hot iron and padlocked his mouth to silence his preaching.

Ransomed by his brethren, he returned to Spain in 1239; tradition makes Pope Gregory IX name him a cardinal, a dignity modern historians doubt. He died at Cardona on 31 August 1240, and in 1657 Alexander VII placed his name in the Roman Martyrology. Because of the manner of his birth he is invoked by women in labour, and the padlock of his legend has made him a patron of the falsely accused.
saints.knownFor: Ransoming captives and offering himself in their place.

saints.name: St. Giles
saints.title: Abbot and Hermit
saints.shortBlurb: A hermit of the forests near the Rhône whose solitary holiness drew a monastery and the veneration of all Christendom…
biography: Giles — in Latin Aegidius — was a hermit of the seventh century in the wild country between Nîmes and the mouth of the Rhône. His legend, first written down centuries later, makes him an Athenian of royal blood who sailed west and withdrew into the forest, where a hind sustained him with her milk.

The king's hunters — the legend names the Visigoth Wamba — pursued the deer to his hermitage, and the arrow loosed at the beast struck Giles instead. In reparation the king founded the monastery of Saint-Gilles-du-Gard, over which the hermit ruled as abbot until his death about 710; because he bore that wound in his own flesh he became the patron of the disabled.

The town that grew around his abbey became one of the great pilgrimage stations on the road to Compostela, and his cult spread across medieval Europe. Counted among the Fourteen Holy Helpers — the only one of them who was not a martyr — he was invoked in time of plague; his relics, hidden at Toulouse in 1562 to escape the Huguenots, were restored to Saint-Gilles in 1862.
saints.knownFor: His life of hermit solitude and the great pilgrim abbey that bears his name.

sources.text: Butler, Lives of the Saints (1866 ed.), 1 September

saints.name: The Martyrs of September
saints.title: Martyrs of the French Revolution
saints.shortBlurb: The bishops, priests, and religious slaughtered in the Paris prisons for refusing the revolutionary oath against the Church…
biography: When the Revolution imposed the Civil Constitution of the Clergy in 1790 and exacted an oath to uphold it, nearly every bishop and about half the clergy of France refused, unwilling to break communion with Rome. After the monarchy fell in August 1792 the non-juring priests were ordered to leave the country within a fortnight on pain of deportation, and many who remained were shut in improvised prisons.

On the afternoon of 2 September 1792 the killers came to the Carmelite convent in the Rue de Vaugirard, where priests were confined. Called one by one before a makeshift tribunal, they were cut down in the garden as they refused the oath; ninety-five died there, among them Jean-Marie du Lau, Archbishop of Arles, the brothers La Rochefoucauld of Beauvais and Saintes, and the De La Salle brother Solomon Leclercq.

More died at the Abbaye, the seminary of Saint-Firmin, and La Force, one hundred and ninety-one in all, three bishops with priests, deacons, and religious. Pius XI beatified them together on 17 October 1926, and Leclercq was canonized in 2016. For their witness unto death they are invoked as patrons of persecuted clergy.
saints.knownFor: Dying rather than swear the oath that would have severed them from the Church.

sources.text: Vatican, Beatification of the Martyrs of Paris of September 1792 (vatican.va)

saints.name: St. Gregory the Great
saints.title: Pope and Doctor of the Church
saints.shortBlurb: The Roman prefect turned monk who as pope styled himself "servant of the servants of God" and shepherded the Church through a broken age…
biography: Born about 540 of a Roman senatorial family, Gregory became prefect of the city, then gave his wealth to found monasteries and made his father's palace on the Caelian Hill the monastery of St. Andrew, where he lived as a monk. He served later as deacon and as papal envoy at Constantinople, where he began his Moralia on Job.

In 590, when Pelagius II died of the plague, clergy and people chose him pope, and he was consecrated on 3 September. He fed the starving city from the Church's estates, made treaties with the Lombards, and in 596 sent Augustine and his monks to convert the English.

His Pastoral Rule formed bishops for centuries, his Dialogues preserved the memory of St. Benedict, and the chant of the Roman Church bears his name. When the Patriarch of Constantinople claimed the title ecumenical, he answered by taking the style 'servant of the servants of God,' which the popes bear still.

Worn out by gout and labor, he died on 12 March 604 and was buried in St. Peter's. One of the four great Latin Doctors, he is patron of musicians for his chant and of teachers for his school of pastoral writings.
saints.knownFor: The mission to the English and his reform of the Church's liturgy and pastoral life.

canonization.canonized: Venerated from antiquity; Doctor of the Church

sources.text: Catholic Encyclopedia (1913), "Pope St. Gregory I (the Great)"
Butler, Lives of the Saints (1866 ed.), 3 September

saints.name: St. Rosalia of Palermo
saints.title: Virgin and Hermit
saints.shortBlurb: The noblewoman who fled the world to live and die in a mountain cave, and whose rediscovered relics were credited with lifting a plague…
biography: Rosalia was born about 1130 into the Norman nobility of Sicily. Tradition makes her a maiden of the court of King Roger II who fled the world for solitude, first in a grotto on Monte Quisquina, then in a cave on Monte Pellegrino above Palermo, where she died about 1160; the inscription found on the cave wall names her a daughter of Sinibald, lord of Quisquina and delle Rose.

Her memory was all but lost for centuries. Then in 1624, as plague ravaged Palermo, tradition holds that she appeared to a sick woman and to a hunter, revealing where her bones lay and bidding that they be carried through the city. Found in the grotto as she had said, the relics were borne in procession around Palermo, and the pestilence ceased.

A sanctuary rose in the cave of the discovery, Pope Urban VIII entered her name in the Roman Martyrology, and Rosalia — la Santuzza, the little saint, as Palermo calls her — was hailed as the city's principal patroness. Her summer festino remains the great festival of Palermo, and she is invoked against plague and epidemics.
saints.knownFor: Her hidden life of penance and the deliverance of Palermo from plague.

saints.name: St. Teresa of Calcutta
saints.title: Religious and Foundress
saints.shortBlurb: The little Albanian sister who left the classroom for the slums of Calcutta and made the dying poor her whole life…
biography: Born Anjezë Gonxhe Bojaxhiu at Skopje on 26 August 1910, of Albanian stock, she joined the Sisters of Loreto in Ireland at eighteen and was sent to India in 1929, taking her name from Thérèse of Lisieux. For nearly twenty years she taught at the Loreto school in Entally, Calcutta.

On 10 September 1946, on the train to Darjeeling, she received what she called a 'call within a call' — to leave the convent and serve the poorest of the poor while living among them. In 1948 she put on the white blue-bordered sari and went into the slums; in 1950 her Missionaries of Charity were approved.

The congregation added to the usual vows a fourth: wholehearted free service to the poorest of the poor. In 1952 she opened the Kalighat Home for the Dying, that the abandoned might die with dignity; the work spread worldwide, and in 1979 she received the Nobel Peace Prize.

She died at Calcutta on 5 September 1997 and was given a state funeral by India. Her letters revealed some fifty years of interior darkness borne in faith. Beatified by John Paul II in 2003, she was canonized by Pope Francis on 4 September 2016.
saints.knownFor: Serving Christ in the poorest of the poor through the Missionaries of Charity.

sources.text: Vatican biography, Canonization of St. Teresa of Calcutta (vatican.va)

saints.name: St. Magnus of Füssen
saints.title: Abbot
saints.shortBlurb: The monk of St. Gall who carried the Gospel into the wild valleys of the Allgäu and founded the abbey of Füssen…
biography: Magnus — in German Mang — is honoured as the Apostle of the Allgäu, the Alpine foothills of southern Bavaria. Almost everything told of him comes from a late and tangled Life; on the soundest reading he laboured in the eighth century under Wikterp, bishop of Augsburg, who entrusted to him the evangelizing of the eastern Allgäu.

With the priest Theodo he founded at Kempten the region's first monastery; then, pressing on alone across the Lech at a ford still called St. Mangstritt, Magnus's step, he built a cell at Füssen on the old Roman road, the Via Claudia Augusta. There a monastery grew under his rule and found favour with King Pepin.

He died at Füssen and was buried in the church he had built; his relics were solemnly raised in 851. Long venerated as the patron of the Allgäu, of Füssen, and of Kempten, he is invoked for the protection of cattle and crops against snakes, mice, and the insects that blight the fields.
saints.knownFor: The evangelization of the Allgäu and the founding of Füssen abbey.

sources.text: The Roman Martyrology (1914 English ed.; public domain), 6 September

saints.name: St. Cloud
saints.title: Priest and Hermit
saints.shortBlurb: A Frankish prince who escaped his brothers' murder, renounced a crown, and chose the poverty of a priest and hermit…
biography: Clodoald, called Cloud, was born in 522, the son of Chlodomer, king of Orléans, and a grandson of Clovis and St. Clotilde. When Chlodomer fell in battle against the Burgundians in 524, the boy's uncles Childebert and Clotaire murdered his brothers Theodoald and Gunthar to seize their inheritance; Cloud alone escaped, carried to safety by loyal men.

Renouncing every claim to the throne, he cut off his long hair, the mark of Frankish royalty, and became a disciple of the hermit Severinus at the gates of Paris. In 551 Eusebius, bishop of Paris, ordained him priest, and afterward he withdrew to a hill above the Seine at Novigentum, where he built a church in honour of St. Martin and gathered a monastery.

He died there on 7 September 560, aged thirty-eight; Gregory of Tours, our earliest witness, says only that, despising an earthly kingdom, he became a cleric and died a priest. The village took the name Saint-Cloud from his tomb. By a play on his name — clou being French for nail — he is invoked as the patron of nail-makers.
saints.knownFor: Trading his royal inheritance for the life of a hermit and priest.

saints.name: The Nativity of the Blessed Virgin Mary
saints.title: Feast of Our Lady's Birth
saints.shortBlurb: The Church keeps the birthday of the Mother of God, dawn of the salvation promised to the world…
biography: Scripture does not record Mary's birth; the earliest account is the second-century Protoevangelium of James, which names her parents Joachim and Anne, an aged and childless couple to whom a daughter was promised. Tradition places her birth at Jerusalem, where a fifth-century basilica rose by the Sheep Pool on the supposed site of her parents' house.

The feast began in the East: a hymn for it survives from the sixth century, when, after the Council of Ephesus in 431 exalted the Mother of God, her cult flourished in Syria and Palestine. Its liturgical keeping is tied to the dedication of that Jerusalem basilica, and, carried to Rome by Eastern monks, it was celebrated there by the end of the seventh century.

Kept on 8 September, nine months after the Immaculate Conception, her nativity is hailed as the dawn before the rising of the Sun of Justice. Only three birthdays stand on the Church's calendar — Christ's, John the Baptist's, and Mary's; for the rest of the saints the Church keeps not the day of birth but the day of death, their birth into heaven.
saints.knownFor: The birth of the Mother of God, herald of the world's salvation.

sources.text: Catholic Encyclopedia (1913), "Nativity of the Blessed Virgin Mary"

saints.name: St. Peter Claver
saints.title: Priest
saints.shortBlurb: A Spanish Jesuit at Cartagena who called himself “the slave of the slaves” and served the Africans of the slave ships…
biography: Born at Verdu in Catalonia in 1581, Peter Claver studied at the University of Barcelona and entered the Jesuit novitiate at Tarragona. Sent to the missions of New Granada, he landed at Cartagena in 1610 and was ordained priest there in 1616, trained for his work by Alfonso de Sandoval, the apostle of the enslaved.

Cartagena was then a chief port of the Atlantic slave trade, receiving thousands of captives a year. For nearly forty years Claver met the ships as they docked, going down into the holds with food, medicine, and interpreters, nursing the sick and baptizing -- three hundred thousand souls, it is reckoned. In his solemn profession he signed himself 'Peter Claver, slave of the slaves forever.'

Broken by illness in 1650 and left largely untended in his last years, he died at Cartagena on 8 September 1654. Leo XIII canonized him on 15 January 1888, together with Alphonsus Rodriguez, the doorkeeper who had first urged him to the Indies, and in 1896 proclaimed him patron of missions among African peoples.
saints.knownFor: His lifelong service to enslaved Africans at Cartagena.

sources.text: Butler, Lives of the Saints (1866 ed.), 9 September

saints.name: St. Nicholas of Tolentino
saints.title: Priest
saints.shortBlurb: An Augustinian friar and preacher of Tolentino, famed for his charity and for his prayers for the souls in purgatory…
biography: Born in 1245 at Sant'Angelo in Pontano in the March of Ancona, Nicholas was named for Nicholas of Bari, at whose shrine his childless parents had prayed for a son. Drawn by the friars' preaching, he entered the Augustinian order about 1264, not long after its Grand Union of 1256, and was ordained priest around 1270.

Sent about 1275 to Tolentino, he served the town for thirty years as preacher, confessor, and visitor of the poor and sick, and was renowned in life for miracles. Once, weakened by long fasting, he was bidden in prayer to eat bread marked with a cross and dipped in water; the blessed 'bread of St. Nicholas' given to the sick from that day is still distributed on his feast.

Devoted above all to prayer for the dead, he became the Church's great intercessor for the souls in purgatory, whose patron he is. He died at Tolentino on 10 September 1305, and in 1446 Pope Eugene IV canonized him, the first friar of his order to be raised to the altars.
saints.knownFor: His preaching, his charity, and his intercession for the holy souls.

saints.name: Sts. Protus and Hyacinth
saints.title: Martyrs
saints.shortBlurb: Two early Roman martyrs, remembered as brothers, whose tombs on the Old Salarian Way were honoured from the earliest centuries…
biography: Protus and Hyacinth were Roman martyrs of the persecution of Valerian, about the years 257-259. Later legend made them brothers and household servants of St. Eugenia, scourged and beheaded for refusing sacrifice; what is certain is their ancient cult, for the Roman calendar of 354 already kept their feast on 11 September.

They were buried in the cemetery of Basilla on the Old Salarian Way, in what was later called the catacomb of St. Hermes. There in 1845 the archaeologist Giuseppe Marchi found the grave of Hyacinth still sealed, its inscription intact and, within, charred bones wrapped in costly stuffs -- the martyr, it seems, had died by fire. Part of the emptied tomb of Protus lay nearby.

The discovery, unique among the Roman martyrs, confirmed the testimony of the ancient itineraries and pilgrim guides. Their feast on 11 September stood in the Roman calendar until the reform of 1969, and their names are still proclaimed in the Roman Martyrology on that day.
saints.knownFor: Their witness of blood in early Roman persecution.

sources.text: The Roman Martyrology (1914 English ed.; public domain), 11 September

saints.name: The Most Holy Name of Mary
saints.title: Memorial of Our Lady's Name
saints.shortBlurb: A day set apart to honour the name of the Virgin Mother, extended to the whole Church in thanksgiving for the deliverance of Vienna…
biography: The feast of the Most Holy Name of Mary grew up in Spain, where it was first granted to the diocese of Cuenca in 1513, to be kept within the octave of Mary's Nativity, and spread through the Carmelite and other orders until it reached the whole Spanish kingdom.

On 12 September 1683 the Ottoman army besieging Vienna was broken by the Christian relief force under King John III Sobieski of Poland, who had commended the battle to Our Lady of Czestochowa. In thanksgiving for that deliverance Pope Innocent XI extended the feast of Mary's name to the universal Church, and Pius X later fixed it on 12 September.

As the feast of the Holy Name of Jesus honours the name at which every knee should bow, so this memorial honours the name of his Mother, the first and purest of redeemed creatures. Restored to the general calendar in 2002 by Pope John Paul II, it bids the faithful bless the name of Mary and fly to her motherly intercession.
saints.knownFor: Honouring the name of the Mother of God.

sources.text: Catholic Encyclopedia (1913), "The Holy Name of Mary"

saints.name: St. John Chrysostom
saints.title: Bishop and Doctor of the Church
saints.shortBlurb: The "golden-mouthed" preacher of Antioch and archbishop of Constantinople, whose eloquence and courage cost him exile…
biography: Born at Antioch about 349, John studied rhetoric under the pagan Libanius, was baptized, and spent six years as a monk in the mountains until austerities broke his health. Ordained priest in 386, he preached at Antioch for twelve years with such power that later ages named him Chrysostomos, 'the golden-mouthed.'

Consecrated archbishop of Constantinople in 398, he reformed a worldly clergy, founded hospitals, and rebuked the luxury of the court. His fearless preaching made an enemy of the Empress Eudoxia and of Theophilus of Alexandria, who engineered his condemnation at the Synod of the Oak in 403; twice exiled, he was ordered at last to Pityus on the farthest shore of the Black Sea.

He died on the forced march, at Comana in Pontus, on 14 September 407, his last words 'Glory to God for all things.' His relics were brought back to Constantinople in 438, and the liturgy that bears his name is still celebrated in the East. A Doctor of the Church, he is the patron of preachers, whose golden model he remains.
saints.knownFor: His matchless preaching and his fearless defence of the poor and the Gospel.

canonization.canonized: Venerated from antiquity; Doctor of the Church

sources.text: Butler, Lives of the Saints (1866 ed.), 13 September

saints.name: The Exaltation of the Holy Cross
saints.title: Feast of the Holy Cross
saints.shortBlurb: The Church lifts up the Cross of Christ, the instrument of shame made the tree of life and victory…
biography: This feast, kept on 14 September in East and West, lifts up the Cross of Christ, the instrument of shame made the sign of victory. Its roots lie in Jerusalem, where Constantine's churches over Calvary and the Holy Sepulchre were dedicated in 335, and where the wood of the Cross, found, tradition holds, by the Empress Helena, was shown to the faithful.

A generation later the pilgrim Egeria found Jerusalem keeping the dedication feast, the Encaenia, for eight days with a solemnity rivaling Epiphany and Easter, the showing of the holy wood at its heart. From Jerusalem the observance spread through the whole Church, Greek Christians naming it the Exaltation of the precious and life-giving Cross.

The day drew fresh meaning when the Emperor Heraclius, having defeated the Persians who had carried the relic off in 614, restored it to Jerusalem in 629. The Latin Church long kept the Finding of the Cross on 3 May as well; that feast was dropped from the general calendar in 1960, while the Exaltation remains, adoring the throne from which Christ reigned.
saints.knownFor: The triumph of Christ's Cross, the tree of life.

saints.name: Our Lady of Sorrows
saints.title: Memorial of the Sorrowful Mother
saints.shortBlurb: The Church contemplates the Mother of Jesus sharing, in her heart, the sufferings of her Son…
biography: Kept on 15 September, the day after the Exaltation of the Holy Cross, this memorial honours Mary standing by the cross of her Son, where Simeon's prophecy was fulfilled: 'a sword shall pierce through thy own soul also.' Devotion to her compassion took fixed shape among the Servite friars, founded at Florence in 1233, who spread the meditation of her Seven Sorrows.

The seven are the prophecy of Simeon, the flight into Egypt, the loss of the Child Jesus in the Temple, the meeting with her Son on the way of the cross, his crucifixion, the taking down of his body, and his burial. From the Servites the feast passed to the whole Latin Church, extended in 1814 by Pope Pius VII, and the Stabat Mater is sung at its Mass.

The Church contemplates in the sorrowful Mother the pattern of every soul that shares in the Passion: she who offered her Son in the Temple stood faithful at Calvary and received from the cross a new motherhood over the beloved disciple and all the redeemed. Under this title Mary is honoured as patroness of Slovakia.
saints.knownFor: The seven sorrows of the Mother of Jesus, faithful at the foot of the Cross.

sources.text: Catholic Encyclopedia (1913), "Feast of the Seven Sorrows of the Blessed Virgin Mary"

saints.name: Sts. Cornelius and Cyprian
saints.title: Pope and Bishop, Martyrs
saints.shortBlurb: A pope who died in exile and the bishop of Carthage who defended him, joined in one memorial as martyrs and friends…
biography: Cornelius, elected Bishop of Rome in 251 after a long vacancy, faced the schism of Novatian over the reconciliation of Christians who had lapsed in the Decian persecution. Upholding mercy toward the penitent, he was supported in letters by Cyprian, Bishop of Carthage. Banished under the Emperor Gallus, Cornelius died in exile at Centumcellae in June 253 and was numbered among the martyrs.

Cyprian, born about 200, was a Carthaginian rhetorician converted in middle life and made bishop of his city about 249. He governed his church through persecution and the great plague, and wrote On the Unity of the Catholic Church, teaching that no one can have God for his Father who has not the Church for his mother.

When the persecution of Valerian fell upon Africa, Cyprian was beheaded outside Carthage on 14 September 258, the first bishop of that church to die a martyr. The two friends, united in life by their letters and their doctrine, are named together in the Roman Canon and keep one memorial in the calendar.
saints.knownFor: Upholding the Church's mercy to the lapsed and their witness of blood.

saints.name: St. Robert Bellarmine
saints.title: Bishop and Doctor of the Church
saints.shortBlurb: The Jesuit cardinal whose learning shaped the Church's response to a divided Christendom, and who taught the faith to children and kings alike…
biography: Born at Montepulciano in 1542, a nephew of Pope Marcellus II, Robert Bellarmine entered the Society of Jesus in 1560 and taught at Louvain and the Roman College. His lectures grew into the Disputations on the Controversies of the Christian Faith, three volumes published between 1586 and 1593 that armed the Catholic reform for generations.

Made cardinal in 1599 against his own wish, and for a few years Archbishop of Capua, he lived austerely and gave his revenues to the poor. His two catechisms, composed at the command of Clement VIII, taught the faith to children and were translated into dozens of tongues; as a consultor of the Holy Office he took part, temperately, in the first proceedings against his friend Galileo in 1616.

He died in Rome on 17 September 1621. Canonized by Pius XI in 1930 and declared a Doctor of the Church the following year, he is the patron of catechists, he who, amid the affairs of popes and kings, never ceased to teach children their first prayers.
saints.knownFor: His theological writing and his catechisms for the whole Church.

canonization.canonized: 1930 by Pope Pius XI; Doctor of the Church (1931)

saints.name: St. Joseph of Cupertino
saints.title: Priest
saints.shortBlurb: The simple Franciscan friar whose ecstasies at prayer were said to lift him bodily from the ground…
biography: Born at Cupertino near Brindisi in 1603, Joseph Desa came into the world in a stable, his father dead before his birth and his mother driven from her home by creditors. Slow and absent-minded, nicknamed 'the Gaper,' he was refused by the Conventual Franciscans and dismissed by the Capuchins before the friars of Grottella took him in as a stable boy.

Admitted to the order in 1625 and ordained priest in 1628, he fell so often into ecstasy at prayer, at the very names of Jesus and Mary, that by many witnesses' testimony he was seen lifted bodily into the air. Crowds pressed upon him; his superiors hid him away, and in 1638 he was denounced to the Inquisition at Naples, examined and absolved, yet sent to live apart at Assisi.

Kept for years from public ministry and moved from friary to friary -- Pietrarubbia, Fossombrone, lastly Osimo -- he bore his seclusion in cheerful obedience. He died at Osimo on 18 September 1663. Canonized in 1767, he is invoked by students facing examinations, for his own poor learning, and by aviators and astronauts, for his flights in prayer.
saints.knownFor: His profound ecstasies at prayer and his childlike humility.

saints.name: St. Januarius
saints.title: Bishop and Martyr
saints.shortBlurb: The bishop of Benevento martyred under Diocletian, whose relic of blood is famously venerated at Naples…
biography: Januarius, in Naples San Gennaro, was Bishop of Benevento when the persecution of Diocletian fell upon the churches. According to his ancient passio he was arrested while visiting imprisoned Christians, thrown to the beasts in the amphitheatre of Pozzuoli, and at last beheaded about the year 305, together with the deacons Sossus, Festus, and Proculus and the lector Desiderius.

A pious woman is said to have gathered his blood into two ampoules, kept to this day in the treasury chapel of Naples cathedral, whither his body also was brought in 1497. Since at least 1389 the congealed blood has been seen to liquefy, thrice in the year: on his feast, 19 September; on the Saturday before the first Sunday of May; and on 16 December.

The Church permits the veneration without pronouncing on the marvel's nature. Principal patron of Naples, Januarius is invoked against the eruptions of Vesuvius, whose threatening in 1631 is held to have been stayed at his intercession, and his relic of blood has made him a patron of blood banks and their donors.
saints.knownFor: His martyrdom and the veneration of his blood-relic at Naples.

saints.name: Sts. Andrew Kim Taegŏn, Paul Chŏng Hasang, and Companions
saints.title: Martyrs
saints.shortBlurb: The first Korean priest, a lay catechist, and a great company of Korean Christians who kept the faith through waves of persecution unto death…
biography: The Church in Korea is the only one founded without missionaries. About 1784 the young scholar Yi Seung-hun, baptized Peter in Beijing, returned home to baptize his countrymen, and the community grew by books and lay witness, persecuted already in 1801, before the first priests of the Paris Foreign Missions reached it in 1836.

Andrew Kim Taegon, the child of converts, studied at Macao and in 1845 was ordained at Shanghai, the first native Korean priest; smuggled home again, he was beheaded at Saenamteo on the Han on 16 September 1846, aged twenty-five. Paul Chong Hasang, a lay catechist whose father had died for the faith in 1801, laboured to obtain bishops for Korea and was martyred in the persecution of 1839.

With them the Church honours one hundred and three martyrs, French bishops and missionaries among them, but above all lay Koreans, men, women, and children, slain in the waves of 1839, 1846, and 1866. John Paul II canonized them together at Seoul on 6 May 1984; they are patrons of Korea.
saints.knownFor: The witness of the Korean martyrs and the faith planted by lay believers.

sources.text: Vatican biography, Canonization of the Martyrs of Korea (vatican.va)

saints.name: St. Matthew
saints.title: Apostle and Evangelist
saints.shortBlurb: A tax collector called from his table to follow Christ, and author of the first Gospel…
biography: Matthew, called Levi in the Gospels of Mark and Luke, was a publican, farming the taxes at Capernaum by the Sea of Galilee, when Jesus passed and said only, 'Follow me.' He rose from the toll booth, left all, and followed, and made the Lord a great feast among his fellow tax-gatherers, drawing the Pharisees' murmur and the answer, 'I came not to call the just, but sinners.'

To him is ascribed the first Gospel, written for Jewish Christians to show Jesus as the promised Messiah, the son of David; the early Fathers, following Papias, held that he composed it first in Aramaic for the Hebrews before going out to other nations. Ancient tradition, kept in the Roman Martyrology, sends him to preach in Ethiopia and to die there a martyr.

His relics are venerated in the cathedral of Salerno, and in art he is figured as a winged man, for his Gospel opens with the human birth of Christ. Because of the trade he abandoned at the Lord's call, he is the patron of tax collectors, bankers, and accountants.
saints.knownFor: Leaving his tax table to follow Christ; writing the first Gospel.

sources.text: Butler, Lives of the Saints (1866 ed.), 21 September

saints.name: St. Maurice and the Theban Legion
saints.title: Martyrs
saints.shortBlurb: A legion of Christian soldiers who, led by their commander Maurice, chose death rather than turn their swords against the innocent or deny their faith…
biography: According to the letter of Eucherius, Bishop of Lyon, written about 450, the Theban Legion was a body of Christian soldiers recruited at Thebes in Egypt and sent by the Emperor Maximian into Gaul against the rebels of Burgundy. When the army reached Agaunum in the Alps, now Saint-Maurice in the Valais, the legion refused to sacrifice to the gods and to turn its weapons against fellow Christians.

Under their commander Maurice, together with Candidus, Innocent, and Exuperius, the soldiers stood firm while the legion was twice decimated, every tenth man put to the sword, and was at last cut down entire, about the year 287. Their confession, recorded by Eucherius, was that they owed the emperor their service but God their innocence.

In the following century Theodore, Bishop of Octodurum, built a basilica over the martyrs' relics, and on the site rose the abbey of Saint-Maurice, founded in 515 on land given by King Sigismund of Burgundy and still occupied today. As soldiers who chose death rather than an impious order, Maurice and his legionaries are patrons of soldiers and infantry and of the Alpine lands.
saints.knownFor: Their refusal to persecute fellow Christians, sealed by martyrdom.

saints.name: St. Pius of Pietrelcina
saints.title: Priest
saints.shortBlurb: The Capuchin friar known to the world as Padre Pio, who bore the wounds of Christ and spent his days in the confessional…
biography: Francesco Forgione was born on 25 May 1887 at Pietrelcina in Campania, the son of peasant farmers. At fifteen he entered the Capuchin novitiate at Morcone, taking the name Pio, and was ordained a priest in 1910. In 1916 he was sent to the friary of Our Lady of Grace at San Giovanni Rotondo, on the Gargano, where he remained until his death.

On 20 September 1918, while hearing confessions, he received the stigmata, the visible wounds of the crucified Christ, which he bore for the remaining fifty years of his life. Examined by physicians and investigated by the Holy Office, he was for a time forbidden to say Mass or hear confessions in public; he obeyed without complaint, and Pius XI restored him to full ministry in 1933.

For decades he heard confessions for hours each day, drawing pilgrims from every country, and in 1956 he opened the hospital he founded, the Casa Sollievo della Sofferenza, the Home for the Relief of Suffering. He died in his cell on 23 September 1968, the stigmata by then healed without a scar. Canonized by John Paul II in 2002, he is invoked as a patron of confessors.
saints.knownFor: The stigmata he bore and his long ministry of confession and healing.

sources.text: Vatican biography, Canonization of St. Pius of Pietrelcina (vatican.va)

saints.name: St. Pacificus of San Severino
saints.title: Priest
saints.shortBlurb: A Franciscan preacher of the Marches who, struck blind, deaf, and lame, turned his long affliction into a hidden life of prayer…
biography: Carlo Antonio Divini was born at San Severino in the March of Ancona on 1 March 1653, the youngest of thirteen children, and was orphaned of both parents while still a child. In 1670 he took the habit of the Franciscan Reformati at Forano, receiving the name Pacificus, and was ordained a priest on 4 June 1678.

After six years teaching philosophy to the younger friars, he laboured as a missionary preacher among the country people. From 1684 his health failed: he grew lame, then deaf, and at last blind, so that he could preach no more. For the remaining thirty-seven years of his life he bore these afflictions in patience, given to prayer before the Blessed Sacrament and to the counsel of those who sought him.

He was said to have foretold the earthquake that devastated the Abruzzi in 1703, and wonders were reported at his tomb. He died at San Severino on 24 September 1721, was beatified by Pius VI in 1786, and canonized by Gregory XVI in 1839. As one who suffered long infirmity without complaint, he is invoked as the patron of the chronically ill.
saints.knownFor: His patient endurance of affliction and his hidden life of prayer.

sources.text: Catholic Encyclopedia (1913), "St. Pacificus of San Severino"

saints.name: St. Finnbarr of Cork
saints.title: Bishop
saints.shortBlurb: The hermit of the lake at Gougane Barra who founded the monastery and school from which the city of Cork arose…
biography: Born about 550 near Bandon and named Lóchán, Finnbarr was the son of Amergin, a craftsman from Galway in Connacht. He studied in Ossory and received the name Fionnbharra, 'fair head', at his tonsure. After a pilgrimage to Rome, he withdrew to a hermitage on an island in the lake called Loch Irce, now Gougane Barra, at the source of the river Lee.

Disciples gathered to his solitude, and about 606 he moved downriver to the place called Corcach Mór, the Great Marsh of Munster, founding there a monastery and school on the ridge above the Lee. The school became renowned -- 'Where Finbarr taught, let Munster learn' -- and around it grew the city of Cork, whose first bishop and abbot he is held to be.

He died on 25 September 623 at Cell na Cluaine, returning from a visit to Gougane Barra, and was buried in the cemetery of his church at Cork. As the founder of the monastery and school from which the city arose, he is venerated as the patron of Cork and of its diocese.
saints.knownFor: Founding the monastery and school that became the city of Cork.

saints.name: Sts. Cosmas and Damian
saints.title: Martyrs
saints.shortBlurb: Twin physicians who healed the sick without payment for the love of Christ, and were crowned with martyrdom…
biography: Cosmas and Damian, held by tradition to be twin brothers born in Arabia, practised medicine at the seaport of Aegeae in Cilicia and would accept no fee for their care, observing the Lord's word, 'Freely you have received, freely give.' For this the Greeks named them the Anargyroi, the moneyless ones, and their charity won many to the faith.

In the persecution under Diocletian they were arrested by order of Lysias, governor of Cilicia, and, refusing to renounce Christ, were beheaded with their brothers Anthimus, Leontius, and Euprepius, about the year 287. Their relics were buried at Cyrrhus in Syria, which became a shrine that the Emperor Justinian adorned in thanksgiving for a cure ascribed to their prayers.

About 530 Pope Felix IV dedicated a basilica to them in the Roman Forum, famed for its sixth-century mosaics, and their names are still invoked together in the Roman Canon of the Mass. As physicians who healed without payment, they are the patrons of physicians, surgeons, and pharmacists.
saints.knownFor: Healing the sick without charge and their martyrdom for the faith.

saints.name: St. Vincent de Paul
saints.title: Priest
saints.shortBlurb: The Gascon priest who organized the charity of an age, gathering priests and laywomen to serve the poor, the galley-slave, and the foundling…
biography: Born on 24 April 1581 at Pouy in Gascony, of peasant stock, Vincent was ordained a priest in 1600. In 1605, sailing from Marseille, he was captured by Barbary pirates and sold into slavery at Tunis, escaping after two years to land in France in 1607, as he himself related in his letters.

The mission sermon he preached at Folleville in 1617 he himself called the first sermon of the mission, and the spiritual neglect of the country people became his life's charge. In 1625 he founded the Congregation of the Mission, the Vincentians, to preach in the villages and form the clergy.

He organized the Ladies of Charity among the women of Paris, was appointed chaplain to the galley-slaves in 1622, and with St. Louise de Marillac founded the Daughters of Charity in 1633 to serve the poor in the streets, hospitals, and prisons. He relieved foundlings and the victims of war.

He died in Paris on 27 September 1660, was beatified in 1729, and was canonized by Clement XII in 1737. For this lifetime of organized mercy the Church honours him as the patron of all works of charity, of hospitals, and of prisoners.
saints.knownFor: Founding the Vincentians and Daughters of Charity for the service of the poor.

sources.text: Butler, Lives of the Saints (1866 ed.), 27 September

saints.name: St. Wenceslaus
saints.title: Martyr
saints.shortBlurb: The Christian duke of Bohemia, raised by his holy grandmother, murdered at the church door by his own brother…
biography: Born about 907, Wenceslaus -- Václav in Czech -- was the son of Duke Vratislaus of Bohemia and was reared in the faith by his grandmother St. Ludmila, who in 921 was strangled at Tetín by agents of his mother Drahomíra. As duke he governed as a Christian prince, building the rotunda of St. Vitus at Prague Castle and relieving the poor with his own hand.

His piety and his submission to the German king Henry the Fowler, who forced him to tribute in 929, made him enemies among the nobles. In 935 his brother Boleslaus invited him to Stará Boleslav for the feast of Saints Cosmas and Damian, and there, at the church door on 28 September, Boleslaus's men set upon him, the brother himself striking the final blow.

Venerated from his death as a martyr, his relics were translated in 938 to St. Vitus's in Prague, and the Emperor Otto I is said to have granted him the royal title, whence the 'king' of legend and of the carol 'Good King Wenceslas'. As the martyred prince of his nation he is the patron of Bohemia and of the Czech people.
saints.knownFor: His just Christian rule and his martyrdom at his brother's hand.

saints.name: Sts. Michael, Gabriel and Raphael
saints.title: Archangels
saints.shortBlurb: The three archangels named in Scripture — the warrior, the messenger, and the healer — honored together on Michaelmas…
biography: Three angels alone are named in the Scriptures, and their names declare their missions. Michael, 'Who is like God?', fought the dragon in the Apocalypse, disputed with the devil in the Epistle of Jude, and rises in the Book of Daniel as the great prince who stands guard over the people of God.

Gabriel, 'the strength of God', is the messenger: he interpreted visions to Daniel and, in the Gospel of Luke, announced the birth of the Baptist to Zechariah and the Incarnation of the Son to Mary at Nazareth. Raphael, 'God heals', appears in the Book of Tobit, where he guided the young Tobias, delivered Sarah from the demon, and restored the sight of old Tobit.

The feast of 29 September, called Michaelmas in England, recalls the dedication of a basilica of St. Michael on the Via Salaria outside Rome. The Church once kept Gabriel's feast on 24 March and Raphael's on 24 October, uniting all three on Michael's day in the calendar reform of 1969. Michael is invoked as patron of soldiers and police, Gabriel of messengers, Raphael of travellers and the sick.
saints.knownFor: The angelic ministry of protection, message, and healing.

saints.name: St. Jerome
saints.title: Priest and Doctor of the Church
saints.shortBlurb: The fiery scholar of Bethlehem who gave the Latin Church its Bible, the Vulgate, translating the Scriptures from the original tongues…
biography: Born about 347 at Stridon on the border of Dalmatia and Pannonia, Jerome studied rhetoric at Rome under the grammarian Donatus and was baptized there as a young man. Going East in 373, he lived for several years as a hermit in the Syrian desert of Chalcis, where he mastered Hebrew.

Ordained priest at Antioch, he heard Gregory of Nazianzus at Constantinople, and in 382 came to Rome, where Pope Damasus made him his secretary and set him to revising the Latin Gospels. His fierce pen and ascetic counsel won him devoted disciples among the Roman matrons, chiefly Paula, and bitter enemies.

After the pope's death Jerome left Rome in 385 for Bethlehem, where Paula built monasteries for men and women. There for thirty-four years he translated the Old Testament from the Hebrew, composed commentaries, and did battle with Jovinian, Vigilantius, Rufinus, and the Pelagians, dying on 30 September 420 near the grotto of the Nativity.

Boniface VIII numbered him in 1298 among the four great Latin Doctors; legend shows him drawing a thorn from a lion's paw. Because he gave the Latin Church its Bible and lived among manuscripts, he is patron of translators, librarians, and scripture scholars.
saints.knownFor: The Vulgate; scripture scholarship; “Ignorance of Scripture is ignorance of Christ.”

canonization.canonized: Pre-Congregation; named a Doctor of the Church in 1298 by Pope Boniface VIII

sources.text: Butler, Lives of the Saints (1866 ed.), 30 September

saints.name: St. Thérèse of the Child Jesus
saints.title: Virgin and Doctor of the Church
saints.shortBlurb: The Little Flower of Carmel, who taught the “little way” of confidence and love and died at twenty-four…
biography: Marie-Francoise-Thérèse Martin was born at Alençon on 2 January 1873, the last of nine children of Louis and Zélie Martin, themselves canonized in 2015. Her mother died when Thérèse was four, and the family then settled at Lisieux in Normandy.

At fifteen, in 1888, she entered the Carmel of Lisieux, where two of her sisters were already nuns, taking the name Sister Thérèse of the Child Jesus and of the Holy Face. In the cloister she lived her 'little way' of spiritual childhood, trusting in God's mercy through small acts of love.

At her superiors' command she wrote the memoir published after her death as The Story of a Soul. She died of tuberculosis on 30 September 1897, aged twenty-four, promising to 'spend her heaven doing good upon earth' and to let fall 'a shower of roses'.

Beatified in 1923 and canonized in 1925, she was proclaimed by Pius XI patroness of the missions with Francis Xavier in 1927, though she never left her cloister. Pius XII named her patroness of France with Joan of Arc in 1944, and John Paul II declared her Doctor of the Church in 1997; from her promised roses she is patron of florists.
saints.knownFor: The “little way” of confidence and love.

canonization.canonized: 1925 by Pope Pius XI; Doctor of the Church (1997)

sources.text: Thérèse of Lisieux, The Story of a Soul (L'Histoire d'une âme, 1898; public domain)

saints.name: The Holy Guardian Angels
saints.title: Angelic Guardians
saints.shortBlurb: The heavenly guardians whom God appoints to watch over, protect, and pray for each human soul…
biography: That God appoints an angel to guard each soul is witnessed across Scripture. In Exodus the Lord sends his angel before Israel, to guard them on the way; the Psalmist sings that God has given his angels charge over us, to keep us in all our ways; and in the Acts of the Apostles the disciples, told that Peter stands at the gate, answer, 'It is his angel.'

The Lord himself set the seal on the doctrine when he warned his hearers not to despise the little ones, for 'their angels in heaven always see the face of my Father who is in heaven.' Jerome exclaimed at the thought: 'how great the dignity of the soul, since each one has from his birth an angel commissioned to guard it.'

A feast of the Guardian Angels was authorized for certain places by Pope Paul V in 1608 and extended to the whole Latin Church by Pope Clement X in 1670, who fixed it to 2 October, the first free day after the feast of the Archangels. Kept the day after Michaelmas, it gives thanks for the unseen guardianship that accompanies every Christian through life.
saints.knownFor: God's appointment of an angel to guard each soul.

saints.name: Sts. Ewald the Fair and Ewald the Dark
saints.title: Priests and Martyrs
saints.shortBlurb: Two English priests, brothers distinguished only by the colour of their hair, martyred while preaching to the Old Saxons…
biography: The two Ewalds were priests of Northumbria who bore the same name and were told apart, says Bede, only by the colour of their hair, as Ewald the Fair and Ewald the Dark, of whom the Dark was the more learned in Scripture. After long training in the schools of Ireland, they crossed to the continent about 690 to preach to the Old Saxons, kinsmen of their own people.

They lodged with the steward of a Saxon ealdorman, meaning to win the chief to Christ; but the pagans, fearing their gods would be abandoned, rose against the priests and killed them about 695 at the place now called Aplerbeck, by Dortmund. Ewald the Fair was slain quickly by the sword; Ewald the Dark was torn limb from limb, and their bodies were cast into the Rhine.

Bede, who tells their story in his Ecclesiastical History, records that a pillar of heavenly light marked where the bodies lay. Pepin of Herstal had them enshrined at Cologne in the church of St. Cunibert, and the brothers are named in the Roman Martyrology on 3 October. Martyred on Saxon soil, they are honoured as patrons of Westphalia.
saints.knownFor: Martyrdom while evangelizing the Old Saxons.

saints.name: St. Francis of Assisi
saints.title: Religious
saints.shortBlurb: The Poverello of Assisi, who wedded Lady Poverty, founded the Friars Minor, and bore in his own flesh the wounds of the Crucified…
biography: Born at Assisi in 1181, the son of the cloth merchant Pietro di Bernardone, Francis passed a carefree youth until captivity in Perugia and an illness turned his heart. Praying in the ruined chapel of San Damiano, he heard the crucifix bid him repair God's church, and in 1206 renounced his inheritance before the bishop for a life of poverty.

In 1209 he won from Pope Innocent III approval of his primitive rule, the beginning of the Order of Friars Minor. In 1219 he crossed the crusader lines to preach before the Sultan al-Kamil in Egypt, and at Greccio in 1223 made the first Christmas crib.

In September 1224, keeping a fast on Mount La Verna, he saw a seraph and received the stigmata, the first such wounds recorded in the Church. He composed the Canticle of the Sun, praising God through Brother Sun and Sister Moon, and died at the Portiuncula on 3 October 1226.

Canonized by Gregory IX in 1228, he was proclaimed patron of ecology by John Paul II in 1979, for he called every creature his brother and sister; he is also honoured as a patron of Italy and of merchants, whose trade he renounced.
saints.knownFor: Radical poverty; love of creation; the stigmata; the first Christmas crèche.

sources.text: Butler, Lives of the Saints (1866 ed.), 4 October

saints.name: St. Faustina Kowalska
saints.title: Virgin
saints.shortBlurb: A humble Polish sister and “secretary” of Divine Mercy, to whom Christ entrusted the message of his boundless mercy…
biography: Helena Kowalska was born on 25 August 1905 at Głogowiec near Łódź, the third of ten children of a poor carpenter. After years as a domestic servant, she entered the Sisters of Our Lady of Mercy in Warsaw in 1925, taking the name Maria Faustina, and served as cook, gardener, and portress.

On 22 February 1931, in her cell at Płock, she saw the Lord, two rays issuing from his heart, and heard the command to paint his image signed 'Jesus, I trust in You' and to work for a feast of mercy on the Sunday after Easter. At Vilnius her confessor Michał Sopoćko arranged the first image, painted in 1934; the chaplet of Divine Mercy followed.

These revelations she recorded in her Diary, styling herself the secretary of Divine Mercy. She died of tuberculosis at Kraków on 5 October 1938, aged thirty-three. The Holy Office forbade the devotion for a time, lifting the ban in 1978.

Beatified in 1993, she was canonized by Pope John Paul II on 30 April 2000, and that day he proclaimed the Sunday after Easter Divine Mercy Sunday. She is venerated as patron of the Divine Mercy apostolate born of her revelations.
saints.knownFor: The Divine Mercy devotion.

sources.text: Vatican biography, Canonization of St. Maria Faustina Kowalska (vatican.va)

saints.name: St. Bruno
saints.title: Priest and Founder
saints.shortBlurb: A learned master of Reims who fled fame for the silence of the mountains and founded the Carthusian Order…
biography: Born at Cologne about 1030, Bruno studied at Reims and rose to head its cathedral school from 1057 to 1075, numbering among his pupils the future Pope Urban II. Made chancellor of the diocese, he opposed the violent and simoniacal Archbishop Manasses of Reims until Manasses was driven from the see in 1080.

With six companions he was settled by Hugh, Bishop of Grenoble, in the wild valley of Chartreuse in 1084, where they built an oratory and scattered cells, the first charterhouse and mother of the Carthusian Order. Called to Rome in 1090 by his former pupil Urban II, Bruno refused the archbishopric of Reggio and begged back his hermit's life.

The pope kept him in Italy, and in 1091 he founded a second charterhouse, Our Lady della Torre in Calabria, under the patronage of Count Roger of Sicily, dying there on 6 October 1101. Never formally canonized, his cult was approved by Leo X in 1514 and extended to the whole Church in 1623; his order, by the old saying, was never reformed because never deformed.
saints.knownFor: Founding the Carthusian Order.

canonization.canonized: Cultus approved 1514 by Pope Leo X; feast extended to the whole Church 1623

saints.name: Our Lady of the Rosary
saints.title: Memorial of the Blessed Virgin Mary
saints.shortBlurb: A memorial giving thanks for the Rosary and for the deliverance of Christendom at Lepanto…
biography: This memorial honours the Blessed Virgin under the title of the Rosary, the prayer that ponders the mysteries of Christ's life, death, and glory upon the beads. It was born of battle: after the Holy League's fleet defeated the Ottoman navy at Lepanto on 7 October 1571, Pius V, who had asked all Christendom to pray the Rosary for the outcome, instituted an annual feast of Our Lady of Victory.

Two years later, in 1573, Gregory XIII renamed it the feast of the Holy Rosary and kept it on the first Sunday of October. Clement XI extended it to the whole Church in 1716 after Prince Eugene of Savoy's victory over the Turks at Peterwardein, and Pius X in 1913 fixed it again on 7 October, the anniversary of the battle.

Leo XIII, the Rosary's great champion, added 'Queen of the Most Holy Rosary' to the Litany of Loreto in 1883. The memorial thus weds a devotion long preached by the sons of St. Dominic to the Church's confidence in the intercession of the Mother of God — a garland of roses, as the name rosarium suggests, laid upon the mysteries of her Son.
saints.knownFor: The Rosary and the deliverance at Lepanto.

sources.text: Catholic Encyclopedia (1913), “Feast of the Holy Rosary”

saints.name: St. Pelagia the Penitent
saints.title: Penitent
saints.shortBlurb: A celebrated dancer of Antioch who turned from a life of sin to a hidden life of penance…
biography: Pelagia's story is told by James, a deacon of the church of Heliopolis, who places her in the fifth century. The foremost actress and dancer of Antioch, she rode through the city laden with gold and pearls while a synod of bishops was gathered there, and her splendor provoked the bishop Nonnus to a sermon on the judgment.

Struck by his preaching, she sought baptism, was received under her birth name with the deaconess Romana as godmother, and distributed her wealth to the widows, orphans, and poor of the city. Then she vanished from Antioch in men's clothing, taking the name Pelagius, and built herself a cell on the Mount of Olives at Jerusalem.

There she lived three or four years in hidden penance, so wasted by austerity that at her death, about 457, the brethren who came to bury the supposed monk discovered a woman. Her relics drew pilgrims from Jericho and the Jordan valley. Remembered as a model of repentance, she is invoked as patron of penitents and, from her former calling, of actresses.
saints.knownFor: Conversion from a life of sin to penitential solitude.

saints.name: St. Denis and Companions
saints.title: Bishop and Martyrs
saints.shortBlurb: The first bishop of Paris, martyred with his companions and honoured as an apostle of Gaul…
biography: According to the earliest tradition Denis was sent from Rome by Pope Fabian about the middle of the third century to restore the Church of Gaul after the Decian persecution. Settling on an island in the Seine with the priest Rusticus and the deacon Eleutherius, he built a church, preached fearlessly, and is venerated as the first bishop of Paris.

Arrested with his two companions by the governor Fescenninus Sisinnius, the three were beheaded, in the tradition under the emperor Valerian about the year 258, on the hill north of the city afterward called Montmartre, a name long explained as the mount of the martyrs. A matron named Catulla buried them, and a shrine rose over their graves.

A later legend made Denis a cephalophore, rising after his execution to carry his own head, and it is from the manner of his death that he is invoked against headaches. The abbey of Saint-Denis, enriched by King Dagobert and the burial place of the kings of France, made him a national patron, of Paris and of the whole realm.
saints.knownFor: First bishop of Paris and martyr of Gaul.

saints.name: St. Francis Borgia
saints.title: Priest
saints.shortBlurb: A Spanish duke who, shaken by the sight of a dead empress's ruined beauty, left his rank to become a Jesuit…
biography: Born at Gandía in Valencia on 28 October 1510, great-grandson of Pope Alexander VI and of King Ferdinand of Aragon, Francis married Eleanor de Castro in 1529 and rose at the court of Charles V to be Viceroy of Catalonia and fourth Duke of Gandía. In 1539 he convoyed the corpse of the Empress Isabella to Granada, and the sight of her ruined beauty turned his heart from the world.

Widowed in 1546, he entered the Society of Jesus and was ordained priest in 1551, as commissary-general in Spain founding a dozen colleges. Elected the order's third Superior General in 1565, he governed its rapid spread through Europe and the missions of the New World so fruitfully that he has been called its second founder. He died in Rome on 30 September 1572.

Beatified in 1624 and canonized by Clement X, he has been invoked against earthquakes since the time of his beatification, a patronage spread through Jesuit churches, and Portugal claimed him as a patron of the kingdom. His feast was long kept on 10 October.
saints.knownFor: Renouncing a dukedom to serve as a Jesuit.

saints.name: St. John XXIII
saints.title: Pope
saints.shortBlurb: The “Good Pope” of peasant stock who, in a brief pontificate, summoned the Second Vatican Council…
biography: Angelo Giuseppe Roncalli was born on 25 November 1881 at Sotto il Monte near Bergamo, the son of peasant sharecroppers. Ordained priest in 1904, he served as secretary to the bishop of Bergamo and as a military chaplain through the First World War.

Made a bishop in 1925, he spent nearly twenty years as a papal representative in Bulgaria, Turkey, and Greece, labouring in the Second World War to rescue Jews from deportation. As nuncio to France from 1944 he steered the French Church through the Liberation, and in 1953 was created cardinal and named Patriarch of Venice.

Elected pope on 28 October 1958 at the age of seventy-six and thought a caretaker, he stunned the Church within three months by announcing an ecumenical council. In a pontificate of under five years he issued the encyclicals Mater et Magistra and Pacem in Terris and visited Rome's hospitals and prisons like a parish priest.

He died of stomach cancer on 3 June 1963, mourned across the world as 'Good Pope John'. Beatified in 2000 and canonized by Pope Francis in 2014, his memorial is kept on 11 October, the anniversary of the Council's opening.
saints.knownFor: Convoking the Second Vatican Council.

sources.text: Vatican biography, Canonization of St. John XXIII (vatican.va)

saints.name: St. Wilfrid
saints.title: Bishop
saints.shortBlurb: A Northumbrian bishop who championed the customs of Rome and carried the faith to the pagan South Saxons…
biography: Born a Northumbrian noble about 633, Wilfrid studied at Lindisfarne, Canterbury, Lyon, and Rome before becoming abbot of Ripon. At the Synod of Whitby in 664 he pleaded the Roman calculation of Easter against Colmán of Lindisfarne and won King Oswiu to the Roman usage, aligning the English Church with the universal West.

Consecrated bishop at Compiègne, he founded monasteries at Ripon and Hexham and introduced the Rule of Benedict, glazed windows, and Roman chant. Quarreling with King Ecgfrith, he was expelled in 678 and became the first Englishman to appeal to Rome; Pope Agatho's synod of 679 judged in his favor, yet he was imprisoned and exiled on his return.

He spent five years converting the pagan South Saxons from Selsey, was restored, driven out again, and vindicated once more at Rome before regaining Ripon and Hexham in 706. He died at Oundle in 709 and was buried at Ripon, his life recorded soon after by Stephen of Ripon.
saints.knownFor: Championing Roman usages at the Synod of Whitby.

saints.name: St. Edward the Confessor
saints.title: King
saints.shortBlurb: The pious last king of the House of Wessex, remembered for gentleness, generosity, and the building of Westminster Abbey…
biography: Born in 1003, a son of King Æthelred II and Emma of Normandy, Edward spent his youth in Norman exile while Danish kings ruled England, and was called to the throne in 1042. His twenty-four-year reign was one of almost unbroken peace: he remitted the Danegelt tax, gave largely to the poor, and was the first English king to touch for the king's evil.

Bound by a vow of chastity, he married Edith, Earl Godwin's daughter, only on her agreement to live with him as a sister, the memory of which, with the strains of that alliance, later made him a patron of difficult marriages. A vowed pilgrimage to Rome being commuted by the pope, he rebuilt instead the abbey of St. Peter at Westminster, dedicated but a week before his death.

He died on 5 January 1066, leaving the succession that ended in the Norman Conquest, and was buried in his abbey. Canonized by Alexander III in 1161, his body was found incorrupt and translated by Thomas Becket on 13 October 1163, the day of his feast. He remained a patron of England and of kings until St. George took his place in the fourteenth century.
saints.knownFor: Piety as king and the founding of Westminster Abbey.

saints.name: St. Callistus I
saints.title: Pope and Martyr
saints.shortBlurb: A former slave who rose to govern the Roman Church and gave his name to its great catacomb…
biography: A slave of the Christian Carpophorus in Rome, Callistus lost his master's money in a failed bank, was condemned to the hand-mill and then to the mines of Sardinia, and won freedom when Marcia, the mistress of Commodus, obtained the release of the confessors there. Pope Zephyrinus recalled him and set him over the Church's burial ground on the Appian Way.

That cemetery, the catacomb that still bears his name, became the resting place of many early popes, the reason he is honored as patron of cemetery workers. Elected pope about 217, he readmitted to Communion, after due penance, those guilty of adultery and fornication, an act of mercy denounced as laxity by the rigorists Tertullian and Hippolytus.

He condemned the heretic Sabellius, and he is the earliest pope named in the fourth-century Depositio Martyrum, the surest witness that he died for the faith about 222; legend adds that his body was thrown into a well in Trastevere. He was buried in the cemetery of Calepodius on the Aurelian Way.
