saints.knownFor: Governing the Roman Church and its catacomb cemetery.

saints.name: St. Teresa of Jesus (Ávila)
saints.title: Virgin and Doctor of the Church
saints.shortBlurb: A Carmelite of Ávila who reformed her order and mapped the soul's ascent to God in the Interior Castle…
biography: Born at Ávila on 28 March 1515, Teresa entered the Carmelite Convent of the Incarnation there in 1535. After years of illness and wavering prayer she was converted to deep recollection, and extraordinary graces followed, among them the transverberation, the piercing of her heart by an angel's dart.

In 1562 she founded St. Joseph's at Ávila, the first convent of her reform, and went on to establish sixteen more across Spain in the teeth of opposition; with John of the Cross she extended the reform to the friars, beginning at Duruelo in 1568. The Discalced Carmelite province was canonically erected in 1580.

Her books, the Life written by herself, the Way of Perfection, and the Interior Castle, map the soul's ascent to God with unmatched practical wisdom. She died at Alba de Tormes on 4 October 1582, the very night the reformed calendar leapt to 15 October, which became her feast.

Canonized in 1622, she was declared by Paul VI in 1970 the first woman Doctor of the Church. She is honored as a patron of Spain, and, having herself endured grievous headaches through life, she is invoked by those who suffer them.
saints.knownFor: Reforming Carmel and her writings on mystical prayer.

canonization.canonized: 1622 by Pope Gregory XV; Doctor of the Church (1970)

sources.text: Butler, Lives of the Saints (1866 ed.), 15 October

saints.name: St. Margaret Mary Alacoque
saints.title: Virgin
saints.shortBlurb: A Visitation nun of Paray-le-Monial to whom Christ revealed the riches of his Sacred Heart…
biography: Born at L'Hautecour in Burgundy on 22 July 1647, Margaret Mary entered the Visitation convent at Paray-le-Monial in 1671 and made her final vows the next year. Between 1673 and 1675 she reported a series of revelations in which Christ showed her his Heart afire with love for men and grieved at their ingratitude.

The revelations asked for a Holy Hour of reparation, for Communion on the First Friday of each month, and for a feast in honor of the Sacred Heart on the Friday after the octave of Corpus Christi, with great promises to those who would practice the devotion. Her own community long treated her as a visionary, but the Jesuit Claude de la Colombière believed her and spread the devotion abroad.

She died at Paray-le-Monial on 17 October 1690. Beatified by Pius IX in 1864 and canonized by Benedict XV in 1920, she is venerated as the apostle of the devotion to the Sacred Heart, which from her convent spread through the whole Church.
saints.knownFor: The revelations of the Sacred Heart of Jesus.

saints.name: St. Ignatius of Antioch
saints.title: Bishop and Martyr
saints.shortBlurb: A bishop of the apostolic age who wrote seven great letters on his way to the beasts at Rome…
biography: Third bishop of Antioch after Evodius and, with his friend Polycarp, a hearer of the Apostle John, Ignatius was condemned to the beasts under Trajan and sent in chains to Rome. His journey became a triumph: at Smyrna, where Polycarp was bishop, and at Troas the churches of Asia Minor sent delegates to honor him.

Along the way he wrote seven letters, to the Ephesians, Magnesians, Trallians, Romans, Philadelphians, Smyrnaeans, and to Polycarp, urging unity around the bishop and calling the Eucharist the medicine of immortality; in them occurs the first recorded use of the name Catholic Church. He begged the Romans not to rob him of martyrdom: 'I am the wheat of God.'

Thrown to the beasts in the Flavian amphitheatre, by tradition about the year 107, he won the crown he had long desired. His companions carried his relics back to Antioch; they now rest in the church of San Clemente at Rome. Long kept on 1 February, his feast is now celebrated on 17 October.
saints.knownFor: His letters on Church unity and the Eucharist; martyrdom at Rome.

sources.text: Butler, Lives of the Saints (1866 ed.), 1 February

saints.name: St. Luke
saints.title: Evangelist
saints.shortBlurb: The “beloved physician,” companion of St. Paul, who wrote the third Gospel and the Acts of the Apostles…
biography: A Greek of Antioch and a physician by profession, Luke joined Paul at Troas and, as the 'we' passages of Acts show, accompanied him to Philippi, to Jerusalem, through the shipwreck voyage, and into his Roman imprisonment; Paul names him 'the beloved physician' and writes in his last letter, 'Luke alone is with me.'

He wrote the third Gospel and its sequel, the Acts of the Apostles, both dedicated to Theophilus, together more than a quarter of the New Testament. His Gospel alone preserves the infancy canticles and the parables of the Good Samaritan and the Prodigal Son, and it opens with the priest Zachary's sacrifice, whence his symbol, the ox.

An ancient preface records that he never married, that he wrote the Gospel in Achaia, and that he died at seventy-four in Boeotia; his relics were translated to Constantinople in 357. Because he was a physician he is the patron of physicians and surgeons, and because a later tradition made him the first painter of the Virgin's image, he is the patron of artists.
saints.knownFor: Writing the third Gospel and the Acts of the Apostles.

sources.text: Butler, Lives of the Saints (1866 ed.), 18 October

saints.name: Sts. John de Brébeuf and Isaac Jogues, and Companions
saints.title: Priests and Martyrs
saints.shortBlurb: The North American Martyrs, French Jesuits who carried the Gospel to the Huron and Iroquois and died for it…
biography: Eight French Jesuits, six priests and two lay helpers, of the mission of Sainte-Marie among the Hurons in New France died by torture between 1642 and 1649 amid the war of the Mohawk against the Huron. René Goupil, a surgeon and donné, was the first, tomahawked at Ossernenon in 1642.

Isaac Jogues, captured with Goupil and ritually mutilated, was ransomed by Dutch traders and returned to France, where the pope dispensed his maimed hands for the offering of Mass; sailing back to his mission, he was killed with the layman Jean de la Lande at Ossernenon in October 1646. Antoine Daniel fell in 1648 in the attack on his Huron mission of Teanaostaye.

In 1649 the Iroquois broke the Huron nation and its mission: John de Brébeuf, the apostle of the Hurons, was tortured to death with Gabriel Lalemant at St. Ignace in March, and Charles Garnier and Noël Chabanel were killed in December. Beatified in 1925 and canonized by Pius XI in 1930, the eight are the patrons of Canada, honored at the shrines of Midland and Auriesville.
saints.knownFor: Martyrdom while evangelizing the peoples of North America.

sources.text: R. G. Thwaites (ed.), The Jesuit Relations and Allied Documents (1896–1901; public domain)

saints.name: St. Paul of the Cross
saints.title: Priest and Founder
saints.shortBlurb: A mystic of the Passion who founded the Passionists to keep the sufferings of Christ before the world…
biography: Paul Francis Danei was born at Ovada in Piedmont in 1694 and raised at Castellazzo, where from his youth he gave himself to prayer and severe penance. In 1720, while keeping a forty-day retreat, he received a vision of the Mother of God in a black habit marked with the cross, and wrote the rule of a new congregation vowed to keep alive the memory of the Passion of Christ.

Ordained priest by Benedict XIII in 1727, he opened with his brother John Baptist the first retreat of the congregation on Monte Argentario in 1737, and Benedict XIV approved the rule in 1741. The Passionists, as they came to be called, add to the usual vows a fourth: to promote among the faithful the remembrance of the Lord's sufferings.

For nearly fifty years he preached missions through the towns and countryside of Italy, moving the hardest hearers to repentance, while as superior he governed his growing family with prudence and wrote letters of direction still treasured. He died at Rome in 1775 and was canonized by Pius IX in 1867.
saints.knownFor: Founding the Passionists and preaching the Passion.

sources.text: Catholic Encyclopedia (1913), “St. Paul of the Cross”

saints.name: St. Hilarion
saints.title: Abbot
saints.shortBlurb: The father of monastic life in Palestine, a disciple of St. Anthony whose life St. Jerome recorded…
biography: Born about 291 of pagan parents at Thabatha near Gaza, Hilarion was sent to study at Alexandria, where he was converted and baptized. Drawn by the fame of Anthony the Great, he spent two months with him in the desert, then, finding his parents dead on his return, gave his inheritance to the poor and withdrew about the year 306 to a wilderness by the sea near Majuma.

On a diet of figs and a little bread he became the first to plant the anchoritic life in Palestine. Disciples gathered and monasteries multiplied, but the crowds drawn by his miracles drove him to flight: after Anthony's death in 356 he wandered through Egypt, then Sicily, where his disciple Hesychius found him only after a three years' search, then Dalmatia, and at last Cyprus.

He died near Paphos in 371, aged eighty, and Hesychius secretly carried his body back to Majuma for burial. Jerome, who wrote his Life at Bethlehem some twenty years later, prized him as the model of the solitary vocation and the true father of Palestinian monasticism.
saints.knownFor: Bringing the monastic life to Palestine.

saints.name: St. John Paul II
saints.title: Pope
saints.shortBlurb: The Polish pope of “Be not afraid,” whose long and missionary pontificate reshaped the modern Church…
biography: Karol Józef Wojtyła was born at Wadowice in Poland in 1920. When the Nazi occupation closed the Jagiellonian University, he laboured in a quarry and studied for the priesthood in a clandestine seminary, being ordained in 1946. Made auxiliary bishop of Kraków in 1958 and archbishop in 1964, he took a leading part in the Second Vatican Council and was created cardinal in 1967.

Elected pope on 16 October 1978 — the first non-Italian in 455 years and the first Slav to hold the office — he opened his pontificate with the words 'Be not afraid.' For nearly twenty-seven years he governed as a missionary pastor: 104 journeys outside Italy, fourteen encyclicals, the Catechism of the Catholic Church, and 483 canonizations, more than all his predecessors of five centuries together.

His witness helped to break communist rule in his homeland, and his last public suffering bore its own testimony before he died on 2 April 2005. Canonized in 2014, he is honoured on 22 October, the anniversary of his inauguration.
saints.knownFor: His long, missionary pontificate and defense of human dignity.

sources.text: Vatican biography, Canonization of St. John Paul II (vatican.va)

saints.name: St. John of Capistrano
saints.title: Priest
saints.shortBlurb: A Franciscan preacher and reformer who, at seventy, rallied the defenders of Belgrade against the Turks…
biography: Born at Capestrano in the Abruzzi in 1386, John studied law at Perugia and in 1412 was made governor of that city. Imprisoned in 1416 during the war with the Malatesta, he began in his cell the study of theology, and on his release entered the Friars Minor, becoming a disciple of Bernardine of Siena and one of the four pillars of the Franciscan Observant reform.

Ordained in 1425, he preached for thirty years across Italy and central Europe to crowds so vast — 126,000 at Brescia — that no church could hold them and he took to the public squares. After the fall of Constantinople, Pope Callixtus III sent him, already seventy, to preach the crusade against the advancing Turks.

In July 1456, beside the Hungarian captain John Hunyadi, he led the peasant host that broke the siege of Belgrade, earning the name of the Soldier Saint. He died of the plague at Ilok on 23 October that same year and was canonized in 1690. A lawyer by training, he is patron of jurists; the hero of Belgrade, of military chaplains.
saints.knownFor: Preaching reform and rallying the defense of Belgrade.

saints.name: St. Anthony Mary Claret
saints.title: Bishop
saints.shortBlurb: A Catalan weaver's son turned tireless missionary, founder of the Claretians and archbishop of Santiago de Cuba…
biography: Born at Sallent in Catalonia in 1807, the son of a weaver, Anthony Mary Claret followed his father's trade before entering the seminary at Vic; he was ordained in 1835 and gave himself to popular missions across Catalonia, preaching with a fire that filled the churches.

In 1849 he founded the Missionary Sons of the Immaculate Heart of Mary, the Claretians, and the next year was named Archbishop of Santiago de Cuba, where he reformed the clergy, visited every corner of his island diocese, and survived an attempt on his life.

Recalled to Spain in 1857 as confessor to Queen Isabella II, he used the court to spread good books until the revolution of 1868 drove him into exile with the queen. A tireless writer whose works number some two hundred, he died at the Cistercian abbey of Fontfroide in France in 1870 and was canonized by Pius XII in 1950. The weaver's son is honoured as patron of weavers.
saints.knownFor: Founding the Claretians and his tireless preaching.

sources.text: Vatican biography, Canonization of St. Anthony Mary Claret (vatican.va)

saints.name: Sts. Crispin and Crispinian
saints.title: Martyrs
saints.shortBlurb: Two brothers who preached the Gospel by day and made shoes by night, martyred at Soissons…
biography: Their legend, which dates from the eighth century, makes Crispin and Crispinian brothers of noble Roman birth who went as missionaries to Gaul and settled at Soissons. In imitation of the apostle Paul they worked with their hands as shoemakers, earning enough to support themselves and to aid the poor while they preached the faith.

In the persecution under Diocletian they were brought before the co-emperor Maximian Herculius, delivered to the cruel prefect Rictiovarus, tortured, and at last beheaded, on 25 October about the year 286. Their relics, first buried at Soissons, were carried in part to Rome and to Osnabrück.

Because they plied the awl and last for their living, they became the patrons of shoemakers, cobblers, tanners, and all workers in leather, whose guilds long kept their feast with processions and merrymaking. Through Shakespeare's Henry V, who fires his army before Agincourt — fought on their feast in 1415 — 'Saint Crispin's Day' holds a place in the language still.
saints.knownFor: Working as shoemakers while preaching the Gospel.

saints.name: St. Cedd
saints.title: Bishop
saints.shortBlurb: A Northumbrian monk trained at Lindisfarne who evangelized the East Saxons and founded Lastingham…
biography: One of four brothers who were all priests, among them Chad, Cedd was born in Northumbria about 620 and formed at Lindisfarne in the school of Aidan. In 653 he was sent with three fellow priests to evangelize the Middle Angles under the sub-king Peada, and soon after was dispatched to the East Saxons at the request of their king Sigeberht.

Consecrated bishop by Finan of Lindisfarne, he founded churches and the monasteries of Tilbury and Bradwell in Essex, and at the petition of Œthelwald of Deira planted Lastingham in Yorkshire, first purifying the site with a forty-day fast. Bede remembers a pastor who feared no man: Cedd excommunicated a nobleman living in an unlawful marriage and rebuked the king himself for defying the sentence.

At the Synod of Whitby in 664 he served as interpreter between the Celtic and Roman parties, and though schooled in the Irish observance he accepted the council's decision for the Roman Easter. Within the year he died of the plague at Lastingham on 26 October, and was succeeded as abbot by his brother Chad.
saints.knownFor: Evangelizing the East Saxons and founding Lastingham.

sources.text: Bede, Ecclesiastical History of the English People (public domain)

saints.name: St. Frumentius
saints.title: Bishop
saints.shortBlurb: A captive youth from Tyre who rose from slavery to become the apostle and first bishop of Ethiopia…
biography: The historian Rufinus, who had the story from Aedesius himself, tells how about the year 316 two brothers of Tyre, Frumentius and Aedesius, sailing with their uncle Meropius, were spared when their ship's company was massacred at a Red Sea port and were carried as slaves to the king of Axum in Ethiopia. Aedesius became the royal cupbearer; Frumentius, the king's secretary and treasurer.

Freed at the king's death, they stayed at the widowed queen's plea to guide the young heir Ezana, and Frumentius gathered the Christian merchants of the land to worship openly. When Ezana came of age, he journeyed to Alexandria and asked Athanasius for a bishop; Athanasius consecrated Frumentius himself, traditionally about the year 328.

Returning to Axum, he baptized King Ezana and countless of his people, planted the Ethiopian Church, and became its first Abuna; when the Arian emperor Constantius II demanded his removal about 356, the king refused. The Ethiopians name him Abba Salama, Father of Peace, and Kesate Birhan, Revealer of Light. He died about 383, honoured as the apostle and patron of Ethiopia.
saints.knownFor: Bringing Christianity to Ethiopia.

saints.name: Sts. Simon and Jude
saints.title: Apostles
saints.shortBlurb: Two of the Twelve honored together — Simon the Zealot and Jude Thaddaeus, invoked in desperate causes…
biography: Simon, called the Zealot for his zeal for the law of God, and Jude, named Thaddaeus and 'Judas of James' to mark him off from the betrayer, are both numbered among the Twelve. After Pentecost the Scriptures are silent about them, and only tradition tells of their later labors.

Jude is the author of the short catholic Epistle that bears his name, urging the faithful to 'contend earnestly for the faith once delivered to the saints' amid false teachers. Eusebius records that two grandsons of Jude, simple farmers, were questioned by the emperor Domitian and lived into the reign of Trajan.

An ancient Western tradition, kept in the Roman Martyrology, holds that Simon preached in Egypt and Jude in Mesopotamia, and that passing together into Persia they won numberless converts and there suffered martyrdom; Simon's emblem is the saw, by which his body is said to have been cut asunder.

Their relics are honoured in St. Peter's Basilica at Rome. Because his Epistle calls for perseverance in harsh and difficult days, Jude is invoked as the patron of hopeless and desperate causes, while Simon is the patron of tanners; the West keeps their feast together on 28 October.
saints.knownFor: Apostolic preaching; Jude, patron of desperate causes.

sources.text: Butler, Lives of the Saints (1866 ed.), 28 October

saints.name: St. Narcissus of Jerusalem
saints.title: Bishop
saints.shortBlurb: A bishop of Jerusalem famed for holiness and miracles who lived to an extreme old age…
biography: Eusebius, our chief witness, presents Narcissus as already a very old man when he became bishop of Jerusalem late in the second century. He presided with Theophilus of Caesarea over a council that decreed Easter should always be kept on a Sunday, and the wonders told of him include the changing of water into oil to supply the lamps of the church at the Easter vigil.

Certain men, the same historian relates, swore false oaths against him, and though the slanders were confuted, Narcissus quietly withdrew into solitude, leaving the see to be governed in his absence by three bishops in succession. When the falsehood was exposed, the people sought him out and unanimously begged him to return.

Because of his extreme age he was given Alexander as coadjutor — the first such arrangement on record — and together they governed the church. He died about the year 216, at an age the tradition reckons far past a hundred; the Church keeps his memory on 29 October, honouring him as a model of patience under calumny and of holiness in a long episcopate.
saints.knownFor: His long episcopate and holiness at Jerusalem.

saints.name: St. Alphonsus Rodríguez
saints.title: Religious
saints.shortBlurb: A widowed merchant who became a Jesuit doorkeeper and found sanctity in a humble office faithfully kept…
biography: Born at Segovia in 1532, the son of a wool merchant, Alphonsus inherited his father's business and married, only to be left a widower by the deaths of his wife and children in quick succession. Turning wholly to God, he was refused more than once before the Jesuits received him as a lay brother in 1571.

Sent to the college of Montesión at Palma de Majorca, he kept the door for more than forty years, running to open it with the words 'I am coming, Lord,' for he greeted every visitor as Christ himself. His hidden penances and wise counsel drew the whole island to his lodge; the young Peter Claver, who sought him out in 1605, he urged to the missions of the New World.

He died at Palma on 31 October 1617, and in 1888 Leo XIII canonized him on the same day as Peter Claver, the doorkeeper and his disciple raised to the altars together. The island he served from behind a door honours him as its patron.
saints.knownFor: Sanctity in the humble office of doorkeeper.

saints.name: St. Wolfgang
saints.title: Bishop
saints.shortBlurb: A monk and reforming bishop of Regensburg who tutored a future emperor and served the poor…
biography: Born in Swabia about 934 and schooled at Reichenau and Würzburg, Wolfgang taught in the cathedral school of Trier before entering the Benedictine abbey of Einsiedeln in 964; Ulrich of Augsburg ordained him priest in 968 and sent him to preach the Gospel to the Magyars in Pannonia.

Made bishop of Regensburg at Christmas 972, he gave the abbey of St. Emmeram back its own abbot, renewed the convents of his city, and founded that of Mittelmünster in 983. He tutored the young Henry, the future emperor and himself a saint, and with Ulrich and Conrad of Constance is counted one of the three great German bishops of his century.

For a year he lived as a hermit by the lake that still bears his name, until a hunter discovered him and he returned to his flock. He died at Pupping on the Danube in 994 while on a journey, was buried at St. Emmeram, and was canonized by Leo IX in 1052. He is patron of Regensburg, and is still invoked against strokes and apoplexy.
saints.knownFor: Reforming his diocese and tutoring an emperor.

saints.name: All Saints
saints.title: Solemnity of All the Saints
saints.shortBlurb: The Church's great feast of all the blessed in heaven, known and unknown, who share the vision of God…
biography: On this solemnity the Church honours the whole company of the blessed in heaven — not only those named in her calendar, but that great multitude which no man can number, out of every nation and people and tongue. The feast celebrates the communion of saints, the bond of prayer and charity uniting the pilgrim Church on earth with the Church triumphant in glory.

A common commemoration of all the martyrs arose early: Antioch kept it on the first Sunday after Pentecost, and the Syrians on 13 May. At Rome, on 13 May 609, Boniface IV consecrated the Pantheon, the gift of the emperor Phocas, as a church of Our Lady and All the Martyrs, and that date long remained the Roman feast.

Gregory III dedicated a chapel in St. Peter's to all the saints on 1 November, and in 835, at the desire of the emperor Louis the Pious, Gregory IV extended the November observance through the whole Frankish empire, whence it spread throughout the West. The day is kept as a holy day of obligation, honouring the known and the unknown blessed together.
saints.knownFor: Honouring the whole multitude of the blessed in heaven.

saints.name: The Commemoration of All the Faithful Departed
saints.title: All Souls' Day
saints.shortBlurb: The day the Church prays for all the faithful departed still being purified before they enter the joy of heaven…
biography: On this day the Church prays for all the faithful departed who died in God's grace yet still await purification in purgatory. The conviction is as old as Scripture: Judas Maccabeus sent an offering to Jerusalem for the sins of his fallen soldiers, and the sacred writer calls it 'a holy and wholesome thought to pray for the dead' (2 Maccabees 12:46).

The catacombs bear the same prayer scratched on the tombs of the first Roman Christians, and St. Monica begged her son Augustine to remember her at the altar. From such practice grew the Church's teaching that the living can aid the dead by Masses, prayers, and alms, and that the dead, once purified, pray for us in turn.

The general commemoration on 2 November spread from the monasteries of Cluny at the close of the tenth century. In 1915, amid the slaughter of the First World War, Benedict XV granted every priest leave to offer three Masses on this day for the dead; a plenary indulgence, applicable to the departed, is attached to visiting a cemetery in the first days of November.
saints.knownFor: Prayer and sacrifice offered for the souls in purgatory.

saints.name: St. Martin de Porres
saints.title: Religious
saints.shortBlurb: A Dominican lay brother of Lima whose charity to the poor and the sick knew no barrier of race or rank…
biography: Born at Lima on 9 December 1579, the illegitimate son of a Spanish nobleman, Juan de Porras, and Ana Velázquez, a freedwoman of African descent, Martin grew up in poverty after his father abandoned the family. Apprenticed as a boy to a barber-surgeon, he learned the trades of barbering and healing that he would practise all his life.

Because his mixed blood barred full profession under Peruvian law, he entered the Dominican priory of the Holy Rosary at Lima at fifteen as a donado, a volunteer servant, and professed vows as a lay brother only in 1603. As infirmarian he tended friars and townsfolk, nobles and African slaves, without distinction; his alms fed some 160 poor daily, and he founded an orphanage and a children's hospital.

A friend of Rose of Lima and Juan Macías, he was famed in his lifetime for humility, penance, and miraculous cures. He died at Lima on 3 November 1639, was beatified by Gregory XVI in 1837, and canonized by John XXIII in 1962. Because of his own parentage and his early trade, he is honoured as patron of mixed-race people, of barbers, and of all who work for interracial harmony.
saints.knownFor: Heroic charity to the poor and the sick as a Dominican lay brother.

sources.text: Vatican biography, Canonization of St. Martin de Porres (vatican.va)

saints.name: St. Charles Borromeo
saints.title: Bishop
saints.shortBlurb: The reforming Archbishop of Milan who turned the decrees of the Council of Trent into pastoral fact…
biography: Born on 2 October 1538 in the castle of Arona on Lake Maggiore, the son of Count Gilbert Borromeo and Margaret de' Medici, Charles took his doctorate in canon and civil law at Pavia. When his uncle was elected Pope Pius IV in 1559, he was called to Rome, created cardinal the next year, and made administrator of Milan at twenty-one.

As the pope's chief minister he laboured to reconvene the Council of Trent for its final sessions of 1562-63 and helped frame its Catechism. Made Archbishop of Milan in 1564, he entered the city the next year — its first resident archbishop in eighty years — and reformed it by synods, visitations, and seminaries, founding the Confraternity of Christian Doctrine to catechize the young.

When famine and plague struck Milan in 1576, he stayed while the governor fled, fed tens of thousands daily at his own cost, and ministered to the dying. Worn out, he died on 3 November 1584, aged forty-six, and was canonized by Paul V in 1610; his feast is kept the following day. As the Church's founder of seminaries and catechism classes, he is patron of bishops, seminarians, and catechists.
saints.knownFor: Reforming the Church after Trent as Archbishop of Milan.

saints.name: Sts. Zachary and Elizabeth
saints.title: Parents of St. John the Baptist
saints.shortBlurb: The righteous priest and his wife, kinswoman of the Virgin Mary, who in old age became parents of the Baptist…
biography: Zachary was a priest of the course of Abia, and his wife Elizabeth, of the daughters of Aaron, a kinswoman of the Blessed Virgin Mary. The Gospel of Luke calls them both righteous before God, walking blamelessly in all the commandments and ordinances of the Lord, yet they had no child, for Elizabeth was barren, and both were well advanced in years.

As Zachary offered incense in the Temple, the angel Gabriel foretold a son who would go before the Lord in the spirit and power of Elijah; struck dumb for his unbelief, the old priest recovered speech only at the boy's naming — 'His name is John' — and sang the Benedictus over the child who would be called the prophet of the Most High.

It was to Elizabeth, six months with child, that Mary hastened after the Annunciation; at her greeting the infant leaped in her womb, and, filled with the Holy Spirit, Elizabeth cried, 'Blessed art thou among women', hailing Mary as the mother of her Lord — words the Church still prays in the Hail Mary. The Roman Martyrology commemorates both parents of the Forerunner on this day.
saints.knownFor: The devout parents of St. John the Baptist.

sources.text: The Roman Martyrology (1914 English ed.; public domain)

saints.name: St. Leonard of Noblac
saints.title: Hermit
saints.shortBlurb: A Frankish hermit near Limoges long invoked by prisoners and by women in childbirth…
biography: According to his medieval Life, Leonard was a Frankish noble of the court of Clovis I, converted with the king at Christmas 496 and instructed by Remigius of Reims. Refusing the offer of a bishopric, he entered the monastery of Micy near Orléans, then withdrew to the forest of Pauvain near Limoges to live as a hermit.

Disciples gathered, and the community he founded at Noblac grew into the abbey and town of Saint-Léonard-de-Noblat. Tradition holds that Clovis granted him the right to visit prisons and set captives free, and that when the queen was safely delivered of a child through his prayers, the grateful king gave him the forest land for his monastery.

He died about 559 and was buried at Noblac. His cult spread swiftly after Bohemond of Antioch, freed from a Muslim prison in 1103, attributed his release to Leonard and made an offering at his tomb, which became a stage on the road to Compostela. Freed prisoners hung their chains at his shrine; hence his patronage of captives and, from the queen's deliverance, of women in childbirth.
saints.knownFor: Intercession for prisoners and women in childbirth.

saints.name: St. Willibrord
saints.title: Bishop
saints.shortBlurb: The Northumbrian monk who became the Apostle of the Frisians and first Archbishop of Utrecht…
biography: Born in Northumbria about 658, Willibrord was given as a child to the monastery of Ripon and formed under Wilfrid; from the age of twenty to thirty-two he lived at Rath Melsigi in Ireland under the abbot Egbert. In 690 he crossed to the Continent with eleven companions to preach the Gospel to the pagan Frisians, under the protection of Pepin of Herstal.

Twice he went to Rome for his mission's sake, and on 21 November 695 Pope Sergius I consecrated him bishop of the Frisians in the church of Santa Cecilia in Trastevere, giving him the name Clement. He fixed his see at Utrecht, as its first bishop, and in 698 founded the abbey of Echternach on land given by Irmina of Oeren.

When the pagan king Radbod retook Frisia in 716 and burned its churches, Willibrord withdrew to Echternach, returning after Radbod's death in 719 to rebuild, with the young Boniface at his side. He died at Echternach on 7 November 739, aged eighty-one, and lies buried there. Honoured as the Apostle of the Frisians, he is patron of the Netherlands and Luxembourg.
saints.knownFor: The evangelization of Frisia and the see of Utrecht.

saints.name: The Four Crowned Martyrs
saints.title: Martyrs
saints.shortBlurb: Roman martyrs of the Diocletian persecution honoured on the Caelian Hill from the earliest centuries…
biography: The Quattuor Coronati are among the most anciently venerated martyrs of Rome; their basilica has stood on the Caelian Hill since the fourth century. Their name gathers two intertwined traditions from the persecution of Diocletian, joined under one feast on 8 November.

One account honours five stonemasons of Sirmium in Pannonia — Claudius, Nicostratus, Symphorian, Castorius, and Simplicius — who, though willing to carve Cupids and the chariot of the Sun, refused to fashion a statue of Aesculapius for a heathen temple; condemned as Christians, they were sealed in leaden caskets and drowned in the River Save about the year 305.

The other tradition tells of four Roman soldiers beaten to death for refusing sacrifice to the same god, buried on the Via Labicana by Pope Miltiades and St. Sebastian; when their names were lost, they were venerated under the masons' names — hence four crowned ones. For the masons' craft they became patrons of stonemasons and sculptors, whose Florentine guild commissioned Nanni di Banco's famous group of them at Orsanmichele.
saints.knownFor: Ancient Roman martyrs venerated as patrons of stonemasons.

saints.name: The Dedication of the Lateran Basilica
saints.title: The Mother Church of Rome and of the World
saints.shortBlurb: The feast of the Lateran, cathedral of the Bishop of Rome and mother of all the churches of the city and the world…
biography: This feast, kept on 9 November since the twelfth century, honours the dedication of the Basilica of the Most Holy Saviour and of Sts. John the Baptist and John the Evangelist at the Lateran — the cathedral of the Pope as Bishop of Rome, which houses his cathedra, and the oldest and first in rank of the four great basilicas.

The site was the palace of the Laterani family, confiscated under Nero and come to Constantine through his wife Fausta; the emperor gave it to Pope Miltiades, and a synod against the Donatists met there in 313. The church was consecrated by Pope Sylvester I in 324 and dedicated to Christ the Saviour; the two St. Johns were added as its patrons in the tenth and twelfth centuries.

For a thousand years the adjoining Lateran Palace was the residence of the popes, and five ecumenical councils met within its halls. The inscription on its front proclaims it the mother and head of all the churches of the city and of the world; its feast is therefore kept by the whole Western Church as a celebration of unity around the See of Peter rather than of any one saint.
saints.knownFor: The cathedral of the Pope, mother of all churches.

saints.name: St. Leo the Great
saints.title: Pope and Doctor of the Church
saints.shortBlurb: The pope whose Tome guided the Council of Chalcedon and who turned back Attila from the gates of Rome…
biography: A Tuscan by birth, Leo was archdeacon of Rome, known even abroad, when he was sent to Gaul on imperial business; in his absence Sixtus III died, and in 440 he was elected Bishop of Rome. He governed for twenty-one years through heresy and invasion, stamping out Manichaeism in Rome and asserting the primacy of his see from Gaul to Africa.

His dogmatic letter to Flavian of Constantinople, the Tome of Leo, confessed the two natures united in the one person of Christ; ignored at the Robber Synod of Ephesus in 449, it was read at the Council of Chalcedon in 451, where the fathers cried, 'Peter has spoken through Leo.'

In 452 he met Attila the Hun near Lake Garda and won his withdrawal from Italy; three years later he faced Genseric's Vandals and, though he could not prevent the sack, saved the city from fire and slaughter and its basilicas from violation. He died on 10 November 461, the first pope buried in St. Peter's; Benedict XIV declared him a Doctor of the Church in 1754.
saints.knownFor: The Tome of Leo and the defence of the faith at Chalcedon.

canonization.canonized: Venerated from antiquity; Doctor of the Church (1754)

sources.text: Catholic Encyclopedia (1913), “Pope St. Leo I (the Great)”

saints.name: St. Martin of Tours
saints.title: Bishop
saints.shortBlurb: The soldier who cut his cloak for a beggar, then left the army to become a monk and bishop of Tours…
biography: Born about 316 at Sabaria in Pannonia, the son of a Roman tribune, Martin was a catechumen at ten and a conscript cavalryman at fifteen. At the gate of Amiens he met a naked beggar and, having nothing else, cut his cloak in two with his sword; that night he saw Christ in a dream wearing the half he had given away.

Baptized at eighteen, he refused at last to fight, telling the Emperor Julian, 'I am the soldier of Christ: it is not lawful for me to fight.' Released, he became the disciple of Hilary of Poitiers and founded Ligugé, the earliest known monastery in Gaul. In 371 the people of Tours made him their bishop against his will.

As bishop he lived as a monk at Marmoutier across the Loire, laboured to convert the pagan countryside, and pleaded in vain at Trier for the life of the heretic Priscillian. He died at Candes on 8 November 397 and was buried at Tours on 11 November, his feast. His cloak gave its name, cappa, to the chapel and the chaplain. He is patron of soldiers, beggars, and France.
saints.knownFor: Sharing his cloak with a beggar; monk and bishop of Gaul.

sources.text: Butler, Lives of the Saints (1866 ed.), 11 November

saints.name: St. Josaphat
saints.title: Bishop and Martyr
saints.shortBlurb: The Ruthenian archbishop and monk who gave his life for the union of the Eastern Church with Rome…
biography: Born about 1580 at Volodymyr in Volhynia and baptized John Kuncevyc, he was apprenticed to a merchant at Vilnius, where he came under the influence of Josyf Rutsky and of the Union of Brest, which had reconciled the Ruthenian Church with Rome while keeping its Byzantine rite. In 1604 he entered the Basilian monastery of the Holy Trinity at Vilnius, taking the name Josaphat.

Ordained priest in 1609, he preached the union tirelessly, winning back nobles, clergy, and whole towns, so that his opponents nicknamed him the soul-snatcher. Consecrated in 1617, he succeeded the next year as Archbishop of Polotsk, rebuilt its cathedral, issued a catechism, held synods, and lived with the austerity of a monk in hair shirt and chains.

On 12 November 1623 a mob at Vitebsk stormed his house, struck him down with an axe, and cast his body into the Dvina. Beatified in 1643 and canonized by Pius IX in 1867, he was the first saint of the Eastern-rite churches formally canonized by Rome; his body rests under the altar of St. Basil in St. Peter's. He is honoured as patron of Christian unity and of Ukraine.
saints.knownFor: Martyrdom for the union of the Eastern churches with Rome.

saints.name: St. Frances Xavier Cabrini
saints.title: Virgin
saints.shortBlurb: The Italian foundress who crossed the ocean to serve immigrants and became the first United States citizen canonized…
biography: Born on 15 July 1850 at Sant'Angelo Lodigiano near Lodi, the youngest of a farmer's thirteen children, Frances Cabrini was frail from birth and twice refused by religious orders for her health. Trained as a teacher, in 1880 she founded at Codogno the Missionary Sisters of the Sacred Heart of Jesus, taking Xavier as her name for the patron of missions, for she longed to go to China.

Summoned to Rome in 1887, she was told by Leo XIII to go not to the East but to the West — to the Italian immigrants of America. Landing in New York on 31 March 1889 with six sisters, she was bidden by the archbishop to sail home; she answered that she had letters from the pope, and stayed.

Over twenty-eight years she founded sixty-seven schools, orphanages, and hospitals across the United States, Latin America, and Europe, crossing the ocean twenty-four times and the Andes by mule. Naturalized an American citizen in 1909, she died at Columbus Hospital in Chicago on 22 December 1917. Canonized by Pius XII in 1946, the first American citizen raised to the altars, she was named patroness of immigrants in 1950.
saints.knownFor: Founding schools and hospitals for immigrants in the Americas.

sources.text: Vatican biography, Canonization of St. Frances Xavier Cabrini (vatican.va)

saints.name: St. Lawrence O'Toole
saints.title: Bishop
saints.shortBlurb: The reforming Archbishop of Dublin who shepherded his people through the Norman conquest of Ireland…
biography: Born in 1128 at Kilkea in County Kildare, the son of a Leinster chieftain, Lorcán Ua Tuathail was handed over at the age of ten as a hostage to Dermot MacMurrough and held for two years in harsh custody. Freed through the abbot of Glendalough, he stayed on as a monk, and at twenty-six was himself elected abbot, reforming the abbey on Augustinian lines.

In 1162 he was chosen Archbishop of Dublin, the first Gael to hold that Hiberno-Norse see; he fed the poor daily at his table and lived in hair shirt and fast. When Norman knights stormed Dublin in 1170 while he negotiated outside its walls, he rushed back and stopped the slaughter; thereafter Gael, Norse, and Norman alike sought him as mediator.

Clubbed down by a madman while saying Mass at Becket's tomb in Canterbury, he rose and finished the Mass. He attended the Third Lateran Council in 1179 and was named papal legate. On a last embassy to Henry II he fell ill and died at Eu in Normandy on 14 November 1180; canonized in 1225, he is patron of the Archdiocese of Dublin.
saints.knownFor: Reform of the Church and peacemaking during the Norman invasion.

saints.name: St. Albert the Great
saints.title: Bishop and Doctor of the Church
saints.shortBlurb: The Dominican polymath and teacher of Thomas Aquinas, called the Universal Doctor…
biography: Born about 1200 at Lauingen in Swabia, Albert entered the Order of Preachers in 1223. After lecturing in the German houses he took his doctorate at Paris in 1245, where the young Thomas Aquinas became his pupil, and in 1248 the two returned together to Cologne to found the order's studium generale there.

His learning embraced theology, philosophy, and the natural sciences so fully that he was called Doctor Universalis, the Universal Doctor. He commented on nearly the whole of Aristotle and laboured to show that the newly recovered pagan wisdom could serve the Christian faith, recording his own observations of plants, animals, and minerals.

Provincial of the German Dominicans from 1254, he was made Bishop of Regensburg by Pope Alexander IV in 1260 but resigned the see after three years to resume teaching, and in old age he journeyed to Paris to defend Aquinas's doctrine against its critics.

He died at Cologne on 15 November 1280. Beatified in 1622, he was canonized and declared a Doctor of the Church by Pope Pius XI in 1931. Because he joined the study of creation to the study of its Maker, he is a patron of natural scientists and students.
saints.knownFor: Uniting the natural sciences with theology and teaching St. Thomas Aquinas.

canonization.canonized: 1931 by Pope Pius XI, who declared him a Doctor of the Church

saints.name: St. Margaret of Scotland
saints.title: Queen
saints.shortBlurb: The saintly queen of Scots who reformed the Scottish Church and spent herself in prayer and care of the poor…
biography: Born about 1045 in Hungary, where her father Edward the Exile, heir of the old English royal line, had found refuge, Margaret was brought back to England in 1057 and fled north after the Norman Conquest; her ship was driven ashore in Scotland, and in 1070 she married King Malcolm III at Dunfermline.

Mother of eight children — among them three kings of Scotland and Matilda, wife of King Henry I of England — she joined assiduous prayer and fasting to daily service of the poor, feeding orphans with her own hands and establishing a ferry across the Firth of Forth for pilgrims on the way to St Andrews.

With the king's support she pressed for the reform of the Scottish Church, holding councils that corrected its practices, building the abbey church of the Holy Trinity at Dunfermline, and restoring the monastery of Iona; she also softened the rough manners of the court.

When Malcolm and their eldest son Edward fell at Alnwick on 13 November 1093, Margaret, already failing, died three days later at Edinburgh Castle, on 16 November 1093. Canonized by Pope Innocent IV in 1250, she was named patroness of Scotland in 1673.
saints.knownFor: Reform of the Scottish Church and her charity as queen.

saints.name: St. Elizabeth of Hungary
saints.title: Religious
saints.shortBlurb: The young princess and widow who spent herself and her wealth on the sick and the poor…
biography: Born in 1207, a daughter of King Andrew II of Hungary, Elizabeth was sent as a small child to the court of Thuringia and married at fourteen, in 1221, to the young Landgrave Louis IV. Their marriage was happy and devout; together they relieved the famine-stricken poor, and Elizabeth built a hospital beneath the Wartburg, tending the sick with her own hands.

When Louis died of plague at Otranto in 1227 on his way to the crusade, the twenty-year-old widow refused a second marriage. Under the direction of her confessor Conrad of Marburg she became one of the first Franciscan tertiaries in Germany, renounced her rank, and spent her dowry founding a hospital at Marburg, where she nursed the most wretched, above all lepers.

Worn out by austerity and ceaseless service, she died at Marburg on 17 November 1231, aged twenty-four, and was canonized by Pope Gregory IX at Perugia only four years later, in 1235. The beloved legend of the loaves she carried to the poor being changed to roses explains her patronage of bakers; she is likewise a patroness of charities and of the Franciscan Third Order.
saints.knownFor: Her charity to the poor and sick as a widowed Franciscan tertiary.

saints.name: St. Rose Philippine Duchesne
saints.title: Virgin
saints.shortBlurb: The French missionary of the Sacred Heart who carried Catholic education to the American frontier…
biography: Born at Grenoble in 1769, Rose Philippine Duchesne entered the Visitation convent there as a young woman, to be driven out with her sisters when the Revolution closed the religious houses. In 1804 she joined the Society of the Sacred Heart under Madeleine Sophie Barat, longing for the missions.

In 1818, at the request of Bishop Louis Du Bourg of Louisiana, she sailed for America with four companions, settling at St. Charles, Missouri, where she opened in a log cabin the first free school west of the Mississippi. From Florissant she founded within a decade six houses of her society, including schools, an orphanage, and its first American novitiate.

At seventy-one she realized her dream, joining the Jesuit mission to the Potawatomi at Sugar Creek in Kansas in 1841. Too frail for work and unable to master the language, she spent long hours before the Blessed Sacrament, and the watching Indians named her Quah-kah-ka-num-ad, the Woman-Who-Prays-Always.

After a year she returned to St. Charles, where she died on 18 November 1852, aged eighty-three. Beatified in 1940 and canonized by Pope John Paul II in 1988, she is honoured in the United States as a patroness of perseverance amid adversity.
saints.knownFor: Pioneering Catholic education on the American frontier.

sources.text: Vatican biography, Canonization of St. Rose Philippine Duchesne (vatican.va)

saints.name: St. Mechtilde of Hackeborn
saints.title: Virgin
saints.shortBlurb: The Benedictine nun of Helfta whose visions of the Heart of Christ were treasured by St. Gertrude the Great…
biography: Born about 1241 at the castle of Helfta near Eisleben, of the noble Thuringian house of Hackeborn, Mechtilde was entrusted as a child of seven to the monastery of Rodarsdorf, where her elder sister Gertrude was a nun and later abbess. In 1258 the community transferred to Helfta.

Gifted with a beautiful voice, she was made choir mistress, and her sisters named her the nightingale of Christ for the sweetness of her chant. To her care the abbess committed the young Gertrude, later called the Great, who revered Mechtilde as her spiritual mother and teacher.

In her later years Mechtilde confided to Gertrude and another sister the graces of her prayer, and they wrote them down, at first without her knowledge; when she learned of it, Christ Himself, she said, bade her name the work the Book of Special Grace. Its pages, steeped in Scripture and the liturgy, are among the earliest witnesses of devotion to the Sacred Heart.

She died at Helfta on 19 November 1298, in her fifty-eighth year. Her book, translated into many tongues, carried the mysticism of the Helfta nuns throughout late medieval Europe, and her cult has continued unbroken in the Church ever since.
saints.knownFor: The mystical revelations recorded in the Book of Special Grace.

sources.text: The Roman Martyrology (1914 English ed.; public domain)

saints.name: St. Edmund the Martyr
saints.title: King and Martyr
saints.shortBlurb: The king of East Anglia who chose death rather than deny Christ or betray his Christian people…
biography: Born about 841, Edmund was chosen king of the East Angles as a boy of about fourteen and crowned, tradition says, on Christmas Day 855. He ruled for fourteen years with a reputation for justice and piety, having, it was remembered, learned the whole Psalter by heart.

In 865 the Great Heathen Army of the Danes fell upon England, and after overrunning Northumbria and Mercia it turned, under Ivar and Ubba, against East Anglia. Edmund's forces were defeated; the king was taken and pressed to renounce Christ and to reign as a vassal of the heathen invaders.

Refusing, he was bound to a tree, scourged, shot through with arrows until, as his earliest biographer wrote, he bristled like a hedgehog, and at last beheaded, on 20 November 869, at a place called Haegelisdun, identified by tradition with Hoxne in Suffolk.

His body was enshrined at the abbey of Bury, which took his name — Bury St Edmunds — and his Passion, written by Abbo of Fleury about 985, spread his cult across England, where he was venerated as a patron of the realm until St George took his place in the later Middle Ages.
saints.knownFor: Dying rather than deny Christ under the Danish invaders.

saints.name: The Presentation of the Blessed Virgin Mary
saints.title: Memorial of the Blessed Virgin Mary
saints.shortBlurb: The memorial of Mary's dedication to God in the Temple as a young girl, all her life consecrated to the Lord…
biography: This memorial, kept on 21 November, honours the presentation of the child Mary in the Temple at Jerusalem. The canonical Gospels do not record the event; it comes from the Protoevangelium of James, an apocryphal writing which relates that at three years of age Mary was brought by her parents to the Temple in fulfillment of a vow, to be reared in the Lord's service.

The feast arose in the Christian East, probably in Syria, the home of those apocrypha; it stands in Byzantine liturgical books by the eleventh century and was a recognized festival under Manuel Comnenus in 1166. In the West it was introduced at Avignon by Philippe de Mazieres and celebrated before the cardinals in 1372, spreading thence to Paris and the German dioceses.

Sixtus IV received it into the Roman Breviary, Pius V struck it from the calendar, and Sixtus V restored it in 1585, and it has been kept in the Roman rite ever since. Its lesson is not a single scene but the truth the scene expresses: that Mary was wholly given to God from her earliest years, a living temple made ready for the coming of the Lord.
saints.knownFor: Mary's consecration to God from her childhood.

sources.text: Catholic Encyclopedia (1913), “Feast of the Presentation of Mary”

saints.name: St. Cecilia
saints.title: Virgin and Martyr
saints.shortBlurb: A Roman virgin and martyr of the early Church, honored from ancient times as the patroness of music…
biography: Cecilia was a noble Roman maiden of the early third century who, according to her ancient Acts, had secretly vowed her virginity to God. Given in marriage to a pagan named Valerian, she told him an angel guarded her vow; Valerian was baptized, as was his brother Tiburtius, and both, with the officer Maximus, died as martyrs.

Refusing to sacrifice, Cecilia was shut in her own bath to be suffocated; emerging unharmed, she was struck three times with a sword and lingered three days, giving her goods to the poor before Pope Urban buried her in the catacomb of Callixtus. Tradition places her death about 230.

In 821 Pope Paschal I translated her relics to the basilica of Santa Cecilia in Trastevere, over the house venerated as hers; when her tomb was opened in 1599, her body lay in the posture in which Stefano Maderno carved it in marble. Her name stands in the Roman Canon of the Mass.

Because her Acts relate that as the wedding music sounded she sang in her heart to the Lord alone, she has been honoured for centuries as the patroness of musicians, composers, and church music, and is still so invoked today.
saints.knownFor: Her martyrdom; patroness of music.

sources.text: Butler, Lives of the Saints (1866 ed.), 22 November

saints.name: St. Clement I
saints.title: Pope and Martyr
saints.shortBlurb: One of the first successors of St. Peter, whose letter to Corinth is among the oldest Christian writings after the New Testament…
biography: Clement was bishop of Rome near the close of the first century, counted third in succession from Peter after Linus and Anacletus; Irenaeus attests that he had seen the Apostles and heard their preaching, and early writers identified him with the Clement whom Paul names as a fellow labourer.

His one sure writing is the letter sent from the Roman Church to Corinth about the year 96, when dissension had cast out the appointed presbyters there. It is the earliest surviving exercise of Rome's authority over another church and was still read aloud at Corinth in the following century.

Later tradition holds that under Trajan he was banished to the Chersonesus and cast into the sea bound to an anchor, dying about the year 100; the anchor became his emblem, and mariners claim him as patron. Cyril and Methodius brought what were held to be his relics from the Crimea to Rome, to the basilica of San Clemente.

His name stands in the Roman Canon of the Mass among the first popes, and his letter to Corinth remains one of the most precious witnesses to the life and order of the Church in the age immediately after the Apostles.
saints.knownFor: His early letter to the Corinthians and his witness as an apostolic pope.

saints.name: St. Andrew Dung-Lac and Companions
saints.title: Martyrs
saints.shortBlurb: The many martyrs of Vietnam — priests, catechists, and laity — who died for the faith across three centuries of persecution…
biography: This memorial honours one hundred and seventeen martyrs of Vietnam put to death for the faith between 1745 and 1862 — ninety-six Vietnamese and twenty-one European missionaries, among them bishops, priests, catechists, and lay men and women. They stand for a far greater company, for in those centuries of persecution an estimated one to three hundred thousand died for Christ.

Their name-saint, Andrew Dung-Lac, was born about 1795 near Bac Ninh; instructed and baptized by a catechist after his family moved to Hanoi, he himself became a catechist and, in 1823, a priest. Arrested more than once, he was beheaded at Hanoi on 21 December 1839 under the Emperor Minh Mang.

Persecution came in waves under the Nguyen emperors, who outlawed the Gospel's preaching and commanded Christians to trample the crucifix; among the martyrs were the Spanish Dominican bishop Ignatius Delgado and the French priest Theophane Venard, beheaded in 1861 after months in a cage.

Beatified in four groups between 1900 and 1951, the one hundred and seventeen were canonized together by Pope John Paul II on 19 June 1988, and through them all of Vietnam's unnamed witnesses are remembered; they are honoured as patrons of the Church in Vietnam.
saints.knownFor: The witness of the Vietnamese martyrs under persecution.

sources.text: Vatican biography, Canonization of the Martyrs of Vietnam (vatican.va)

saints.name: St. Catherine of Alexandria
saints.title: Virgin and Martyr
saints.shortBlurb: A learned virgin-martyr of the early Church, honoured as a patroness of philosophers and students…
biography: According to her ancient and beloved passion, Catherine was a noblewoman of Alexandria of singular learning, born late in the third century. Converted to Christ as a young woman, she rebuked the Emperor Maxentius for persecuting the Church, whereupon he summoned fifty of the empire's best philosophers to refute her; she confuted them, and they, converted, were put to death.

Imprisoned and scourged, she converted the empress herself and the officer set to guard her. Condemned to die upon a spiked wheel, she saw it shattered at her prayer, and was at last beheaded, about the year 305; legend holds that angels bore her body to Mount Sinai.

Her relics are venerated to this day in the monastery on Sinai built by the Emperor Justinian, which bears her name, and her cult, carried west by returning crusaders, made her one of the most beloved saints of the Middle Ages and one of the Fourteen Holy Helpers.

Her feast, removed from the general calendar in 1969, was restored in 2002. Because she overcame the learned in debate, she is a patroness of philosophers and students; because of the wheel of her passion, of wheelwrights and all who work with wheels.
saints.knownFor: Confounding pagan philosophers and dying for the faith.

saints.name: St. Leonard of Port Maurice
saints.title: Priest
saints.shortBlurb: The great Franciscan missionary preacher of Italy who spread the devotion of the Stations of the Cross…
biography: Born Paolo Girolamo Casanova at Porto Maurizio on the Ligurian coast in 1676, Leonard studied with the Jesuits at the Roman College and in 1697 joined the Franciscans of the Strict Observance at the friary of San Bonaventura on the Palatine. Ordained in 1703, he gave himself for nearly fifty years to the preaching of popular missions.

In more than three hundred missions across Italy he drew crowds the churches could not hold, preaching in the open air; Clement XII and Benedict XIV both employed him on delicate commissions. He also ardently promoted devotion to the Blessed Sacrament, the Sacred Heart, and the Immaculate Conception.

He did more than any man of his age to spread the Way of the Cross, erecting nearly six hundred sets of Stations across Italy, including those within the Colosseum in Rome, where the popes still walk the Way on Good Friday.

True to a promise made to Benedict XIV, he came to Rome to die, at San Bonaventura on 26 November 1751. Beatified in 1796 and canonized in 1867, he was declared by Pope Pius XI in 1923 the heavenly patron of all who preach parish missions.
saints.knownFor: Popular missions and the spread of the Stations of the Cross.

sources.text: Catholic Encyclopedia (1913), “St. Leonard of Port Maurice”

saints.name: St. Virgil of Salzburg
saints.title: Bishop
saints.shortBlurb: An Irish monk and man of learning who became Bishop of Salzburg and Apostle of Carinthia…
biography: Born in Ireland about the year 700 and named Fergal, Virgil was a monk of great learning who left his homeland about 741 and spent two years at the court of Pepin the Short. Sent by Pepin to Duke Odilo of Bavaria, he was made abbot of St. Peter's at Salzburg and governed the church of that city as abbot for many years before being consecrated its bishop, about 767.

A man of unusual scientific curiosity, he taught that the earth is a sphere with another world and other men beneath it — the so-called antipodes — a cosmological opinion for which St. Boniface denounced him to Pope Zachary about 748. The pope ordered an inquiry, but the charge, which touched no article of faith, came to nothing.

Virgil built Salzburg's first cathedral, consecrated in 774, translating thither the relics of St. Rupert from Worms, and he sent missionaries among the pagan Slavs of Carinthia, for whom he is called the Apostle of Carinthia. He died at Salzburg on 27 November 784 and was canonized by Pope Gregory IX in 1233.
saints.knownFor: The see of Salzburg and the evangelization of Carinthia.

saints.name: St. Catherine Labouré
saints.title: Virgin
saints.shortBlurb: The humble Daughter of Charity to whom Our Lady entrusted the Miraculous Medal…
biography: Born Zoé Labouré on 2 May 1806 at Fain-lès-Moutiers in Burgundy, the ninth of eleven children of a farming family, Catherine lost her mother while still a child and thereafter kept her father's house. In 1830 she entered the Daughters of Charity of St. Vincent de Paul, joining the novitiate in the Rue du Bac, Paris, that April.

That same year the Blessed Virgin appeared to her in the convent chapel: first in July, foretelling sorrows to come upon France, then on 27 November 1830, standing upon a globe with rays of grace streaming from her hands, encircled by the invocation 'O Mary, conceived without sin, pray for us who have recourse to thee,' and bidding her have a medal struck after this model.

Catherine confided the visions only to her confessor, Father Aladel; the medal, struck in 1832, spread so swiftly that it was called the Miraculous Medal, its maker unknown. Sent in 1831 to a hospice at Reuilly, she spent nearly half a century caring for aged men in obscurity, revealing her secret only months before her death on 31 December 1876. She was canonized by Pope Pius XII in 1947.
saints.knownFor: The apparitions that gave the Church the Miraculous Medal.

sources.text: Vatican biography, Canonization of St. Catherine Labouré (vatican.va)

saints.name: St. Saturninus of Toulouse
saints.title: Bishop and Martyr
saints.shortBlurb: The first bishop of Toulouse, dragged to his death by a bull for refusing to worship idols…
biography: Saturninus, venerated in his own city as Sernin, was sent from Rome by Pope Fabian about the year 245, one of the seven bishops tradition assigns to the evangelization of Gaul. Fixing his see at Toulouse in 250, in the consulate of Decius and Gratus, he is accounted the first bishop of that city, converting many idolaters, says Fortunatus, by his preaching and miracles.

His ancient acts relate that his daily path to his church led past the Capitol, the chief temple of the city, where the oracles fell dumb at his passing. The pagan priests seized him and demanded that he sacrifice; when he refused, confessing one God, they bound him to a bull kept for the altar and goaded the beast, which dashed his head against the Capitol steps.

Thus he won his crown about the year 257, on 29 November. His relics were later gathered by Bishop Exuperius and now rest in the great basilica of Saint-Sernin, begun in 1080 and still the glory of Toulouse, while the church of Notre-Dame du Taur marks the place where the bull halted and his body was recovered.
saints.knownFor: The first bishop and martyr of Toulouse.

saints.name: St. Andrew
saints.title: Apostle
saints.shortBlurb: The brother of Simon Peter, first-called of the Apostles, who brought others to Christ and died on the X-shaped cross…
biography: A fisherman of Bethsaida in Galilee, son of Jonah and brother of Simon Peter, Andrew was first a disciple of John the Baptist. Hearing John cry, 'Behold the Lamb of God,' he followed Jesus and found his brother, saying, 'We have found the Messiah' — whence the East calls him Protokletos, the First-Called.

In the Gospels he is ever bringing others to Christ: the boy with the five barley loaves, and the Greeks who wished to see Jesus. After Pentecost the Fathers assign him mission fields — Scythia to Eusebius, Achaia to Jerome, Epirus to Gregory Nazianzen.

Tradition holds him crucified at Patras by order of the proconsul Aegeas, bound to a cross on which he hung two days preaching; later ages picture his cross as X-shaped. His relics were carried to Constantinople in 357, and what was brought to Rome was returned to Patras by Pope Paul VI in 1964.

He is patron of fishermen, whose trade he plied on the Sea of Galilee; of Scotland, where legend says St. Rule brought his relics and where his saltire flies; of Greece, where he died; and of Russia, whose chroniclers told of his journey up the Dnieper.
saints.knownFor: The first-called Apostle who brought others to Christ.

sources.text: Butler, Lives of the Saints (1866 ed.), 30 November

saints.name: St. Edmund Campion
saints.title: Priest and Martyr
saints.shortBlurb: An Oxford scholar who became a Jesuit and returned in secret to Elizabethan England, where he was betrayed, racked, and hanged for the faith…
biography: Born in London on 25 January 1540, the son of a Catholic bookseller, Edmund Campion rose to be one of the brightest lights of Oxford: a scholar and junior fellow of St. John's College at seventeen, he delivered the Latin address welcoming Queen Elizabeth to the university in 1566, and was marked out by the great for advancement.

Conscience drew him another way. He left England, was reconciled to the Church at Douai, and in Rome in 1573 entered the Society of Jesus, being ordained priest at Prague in 1578. Sent on the English mission, he landed at Dover in disguise in June 1580 and ministered in secret to persecuted Catholics, publishing his Ten Reasons (Decem Rationes) from a hidden press at Stonor Park.

Betrayed, he was taken at Lyford Grange in July 1581 and imprisoned in the Tower, where he was racked and offered freedom if he would conform. Condemned at Westminster on a fabricated charge of treason, he was hanged, drawn, and quartered at Tyburn on 1 December 1581 with Ralph Sherwin and Alexander Briant. Canonized in 1970 by Pope Paul VI among the Forty Martyrs of England and Wales.
saints.knownFor: The most celebrated of the English Jesuit martyrs under Elizabeth I.

canonization.canonized: 1970 by Pope Paul VI, among the Forty Martyrs of England and Wales

sources.text: Vatican biography, Canonization of the Forty Martyrs of England and Wales (vatican.va)

saints.name: St. Chromatius of Aquileia
saints.title: Bishop of Aquileia
saints.shortBlurb: The bishop of Aquileia and biblical commentator who befriended Jerome and worked as a craftsman of peace in a troubled age…
biography: Born at Aquileia about 345, Chromatius was a priest of that church — it was he who baptized Rufinus about 371 — and in 388, on the death of Bishop Valerian, was chosen bishop of his native city, one of the great sees of the West. He ruled it for some twenty years, a pastor after the pattern of his friend Ambrose.

A man of letters, he was the friend and encourager of St. Jerome, who dedicated to him his translations of Chronicles, Tobit, and the books of Solomon, and who undertook the Latin translation of the Old Testament at his urging. To Rufinus he gave the task of translating Eusebius's Ecclesiastical History, and when Jerome and Rufinus fell out bitterly over Origen, he labored to reconcile them.

His own sermons and tractates on St. Matthew's Gospel survive. He defended St. John Chrysostom, writing to the Emperor Honorius in his cause, and shepherded his flock through the terror of Alaric's invasion, Aquileia being besieged in 401. He died about 407, on the eve of the Goth's second descent upon Italy.
saints.knownFor: Bishop of Aquileia, biblical commentator, and friend of St. Jerome.

sources.text: The Roman Martyrology (1914 English ed.; public domain)

saints.name: St. Francis Xavier
saints.title: Priest
saints.shortBlurb: A companion of Ignatius Loyola and the greatest missionary since the Apostles, who carried the Gospel to India and Japan…
biography: Born 7 April 1506 at the castle of Xavier in Navarre, Francis studied at Paris, where he lodged with Ignatius of Loyola and became one of seven companions who took vows at Montmartre on 15 August 1534. Ordained at Venice in 1537, he was sent by Ignatius at King John III of Portugal's request to evangelize the Indies, sailing from Lisbon in April 1541 as papal legate.

Landing at Goa on 6 May 1542, he labored for ten years with tireless charity — among the pearl fishers of the Fishery Coast, in Malacca and the Moluccas, and in Japan, which he entered at Kagoshima in August 1549, the first to plant the faith there. Wherever he went he taught, baptized, and lived among the poorest.

Resolved to enter China, then closed to foreigners, he died of fever on the island of Shangchuan within sight of its coast on 3 December 1552, aged forty-six. His body, brought to Goa, rests in the church of Bom Jesus. Canonized in 1622, he was declared by Pope Pius XI in 1927 patron of the missions he so greatly served.
saints.knownFor: The Apostle of the Indies and of Japan.

sources.text: Butler, Lives of the Saints (1866 ed.), 3 December

saints.name: St. John Damascene
saints.title: Priest and Doctor of the Church
saints.shortBlurb: A monk of the Judean desert whose defense of holy images and vast synthesis of the faith earned him the title Doctor of the Church…
biography: Born about 675 into the Mansur family, a Christian house of Damascus whose men served as financial officers of the caliphs, John succeeded his father in that charge before renouncing it to become a monk at the laura of St. Sabas near Jerusalem, whither he went with his adopted brother Cosmas. There he was ordained priest by the Patriarch of Jerusalem.

From that desert safety, beyond the emperor's reach, he wrote his three discourses in defense of the holy images when Leo the Isaurian ordered their destruction, distinguishing the worship due to God from the veneration of icons and saints. For this the iconoclast council of 754, after his death, cursed him by name.

His great work, the Fount of Knowledge, crowned by the Exact Exposition of the Orthodox Faith, gathered the teaching of the Greek Fathers into an ordered whole that served both East and West; he wrote also hymns still sung. He died about 749 and was declared a Doctor of the Church by Leo XIII in 1890.
saints.knownFor: Defending sacred images and summing up the theology of the Greek Fathers.

canonization.canonized: Venerated from antiquity; declared Doctor of the Church in 1890 by Pope Leo XIII

sources.text: Butler, Lives of the Saints (1866 ed.), 4 December

saints.name: St. Sabbas
saints.title: Abbot
saints.shortBlurb: A father of Eastern monasticism who founded the Great Lavra above the Kidron valley and defended the faith of Chalcedon…
biography: Born in 439 at Mutalaska near Caesarea in Cappadocia, Sabbas entered a neighboring monastery at the age of eight. At eighteen he went to Jerusalem and placed himself under St. Euthymius the Great, and after his master's death withdrew to a cave in the ravine of the Kidron, southeast of the city, living as a solitary.

Disciples gathered, and in 483 he founded there the Great Lavra, called after him Mar Saba, which grew to a hundred and fifty monks and stands to this day. Ordained priest in 491, he was made archimandrite of all the lauras of the Judaean desert in 494, the acknowledged father of Palestinian monasticism.

Twice he journeyed to Constantinople on behalf of his people: to Anastasius for the exiled Patriarch Elias, and in 531 to Justinian, winning relief for Palestine after the Samaritan revolt. He died at the Lavra on 5 December 532, aged ninety-four; his life was written by Cyril of Scythopolis, and Mar Saba later sheltered St. John Damascene.
saints.knownFor: Founder of the Great Lavra (Mar Saba) and father of Palestinian monasticism.

sources.text: Butler, Lives of the Saints (1866 ed.), 5 December

saints.name: St. Nicholas
saints.title: Bishop of Myra
saints.shortBlurb: The fourth-century bishop of Myra whose renown for secret generosity made him, in legend and love, the patron of children and of sailors…
biography: Born about 270 at Patara in Lycia, Nicholas was orphaned of wealthy parents and gave his substance to the poor. Made bishop of Myra, he suffered imprisonment, by tradition, under Diocletian and was released under Constantine. Beyond his see and his early and vast renown, little is known of him with certainty.

His fame rests on his hidden charity. Hearing that a ruined father of three daughters meant to sell them to shame, Nicholas thrice threw by night a bag of gold through the window, providing their dowries — whence the three golden balls of pawnbrokers, and his patronage of children, to whom his feast still brings secret gifts, the root of the Christmas gift-bearer.

Sailors too claim him, for the legend that he calmed a storm at sea on a voyage to the Holy Land. He died at Myra on 6 December, about 345, and in 1087 sailors of Bari carried his relics to their city, where the basilica of San Nicola was consecrated in 1089; from Bari his devotion spread through the whole West.
saints.knownFor: Secret almsgiving that made him patron of children and sailors.

sources.text: Butler, Lives of the Saints (1866 ed.), 6 December

saints.name: St. Ambrose
saints.title: Bishop and Doctor of the Church
saints.shortBlurb: The governor acclaimed bishop of Milan by the people, who baptized Augustine and taught kings the limits of their power…
biography: Ambrose was born about 340 at Trier, son of the praetorian prefect of Gaul. A lawyer, he became governor of Liguria and Aemilia, resident at Milan. When the Arian bishop Auxentius died in 374, Ambrose, keeping order at the election, heard a child's cry of 'Ambrose, bishop' taken up by all.

Though still a catechumen, he was baptized, and eight days later, on 7 December 374, consecrated bishop — the day the Church still keeps his feast. He gave his goods to the poor, his lands to the Church, and himself to Scripture, the Fathers, and preaching.

He withstood the Arian empress Justina's demand for a basilica, a struggle in which he laid the foundations of Latin hymnody, and at Easter 387 baptized Augustine. When Theodosius massacred seven thousand citizens of Thessalonica in 390, Ambrose required public penance of the emperor before readmitting him to the sacraments.

He died on 4 April 397 and was buried beside the martyrs Gervasius and Protasius. With Augustine, Jerome, and Gregory he is one of the four great Latin Doctors; and because his biographer Paulinus tells of bees alighting on the infant's lips, an omen of honeyed speech, he is patron of beekeepers.
saints.knownFor: Bishop of Milan, teacher of Augustine, Doctor of the Church.

canonization.canonized: Venerated from antiquity; Doctor of the Church

sources.text: Butler, Lives of the Saints (1866 ed.), 7 December

saints.name: The Immaculate Conception of the Blessed Virgin Mary
saints.title: Solemnity of the Blessed Virgin Mary
saints.shortBlurb: The Church honors Mary preserved from the first instant of her conception free from every stain of original sin…
biography: This solemnity honours the Blessed Virgin Mary, conceived in the womb of her mother Anne without any stain of original sin by a singular grace in view of the merits of her Son. It falls on 8 December, nine months before the feast of her Nativity, and ranks as a holy day of obligation.

The feast began in the East as the Conception of St. Anne, kept in Palestinian monasteries by the seventh century. Reaching England before the Norman Conquest, it was for a time suppressed, then spread so widely from Normandy that it was called the feast of the Norman nation.

The schoolmen long debated the privilege: Bernard of Clairvaux and Thomas Aquinas held back, but Duns Scotus made the defense his own — 'God could do it, it was fitting, therefore he did it.' Sixtus IV gave the feast a proper Mass and Office in 1477, and Clement XI in 1708 bound the whole Church to keep it.

Pius IX solemnly defined the dogma in 1854. The bishops of the United States, assembled at Baltimore, had already chosen her under this title as their country's patroness in 1846, and the Holy See confirmed the choice the following year.
saints.knownFor: Mary conceived without sin, the fitting dwelling prepared for the Son of God.

saints.name: St. Juan Diego Cuauhtlatoatzin
saints.title: Layman and Seer of Guadalupe
saints.shortBlurb: The humble Indian convert of Mexico to whom the Virgin of Guadalupe appeared, leaving her image upon his cloak…
biography: Born in 1474 at Cuauhtitlán, north of the Aztec capital, he bore the Nahuatl name Cuauhtlatoatzin, 'the talking eagle,' and lived as a poor farmer and mat-weaver. About 1525 he and his wife María Lucía were baptized by the first Franciscan missionaries, and Juan Diego walked daily to the mission at Tlatelolco for Mass and instruction.

On 9 December 1531, crossing the hill of Tepeyac, he beheld a lady who, speaking in Nahuatl, declared herself the Virgin Mary and asked that a church be built there. When Bishop Juan de Zumárraga sought a sign, on 12 December she bade him gather Castilian roses blooming out of season; unfolding his tilma before the bishop, he revealed her image imprinted upon it.

Juan Diego gave his remaining years to the shrine as its first keeper, dwelling beside it in prayer until his death on 30 May 1548. The image, Our Lady of Guadalupe, drew millions of the native peoples into the Church. Beatified in 1990, he was canonized by Pope John Paul II in Mexico City on 31 July 2002, the first indigenous saint of the Americas.
saints.knownFor: The seer of Our Lady of Guadalupe, whose tilma bears her image.
patronage: the indigenous peoples of the Americas

sources.text: Vatican biography, Canonization of St. Juan Diego (vatican.va)

saints.name: St. Eulalia of Mérida
saints.title: Virgin and Martyr
saints.shortBlurb: A young girl of Roman Spain who defied the persecutors of Diocletian and was put to death for confessing Christ…
biography: Eulalia was born of a noble Christian family of Emerita Augusta, the Roman capital of Lusitania, now Mérida in Spain, and was but twelve years old when the edicts of Diocletian commanded all to sacrifice to the gods. Her mother, dreading her ardor, carried her to a country villa, but the girl slipped away by night and reached the city by morning.

Presenting herself before the governor Dacian, she reproached him for compelling Christians to sacrifice, confessed Christ, and spurned the idols. Neither caresses nor threats moved her; her sides were torn with iron hooks and lighted torches applied to her wounds, and, her hair catching fire, she died in the flames on 10 December 304.

The poet Prudentius, within the same century, sang her passion in his Peristephanon: at her death the bystanders saw her soul fly forth from her mouth as a dove whiter than snow, and snow fell to cover her body. She was buried at Mérida, where a basilica rose over her tomb, and she is venerated as the patroness and glory of that city.
saints.knownFor: One of the most celebrated virgin-martyrs of Roman Spain.

sources.text: The Roman Martyrology (1914 English ed.; public domain)

saints.name: St. Damasus I
saints.title: Pope
saints.shortBlurb: The pope who set Jerome to work on the Latin Bible and adorned the tombs of the martyrs in the Roman catacombs…
biography: Born about 305, said to be of Spanish origin and raised in the clergy of Rome, Damasus served as deacon under Pope Liberius before his own election to the see in 366. A rival faction chose Ursinus, and the ensuing schism was marked by bloodshed in the churches before the civil authority confirmed Damasus in possession.
