His eighteen-year pontificate was a defense of the faith: he withstood the Arians, condemned the teaching of Apollinaris, and at a Roman synod in 382 declared that the primacy of his see rested not on the decrees of men but on the succession of Peter — he was the first pope to style Rome the Apostolic See.

He took Jerome as his secretary and set him to revising the Latin Scriptures on the Greek text, the labor from which the Vulgate grew. Loving the martyrs, he opened and adorned their tombs in the catacombs and composed verse epigrams in their honor, which the calligrapher Furius Dionysius Filocalus engraved on marble. He died on 11 December 384; for his care of the martyrs' graves he is honored as a patron of archaeologists.
saints.knownFor: Commissioning the Vulgate and honoring the martyrs of the catacombs.

sources.text: Butler, Lives of the Saints (1866 ed.), 11 December

saints.name: Our Lady of Guadalupe
saints.title: Patroness of the Americas
saints.shortBlurb: The Mother of God, appearing on the hill of Tepeyac and leaving her image on a poor man's cloak, drew a whole people to Christ…
biography: In December 1531, ten years after the Spanish conquest of Mexico, the Mother of God appeared four times on the hill of Tepeyac to Juan Diego Cuauhtlatoatzin, an Indian convert on his way to Mass, speaking to him in his own Nahuatl tongue and asking that a church be built on that spot in her honor.

The bishop of Mexico, the Franciscan Juan de Zumárraga, asked for a sign. On 12 December the Virgin sent Juan Diego to gather Castilian roses blooming out of season on the stony hill, and when he opened his cactus-fiber cloak before the bishop, out fell the roses, and upon the cloak appeared her image — the tilma venerated ever since as Our Lady of Guadalupe.

The image drew multitudes of the native peoples to baptism, and the shrine at Tepeyac grew into the most visited Marian sanctuary in the world. Pius XII proclaimed her Queen of Mexico and Empress of the Americas in 1945, and John Paul II canonized the seer Juan Diego in 2002, the first indigenous saint of the Americas.
saints.knownFor: Her apparition at Tepeyac and the miraculous image on the tilma.

saints.name: St. Lucy
saints.title: Virgin and Martyr
saints.shortBlurb: A virgin martyr of Syracuse in the persecution of Diocletian, honored as a bringer of light in the dark of winter…
biography: Born about 283 into a wealthy family of Syracuse in Sicily, Lucy had secretly vowed her virginity to God. When her mother Eutychia was healed of a long issue of blood after prayer at the tomb of Agatha at Catania, Lucy won her consent to refuse marriage and to give her dowry to the poor.

Her rejected suitor denounced her as a Christian to the governor Paschasius in the persecution of Diocletian. Sentenced to be dragged away to dishonor, she could not be moved, even by a team of oxen; the fire kindled around her did not burn her; and at length she perished by the sword, about the year 304.

Her very name, from the Latin lux, means light; and her feast, falling in the old calendar near the shortest day, made her the light-bearer of the North, where maidens still wear crowns of candles on her morning. From her name, and from the later legend of her eyes, she is invoked as patroness of the blind and of all with diseases of the eye. Her name stands in the Roman Canon of the Mass.
saints.knownFor: Her virgin martyrdom; patroness of the blind and of light.

sources.text: Butler, Lives of the Saints (1866 ed.), 13 December

saints.name: St. John of the Cross
saints.title: Priest and Doctor of the Church
saints.shortBlurb: A Carmelite reformer and poet of the mystical life, who sang of the dark night of the soul and its union with God…
biography: Juan de Yepes was born in 1542 at Fontiveros, near Ávila, and grew up in poverty after his father's early death. He entered the Carmelites at Medina del Campo in 1563, studied at Salamanca, and was ordained priest in 1567. That same year he met Teresa of Ávila, who won him to her reform; in 1568 he established the first house of Discalced friars at Duruelo, taking the name John of the Cross.

The unreformed friars seized him in 1577 and held him nine months in a narrow cell at Toledo, where he composed the first stanzas of the Spiritual Canticle; escaping in 1578, he continued the reform in Andalusia. His treatises — the Ascent of Mount Carmel, the Dark Night, the Spiritual Canticle, the Living Flame of Love — chart the soul's way through purification to union with God and are classics both of theology and of Spanish verse.

He died at Úbeda on 14 December 1591, was canonized by Benedict XIII in 1726, and was declared a Doctor of the Church by Pius XI in 1926. The poet of the dark night is the patron of mystics, of contemplatives, and of Spanish poets.
saints.knownFor: His mystical poetry and the reform of Carmel.

canonization.canonized: 1726 by Pope Benedict XIII; Doctor of the Church (1926)

sources.text: Catholic Encyclopedia (1913), “St. John of the Cross”
Butler, Lives of the Saints (1866 ed.), 24 November

saints.name: St. Valerian of Abbenza
saints.title: Bishop and Confessor
saints.shortBlurb: An aged African bishop who, rather than surrender the goods of the Church to the Arian Vandals, was cast out to die in the open road…
biography: Valerian was bishop of Abbenza in Roman Africa when Genseric, the Arian king of the Vandals, persecuted the Catholic Church in the fifth century. About the year 457 the king's deputy Proculus was sent through the province to strip the churches, and the bishops who would not surrender their sacred vessels and books were driven from their sees.

Valerian, though more than eighty years old, refused to deliver up the vessels of his church, and was cast out alone beyond the city. By the king's command no man might receive him into house or field, and so the aged bishop lay long in the public road under the open sky, until he ended his days — a confessor, for he bore his passion for the faith without the shedding of blood.

His witness was recorded by the contemporary historian Victor of Vita, who wrote the history of that persecution, and the Roman Martyrology keeps his memory on 15 December: an old man faithful unto death, a confessor of the orthodox truth.
saints.knownFor: An aged confessor of the faith under the Arian Vandal persecution.

sources.text: The Roman Martyrology (1914 English ed.; public domain)

saints.name: St. Adelaide
saints.title: Empress
saints.shortBlurb: A queen imprisoned and delivered, empress of the Romans, who in widowhood gave herself to peace-making and the poor…
biography: Born in 931, the daughter of Rudolph II, king of Burgundy, and Bertha of Swabia, Adelaide was married at sixteen to Lothair, king of Italy, and left a widow within three years. The usurper Berengar II, seeking to force her into marriage with his own son, imprisoned her in 951; escaping, she was delivered by Otto the Great of Germany, who married her at Pavia that same year.

Crowned empress with Otto at Rome in 962, she shared his care for the Church, and after his death in 973 guided the realm as mother of Otto II and, from 991, as regent for her grandson Otto III. A friend of Cluny and its reform, she founded and endowed monasteries — among them Selz in Alsace — and spent her influence on the peace of the realm and the relief of the poor.

Retiring to her monastery of Selz, she died there on 16 December 999 and was canonized by Urban II in 1097. Crowned in a second marriage and once a prisoner for refusing a third, she is fittingly invoked as patroness of brides, of widows, and of second marriages.
saints.knownFor: Holy Roman Empress and benefactress of the Church.

canonization.canonized: Canonized in 1097 by Pope Urban II

sources.text: Butler, Lives of the Saints (1866 ed.), 16 December

saints.name: St. John of Matha
saints.title: Priest
saints.shortBlurb: A Paris theologian who founded an order to ransom Christians held captive by the Moors…
biography: Born at Faucon in Provence in 1160, John was educated at Aix, lived for a time as a hermit, and went up to Paris, where he took the doctorate in theology and was ordained priest. Tradition relates that at his first Mass he beheld an angel clothed in white, bearing a cross of red and blue, with his hands resting upon two captives, a Christian and a Moor.

To discern the vision he joined the hermit Felix of Valois at Cerfroid, and together they founded the Order of the Most Holy Trinity for the redemption of captives — the Trinitarians — which Innocent III approved in 1198. By their rule a third part of all revenues went to ransom Christians enslaved by the Muslims of Africa and Spain, and the friars were bound, if need be, to give themselves in exchange.

John himself journeyed to spread the order in France, Italy, and Spain, and over the centuries the Trinitarians freed many thousands from bondage. He died at Rome on 17 December 1213, and is invoked as the patron of captives and of the order he founded.
saints.knownFor: Founding the Trinitarian Order for the ransom of captives.

sources.text: Butler, Lives of the Saints (1866 ed.), 8 February

saints.name: St. Gatian of Tours
saints.title: First Bishop of Tours
saints.shortBlurb: One of the missionary bishops sent from Rome into Gaul, who planted the faith at Tours amid persecution…
biography: According to Gregory of Tours, Gatian was sent from Rome in the days of Pope Fabian, about the year 250, one of seven bishops dispatched to preach the Gospel in Gaul — Dionysius to Paris, Saturninus to Toulouse, and their companions to other cities. Gatian fixed his episcopal see at Tours, whose people were still given to the worship of idols.

For some fifty years he labored in that city amid the hostility of the pagans, often lying hid to escape the death with which they threatened him, and gathering his little flock in caves and secret places to celebrate the divine mysteries. He died in peace about the year 301, having planted a church where few had believed.

Three generations later his see was made illustrious by Martin, who sought out and venerated his predecessor's tomb. As the first herald of the Gospel in their city, Gatian is honored as patron of Tours, and his memory is kept on 18 December.
saints.knownFor: The apostle and first bishop of Tours.

sources.text: The Roman Martyrology (1914 English ed.; public domain)

saints.name: St. Anastasius I
saints.title: Pope
saints.shortBlurb: A pope praised by Jerome for his holiness, who condemned the errors drawn from the writings of Origen…
biography: A Roman by birth, the son of Maximus, Anastasius succeeded Siricius as bishop of Rome in 399 and reigned little more than two years. Brief as his pontificate was, he was esteemed for his poverty of life and apostolic zeal; Jerome, who knew him, praised the holiness of his rule.

His days fell in the first Origenist controversy. Moved by the pleas of Theophilus of Alexandria, he formally condemned the errors drawn from Origen's writings, and when Rufinus of Aquileia sent him an apology for his translation of Origen, the pope, writing to John of Jerusalem in 401, made no secret of his distrust.

He died on 19 December 401 and was buried in the cemetery of Pontian on the Via Portuensis, where his tomb was found in later ages near that of his successor Innocent I — said by the Liber Pontificalis to have been his son, born before his ordination. His feast is kept on the day of his death.
saints.knownFor: Condemning Origenism and his repute for holiness among the Fathers.

sources.text: The Roman Martyrology (1914 English ed.; public domain)

saints.name: St. Dominic of Silos
saints.title: Abbot
saints.shortBlurb: A Spanish abbot who rebuilt the monastery of Silos and was long invoked by mothers and by captives…
biography: Born about the year 1000 at Cañas in Navarre, Dominic kept his father's flocks as a boy before entering the Benedictine monastery of San Millán de la Cogolla, where he rose to be prior. Refusing King García Sánchez III of Navarre the surrender of the monastery's lands, he was driven into exile with two of his brethren.

Ferdinand I of Castile and León received the exiles, and in 1041 set Dominic over the decayed monastery of Saint Sebastian at Silos, where only six monks remained. Under his rule Silos was renewed in cloister and scriptorium until it stood among the renowned houses of Spain, and the abbot grew famous for his works of healing and for ransoming Christian captives from the Moors.

He died at Silos on 20 December 1073. A century later Joan of Aza prayed at his tomb for a child and bore the son she named Dominic — the future founder of the Friars Preachers. For that grace he is invoked by expectant mothers, and his abbatial staff was long laid by the queens of Spain in their labor; for his own youth and his ransoms he is the patron of shepherds and of captives.
saints.knownFor: Restorer of the abbey of Silos and helper of captives and mothers.

sources.text: Butler, Lives of the Saints (1866 ed.), 20 December

saints.name: St. Peter Canisius
saints.title: Priest and Doctor of the Church
saints.shortBlurb: The Jesuit catechist called the Second Apostle of Germany, whose catechisms held countless souls to the faith…
biography: Born at Nijmegen on 8 May 1521, the son of the city's burgomaster, Peter Kanis studied at Cologne and, won by the direction of Peter Faber, entered the young Society of Jesus in 1543 — the first Dutchman to do so. Ordained priest in 1546, he twice served at the Council of Trent as theologian to Cardinal Otto Truchsess of Augsburg.

Sent into the German lands as the Reformation advanced, he taught at Ingolstadt and Vienna, preached in the cathedral of Saint Stephen, governed his order's Upper German province, and founded colleges from Vienna and Prague to Fribourg, where he settled in 1580. His three catechisms — the great Summa of 1555 with two shorter forms for students and children — passed through some two hundred editions in his lifetime and earned him the name of Second Apostle of Germany.

He died at Fribourg on 21 December 1597; beatified in 1864, he was canonized by Pius XI in 1925 and at the same time declared a Doctor of the Church. The tireless catechist is the patron of Germany and of catechists.
saints.knownFor: His catechisms and the defense of the faith in Germany.

canonization.canonized: 1925 by Pope Pius XI, who declared him a Doctor of the Church

sources.text: Vatican biography, Canonization of St. Peter Canisius (vatican.va)

saints.name: St. Chaeremon and the Martyrs of Egypt
saints.title: Bishop and Martyrs
saints.shortBlurb: An aged Egyptian bishop and the many Christians who perished in the deserts fleeing the persecution of Decius…
biography: When the emperor Decius commanded sacrifice to the gods about the year 250, the persecution fell heavily upon the Church of Egypt. Many Christians were slain outright in the cities and villages, while others fled into the deserts and mountains rather than deny Christ, and there perished — some of hunger and thirst, some by wild beasts, some taken by robbers — and all were reckoned martyrs.

Among them was Chaeremon, the very aged bishop of Nilopolis, a city on the Nile. Fleeing with his wife into the mountain country east of the river, he was seen no more; though the brethren searched diligently, neither the two nor their bodies were ever found, and the Church numbered them with the martyrs.

These things were recorded by Dionysius of Alexandria, himself a fugitive in that persecution, in a letter to Fabius of Antioch from which the historian Eusebius preserved the account. The Roman Martyrology joins Chaeremon with the many martyrs of Egypt on 22 December.
saints.knownFor: The confessors and martyrs of the Decian persecution in Egypt.

sources.text: The Roman Martyrology (1914 English ed.; public domain)

saints.name: St. John of Kanty
saints.title: Priest
saints.shortBlurb: A Polish priest and professor of Kraków, famed for learning matched by humility and boundless charity to the poor…
biography: John was born at Kęty, near Oświęcim in the diocese of Kraków, about 1390, the son of devout country folk, Stanislaus and Anne. Sent to the Academy of Kraków, he took degrees in philosophy and theology, was ordained priest, and became a beloved professor of the university.

He served briefly as parish priest at Olkusz, but, shrinking from the burden of souls, soon returned to Kraków to the chair of Sacred Scripture, which he held until his death. His austerity was proverbial: he slept little and on the floor, ate sparingly, abstained from meat, and gave the poor all he had beyond bare need.

He made four pilgrimages to Rome on foot and one to Jerusalem, desiring, it was said, martyrdom among the Turks. On his manuscripts he wrote a warning against strife and slander: 'Conturbare cave: non est placare suave; infamare cave: nam revocare grave' — avoid contention; avoid slander, which cannot be recalled.

He died at Kraków on Christmas Eve, 1473, and was buried beneath the church of St. Anne, where his tomb grew famed for miracles. Canonized by Pope Clement XIII in 1767, he is venerated as a patron of Poland and of teachers and students.
saints.knownFor: A learned and charitable priest, patron of Poland and of scholars.

sources.text: Butler, Lives of the Saints (1866 ed.), 20 October

saints.name: St. Delphinus
saints.title: Bishop of Bordeaux
saints.shortBlurb: The bishop of Bordeaux who baptized St. Paulinus of Nola and opposed the Priscillian heresy…
biography: Delphinus was bishop of Bordeaux in Aquitaine in the last decades of the fourth century. In 380 he attended the Council of Saragossa, where bishops of Spain and Aquitaine condemned the errors of Priscillian, and in 384 a synod in his own city of Bordeaux deposed the Priscillianist bishop Instantius.

He corresponded with St. Ambrose of Milan, who wrote to him on the affairs of the troubled churches. When Pontius Paulinus, the rich senator of Bordeaux and future St. Paulinus of Nola, sought baptism, it was Delphinus who baptized him, together with his brother, about the year 389.

Paulinus revered him ever after as a father in God, writing to him from Spain and Nola with filial affection, and the presbyter Amandus, his successor, continued the care of the convert. Delphinus died about 403 and is named in the Roman Martyrology on 24 December; he is honoured as patron of Bordeaux, the see he governed through the Priscillianist storms.
saints.knownFor: Baptizing St. Paulinus of Nola and opposing Priscillianism.

sources.text: The Roman Martyrology (1914 English ed.; public domain)

saints.name: St. Anastasia
saints.title: Martyr
saints.shortBlurb: An ancient martyr honored at the dawn Mass of Christmas, whose name is spoken in the Roman Canon…
biography: Anastasia suffered martyrdom at Sirmium in Pannonia, the modern Sremska Mitrovica in Serbia, in the persecution of Diocletian, about the year 304. The later Roman legend that made her a patrician widow and a disciple of St. Chrysogonus is now held to be a pious fiction gathered about her name.

Her relics were carried to Constantinople and solemnly received under the Patriarch Gennadius I (458-471) in the church of the Resurrection, and the East keeps her feast on 22 December. In Rome the ancient titulus Anastasiae, at the foot of the Palatine, bore her name from the fourth century.

That church was the station of the second Mass of Christmas, offered at dawn, and so Anastasia came to be commemorated on 25 December, her memory kept for centuries at the dawn Mass. Her name also stands in the Communicantes of the Roman Canon, last of the holy women there invoked with Felicitas, Perpetua, Agatha, Lucy, Agnes, and Cecilia.
saints.knownFor: The martyr commemorated at the Christmas dawn Mass.

sources.text: The Roman Martyrology (1914 English ed.; public domain)

saints.name: St. Stephen
saints.title: The First Martyr
saints.shortBlurb: The first of the seven deacons and the first martyr of the Church, who saw heaven open as he was stoned…
biography: Stephen — his Greek name means a crown — stands first among the seven deacons chosen to serve the poor of Jerusalem. Full of faith and the Holy Spirit, he worked wonders and disputed with the synagogues of the Libertines, Cyrenians, Alexandrians, Cilicians, and Asians, who could not withstand his wisdom (Acts 6).

Accused by hired witnesses of blasphemy against Moses and the Temple, he stood before the Sanhedrin, his face shining as an angel's. His defence closed in a cry: 'Behold, I see the heavens opened, and the Son of man standing on the right hand of God.'

Cast out of the city, he was stoned, the witnesses laying their garments at the feet of young Saul. Kneeling, he prayed, 'Lord Jesus, receive my spirit,' and, 'Lord, lay not this sin to their charge'; and so fell asleep, about the year 34.

Devout men buried him with great mourning. In 415 his tomb was revealed to the priest Lucian at Caphar Gamala, and the relics were enshrined in the basilica built by the Empress Eudocia. First of the deacons, he is patron of deacons; slain by stones, of stonemasons, and invoked against pains of the head.
saints.knownFor: The Church's first martyr; deacon of Jerusalem.

sources.text: Butler, Lives of the Saints (1866 ed.), 26 December

saints.name: St. John
saints.title: Apostle and Evangelist
saints.shortBlurb: The beloved disciple who leaned on the Lord's breast, stood by the Cross, and wrote the fourth Gospel…
biography: John, son of Zebedee and Salome and brother of James the Greater, was called from his nets on the Lake of Galilee; Jesus named the brothers Boanerges, 'sons of thunder.' With Peter and James he belonged to the inner three, witnesses of the raising of Jairus's daughter, the Transfiguration, and the agony in Gethsemane.

He is 'the disciple whom Jesus loved': he leaned on the Lord's breast at the Last Supper, stood by the Cross and received the Mother of Jesus into his care, and outran Peter to the empty tomb, where he saw and believed.

In later years he governed the churches of Asia from Ephesus. Tertullian relates that under Domitian he emerged unharmed from a cauldron of boiling oil before the Porta Latina at Rome and was banished to Patmos, where he received the Apocalypse.

Tradition ascribes to him the fourth Gospel — written at Ephesus, says St. Irenaeus — three Epistles, and the Apocalypse. He died at Ephesus about 100, under Trajan, the only Apostle not to shed his blood, repeating, 'Little children, love one another.' He is patron of theologians, writers, and friendship.
saints.knownFor: The beloved disciple; author of the fourth Gospel.

sources.text: Butler, Lives of the Saints (1866 ed.), 27 December

saints.name: The Holy Innocents
saints.title: Martyrs
saints.shortBlurb: The children of Bethlehem slain by Herod in his rage against the newborn King, the first to die for Christ…
biography: The Gospel of Matthew records that Herod the Great, deceived by the wise men, sent and slew all the boys of Bethlehem and its borders from two years old and under, fulfilling the prophet Jeremias: 'A voice in Rama was heard... Rachel bewailing her children.' The Holy Family had already fled into Egypt at an angel's warning.

The Greek liturgy numbers the slain at 14,000, the Syrians at 64,000, medieval writers at 144,000; but Bethlehem was small, and modern commentators reckon the victims between six and twenty. Josephus does not record the deed, so slight was it beside Herod's other cruelties.

The Church venerates these children as martyrs — flores martyrum, the first flowers of the Church, in the hymn of Prudentius. St. Augustine says they died not only for Christ but in His stead: martyrs by blood alone, confessing Him not by speaking but by dying.

Their feast first appears, with those of St. Stephen and St. John, in the Leonine Sacramentary about 485; the West keeps it on 28 December, within the Christmas octave, and England called it Childermas. As the first to die for Christ, they are patrons of infants and children.
saints.knownFor: The infant martyrs of Bethlehem, first to die for Christ.

sources.text: The Roman Martyrology (1914 English ed.; public domain)

saints.name: St. Thomas Becket
saints.title: Bishop and Martyr
saints.shortBlurb: The chancellor turned archbishop of Canterbury, who defended the Church's liberty against his king and was murdered at his own altar…
biography: Born in 1118 in Cheapside, London, the son of a Norman merchant, Thomas entered the household of Archbishop Theobald of Canterbury, who made him archdeacon and sent him to study canon law at Bologna and Auxerre. In 1155 Henry II made him chancellor of England.

In 1162 Henry had him made archbishop of Canterbury, expecting a compliant prelate; instead Thomas resigned the chancellorship, embraced austerity, and defended the Church's liberties, above all the immunity of clergy from the king's courts. Condemned at Northampton in 1164, he fled to six years of exile in France.

Reconciled with Henry at Fréteval in July 1170, he returned to Canterbury that December, still refusing to absolve the bishops who had defied him; on 29 December four knights cut him down in his cathedral as the monks sang Vespers. Within days miracles were reported at his tomb, and in 1173 Alexander III declared him a saint.

His shrine at Canterbury drew pilgrims from all Europe for three centuries, until Henry VIII destroyed it in 1538 and struck his name from the service books. Because he gave his life defending the clergy's freedom from the crown, he is honoured as the patron of the secular clergy.
saints.knownFor: Martyred archbishop who defended the liberty of the Church.

canonization.canonized: Canonized in 1173 by Pope Alexander III

sources.text: Butler, Lives of the Saints (1866 ed.), 29 December

saints.name: Pope St. Felix I
saints.title: Pope
saints.shortBlurb: A pope of the third century who governed the Roman Church in a time of peace between persecutions…
biography: Felix succeeded St. Dionysius as bishop of Rome early in 269, under the Emperor Aurelian. In that year the synod of Antioch that deposed Paul of Samosata for heresy addressed its report to Rome, and a letter sent eastward under Felix's name expounded the doctrine of the Trinity against the error.

Only a fragment of that letter survives, interpolated by an Apollinarist hand and read at the Council of Ephesus in 431. The Liber Pontificalis further credits Felix with decreeing that Mass be celebrated over the tombs of the martyrs, though this more likely mirrors the custom of his day than any ordinance of his own.

Later legend made Felix a martyr, confusing him with a Roman namesake buried on the Via Aurelia, but the ancient Depositio episcoporum lists him among the bishops, not the martyrs. He died in 274 and was buried on 30 December in the catacomb of St. Callixtus on the Appian Way, where the calendar of 354 keeps his memory.
saints.knownFor: A third-century pope of the Roman Church under Aurelian.

sources.text: The Roman Martyrology (1914 English ed.; public domain)

saints.name: St. Sylvester I
saints.title: Pope
saints.shortBlurb: The pope of the peace of the Church under Constantine, in whose reign Nicaea met and the great Roman basilicas rose…
biography: Sylvester, a Roman, son of Rufinus, became bishop of Rome in January 314 on the death of Miltiades, and governed the Church for twenty-one years. His pontificate spans the turning of the age: the Edict of Milan had just granted peace, and in his first year Constantine's council at Arles judged the Donatist schism.

In 325 the first ecumenical council assembled at Nicaea to condemn the teaching of Arius. The aged pope did not attend but sent as his legates the priests Vitus and Vincentius, while Hosius of Cordoba presided; the word homoousios was probably settled with him beforehand.

In his years rose Constantine's great Roman basilicas: the Lateran with its baptistery beside the palace where the pope dwelt, St. Peter's on the Vatican, the Sessorian church of the Holy Cross, and churches over the martyrs' graves; the first Roman martyrology, too, was likely drawn up under him.

Later legend made him the healer and baptizer of Constantine and the recipient of his 'Donation,' but these tales are apocryphal. He died on 31 December 335 and was buried in the church he had built over the catacomb of Priscilla on the Via Salaria; his feast closes the civil year.
saints.knownFor: Pope during the age of Constantine and the Council of Nicaea.

sources.text: Butler, Lives of the Saints (1866 ed.), 31 December
